The [places of worship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Places_of_worship "Places of worship") are predominantly [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") churches and temples: [Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Nairobi "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Nairobi") ([Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church")), [Anglican Church of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church_of_Kenya "Anglican Church of Kenya") ([Anglican Communion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion "Anglican Communion")), [Presbyterian Church of East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian_Church_of_East_Africa "Presbyterian Church of East Africa") ([World Communion of Reformed Churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Communion_of_Reformed_Churches "World Communion of Reformed Churches")), [Baptist Convention of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptist_Convention_of_Kenya "Baptist Convention of Kenya") ([Baptist World Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptist_World_Alliance "Baptist World Alliance")), and [Assemblies of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assemblies_of_God "Assemblies of God").[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-157) There are also [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") mosques including [Jamia Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamia_Mosque_(Kenya) "Jamia Mosque (Kenya)").

The majority of schools follow the Kenyan Competence Based Education (CBE). Nairobi Innovation Week (NIW) is an annual that was started in 2015. It is organized by the University of Nairobi and in collaboration with government agencies. It focuses on partnerships, innovations, incubation, and startups. It promotes an entrepreneurial culture. It is an event for local and international innovators to showcase innovations, and to network.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-158)[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-159)

The [University of Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi "University of Nairobi")

Nairobi is home to several Universities and Colleges.

*   The [University of Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi "University of Nairobi") is the largest and oldest university in Kenya. It was established in 1956, as part of the [University of East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_East_Africa "University of East Africa"), but became an independent university in 1970. The university has approximately 84,000 students.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-uonbi.ac.ke-160)
*   [Kenyatta University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyatta_University "Kenyatta University") is situated 16 km (9.9 mi) from Nairobi on the Nairobi road Thika dual carriageway on 450 hectares (1,100 acres) of land. The university was chartered in 1985, offering mainly education-related courses, but has since diversified, offering medicine, environmental studies, engineering, law, business, statistics, agriculture, and economics. It has a student body of about 32,000, the bulk of whom (17,000) are in the main campus. It is one of the fastest-growing public universities.

[Jomo Kenyatta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomo_Kenyatta_International_Airport "Jomo Kenyatta International Airport")

[Jomo Kenyatta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomo_Kenyatta_International_Airport "Jomo Kenyatta International Airport") is the largest airport in Kenya. Domestic travellers made up 40% of overall passengers in 2016, an increase of 32% since 2012. JKIA had more than 7 million passengers pass through it in 2016. In February 2017, JKIA received a Category One Status from the [FAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FAA "FAA"), boosting the airport's status as a Regional Aviation hub.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-162)

[Wilson Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Airport "Wilson Airport") is a general-aviation airport handling smaller aircraft, mostly propeller-driven. In July 2016, construction of a new air traffic control tower commenced at a cost of KES 163 million (approximately US$1.63 million).[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-163)

[Moi Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moi_Air_Base "Moi Air Base") is a military airport. In its earlier years, it was utilised as a landing strip in the pre-[jet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_aircraft "Jet aircraft") airline era. It was mostly used as a British passenger and mail route from [Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton "Southampton") to [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town") in the 1930s and 1940s. This route was served by [flying boats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_boat "Flying boat") between Britain and [Kisumu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kisumu "Kisumu") and then by land-based aircraft on the routes to the south.

[![Image 47](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/A_matatu.jpg/250px-A_matatu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_matatu.jpg)

A matatu

Matatus are the most common form of public transport in Nairobi. [Matatu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matatu "Matatu"), which literally translates to "three cents for a ride" (nowadays much more) are privately owned minibuses.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-164) They generally seat 14 to 33 riders. Matatus operate within Nairobi, its environs and suburbs and from Nairobi to other towns around the country.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-uonbi.ac.ke-160) The matatu's route is imprinted along a yellow stripe on the side of the bus, and matatus plying specific routes have specific route numbers.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-165)

In 2004, a [law was passed, requiring all matatus to include seat belts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seat_belt_legislation "Seat belt legislation"), [speed governors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_governor "Speed governor") and to be painted with a yellow stripe.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-166) At first, this caused a furore amongst Matatu operators, but they were pressured by government and the public to make the changes. Matatus are now limited to 80 km/h (50 mph).

In November 2014 President Uhuru Kenyatta lifted the ban on the yellow stripe and allowed matatus to maintain the colourful graphics in an effort to support the youth in creating employment. Matatus in Nairobi were easily distinguishable by their extravagant paint schemes, as owners would paint their matatu with various colourful decorations, such as their favourite [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") team or [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop") artist. They are notorious for their poor safety records, which are a result of overcrowding and reckless driving.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-167) Due to the intense competition between matatus, many are equipped inside with powerful sound systems and television sets to attract more customers.

[![Image 48](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Nairobi_Public_Transport.jpg/250px-Nairobi_Public_Transport.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nairobi_Public_Transport.jpg)

Public transport in Nairobi

Buses are increasingly becoming common in the city with some even going to the extents of installing complimentary WiFi systems in partnership with the leading mobile service provider. There are four major bus companies operating the city routes and are the traditional Kenya Bus Service (KBS), and newer private operators Citi Hoppa, Compliant MOA and Double M. The Citi Hoppa buses are distinguishable by their green livery, the Double M buses are painted purple, Compliant MOA by their distinctively screaming names and mix of white, blue colours while the KBS buses are painted blue.

Companies such as Easy Coach, Guardian Angel, Transline, Tahmeed, NorthWest, Kisii Classic and Ena coach scheduled buses and luxury coaches to other cities and towns.

A [Bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") will commence operating with 100 high capacity buses along [Thika Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thika_Road "Thika Road") in July 2022 between [Kasarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasarani "Kasarani") and the [Kenyatta National Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyatta_National_Hospital "Kenyatta National Hospital"). After the pilot, Nairobi Metropolitan Area Transport Authority (Namata) will implement another 300 buses as the first phase that will expand the BRT line to run from [Ruiru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruiru "Ruiru") to Kenyatta National Hospital. A second phase will later extend the line to run between Kenol in [Murang'a County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murang'a_County "Murang'a County") to [Ongata Rongai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ongata_Rongai "Ongata Rongai") in [Kajiado County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kajiado_County "Kajiado County").

[![Image 49](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Nairobi_Terminus.jpg/250px-Nairobi_Terminus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nairobi_Terminus.jpg)

[Nairobi Terminus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_Terminus "Nairobi Terminus")

Nairobi was founded as a [railway town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_town "Railway town"), and the main headquarters of [Kenya Railways (KR)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Railways "Kenya Railways") is still situated at [Nairobi railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_railway_station "Nairobi railway station"), which is located near the city centre. The line runs through Nairobi, from [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa") to [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala"). Its main use is freight traffic connecting Nairobi to Mombasa and [Kisumu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kisumu "Kisumu"). A number of morning and evening commuter [trains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_rail_service "Nairobi rail service") connect the centre with the suburbs, but the city has no proper light rail, tramway, or rapid transit lines. A proposal has been passed for the construction of a commuter rail line.

In November 2012, President [Mwai Kibaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwai_Kibaki "Mwai Kibaki") launched the Syokimau Rail Service, marking a major milestone in the history of railway development in Kenya. The opening of the station marked another milestone in efforts to realise various projects envisaged under the Vision 2030 Economic Blueprint. The new station has a train that ferries passengers from [Syokimau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syokimau "Syokimau") to the city centre cutting travel time by half.

The opening of the station marks the completion of the first phase of the Sh24b Nairobi Commuter Rail Network that is geared at easing traffic congestion in Nairobi, blamed for huge economic losses. Other modern stations include Imara Daima Railway Station and Makadara Railway Station.

The new [Mombasa–Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa%E2%80%93Nairobi_Standard_Gauge_Railway "Mombasa–Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway") connects the port city of Mombasa and Nairobi. The new railway line has virtually replaced the old metre-gauge railway. The [Nairobi Terminus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_Terminus "Nairobi Terminus") is located at [Syokimau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syokimau "Syokimau"), some 20 km from the city centre. Passengers travelling from Mombasa are transferred the short distance into the CBD with the metre-gauge trains.

The A104 heading to Nairobi CBD

Two trans-African automobile routes pass through Nairobi: the [Cairo-Cape Town Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo-Cape_Town_Highway "Cairo-Cape Town Highway") and the [Lagos-Mombasa Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos-Mombasa_Highway "Lagos-Mombasa Highway"). Nairobi is served by highways that link Mombasa to Kampala in Uganda and Arusha in Tanzania. These are earmarked to ease the daily motor traffic within and surrounding the metro area. However, driving in Nairobi is chaotic. Most of the roads are tarmacked and there are signs showing directions to certain neighbourhoods.

Nairobi is connected to the [Jomo Kenyatta International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomo_Kenyatta_International_Airport "Jomo Kenyatta International Airport") by the Mombasa Highway, which passes through Industrial Area, South B, South C and Embakasi. [Ongata Rongai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ongata_Rongai "Ongata Rongai"), Langata and Karen are connected to the city centre by Langata Road, which runs to the south. Lavington, Riverside, and Westlands are connected by Waiyaki Way. Kasarani, Eastlands, and Embakasi are connected by [Thika Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thika_Road "Thika Road"), Jogoo Road, and Outer Ring Road.

Highways connect the city with other major towns such as Mombasa, Machakos, Voi, (A109), [Eldoret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldoret "Eldoret"), [Kisumu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kisumu "Kisumu"), [Nakuru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakuru "Nakuru"), [Naivasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naivasha "Naivasha"), and Namanga Border Tanzania (A104).

Nairobi is undergoing major road constructions to update its infrastructure network. The new system of roads, flyovers, and bridges are intended to better cope with high traffic levels. It is also a major component of Kenya's Vision 2030 and Nairobi Metropolis plans. Most roads now are well lit and surfaced with adequate signage.

In 2020, the construction of The [Nairobi Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_Expressway "Nairobi Expressway") began. The Nairobi expressway is a 27 km toll road connecting the Eastern Nairobi neighbourhood of Mulolongo to the uptown neighbourhood of Westlands at James Gichuru junction through Nairobi CBD. The road is directly to the Jomo Kenyatta International Airport enabling travellers to access the airport faster avoiding the heavy traffic on Mombasa Road and Waiyaki Way. The road has an 11.025 km elevated section between Airtel Center and Westlands.

This road, is intended to ease traffic from Jomo Kenyatta International Airport that accesses Nairobi city centre. Also traffic from Central Nairobi is expected to be facilitated, to reduce the number of departing passengers who miss their fights, while stuck in road traffic jams on the city streets.[5] The work involves expansion of the existing road to four-lanes one-way, (8 lanes total), with foot paths, drainage channels, overpass bridges and street lighting. It was opened to the public in May 2022.

### Water supply and sanitation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nairobi&action=edit&section=44 "Edit section: Water supply and sanitation")]

94% of the piped water supply for Nairobi comes from rivers and reservoirs in the [Aberdare Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdare_Range "Aberdare Range") north of the city, of which the reservoir of the [Thika Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thika_Dam "Thika Dam") is the most important one. Water distribution losses – technically called [non-revenue water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-revenue_water "Non-revenue water") – are 40%, and only 40% of those with house connections receive water continuously. Slum residents receive water through [water kiosks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_kiosk "Water kiosk") and end up paying much higher water prices than those fortunate enough to have access to piped water at their residence.

There is a wide variety of housing options in Nairobi. The options range from privately owned housing units/apartments, rented units, leased spaces and even houses on mortgage. Most wealthy Kenyans live in Nairobi, but the majority of Nairobians are of average and low income. Half of the population has been estimated to live in [slums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slum "Slum") which cover just 5% of the city area.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-169) The growth of these slums is a result of urbanisation, poor town planning, lack of good governance and proper leadership in these settlements and lack of empowerment and social capital among other factors.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-170)

[![Image 51](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Nairobi_Kibera_04.JPG/250px-Nairobi_Kibera_04.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nairobi_Kibera_04.JPG)

A view of [Kibera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibera "Kibera"), Nairobi

[Kibera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibera "Kibera") is one of the largest slums in Africa,[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-171) and is situated to the west of Nairobi. (Kibera comes from the Nubian word Kibra, meaning "forest" or "jungle").[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-172) The slums cover two square kilometres[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-173) and are on government land. Kibera has been the setting for several films, the most recent being _[The Constant Gardener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Constant\_Gardener\_(film) "The Constant Gardener (film)")_.

Other notable slums include [Mathare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathare "Mathare") and [Korogocho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korogocho "Korogocho"). Altogether, 66 areas are counted as slums within Nairobi.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-174)

Many Nairobi non-slum-dwellers live in relatively good housing conditions. Large houses can be found in many of the upmarket neighbourhoods, especially to the west of Nairobi. Middle and high income estates include [Gigiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigiri "Gigiri"), [Muthaiga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muthaiga "Muthaiga"), [Langata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langata "Langata") and [Karen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen,_Kenya "Karen, Kenya"). Other middle and high income estates include [Parklands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parklands,_Nairobi "Parklands, Nairobi"), [Westlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westlands,_Nairobi "Westlands, Nairobi"), Hurlingham, Kilimani, Milimani, Spring Valley, Lavington, Rosslyn, Kitisuru, and Nairobi Hill.

To accommodate the growing middle class, many new apartments and housing developments are being built in and around the city. The most notable development is _Greenpark_, at [Athi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athi_River_(town) "Athi River (town)"), [Machakos County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machakos_County "Machakos County")25 km (16 mi) from Nairobi's Central Business District. Over 5,000 houses, villas and apartments are being constructed at this development, including leisure, retail and commercial facilities.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-175) The development is being marketed to families, as are most others within the city. Eastlands also houses most of the city's middle class and includes [South C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_C "South C"), [South B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_B "South B"), [Embakasi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embakasi "Embakasi"), [Buru Buru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buru_Buru "Buru Buru"), Komarock, Donholm, Umoja, Saika, Ruai, Kasarani and various others.

## Crime and law enforcement

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nairobi&action=edit&section=46 "Edit section: Crime and law enforcement")]

Crime levels and safety have very much improved in Nairobi over recent years. Violent crime is rare but petty crime can still be an issue. In general, petty crime in Nairobi mostly involves pickpocketing and theft, and on rare occasions can be confrontational. Although there have been a handful of isolated attacks in Kenya by [Al Shabaab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Shabaab_(militant_group) "Al-Shabaab (militant group)") from neighbouring Somalia, these incidences are rare.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-176)

Nairobi is home to most of Kenya's news and media organisations. The city is also home to the region's largest newspapers: the _[Daily Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Nation "Daily Nation")_ and _[The Standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Standard\_(Kenya) "The Standard (Kenya)")_. These are circulated within Kenya and cover a range of domestic and regional issues. Both newspapers are published in English. People Daily is also the leading free newspaper distributed on the streets of Nairobi. It is published by Mediamax Limited.

[Kenya Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Broadcasting_Corporation "Kenya Broadcasting Corporation"), a state-run television and radio station, is headquartered in the city. [Kenya Television Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Television_Network "Kenya Television Network") is part of the Standard Group and was Kenya's first privately owned TV station. The Nation Media Group runs NTV which is based in Nairobi, The Royal Media Services (RMS). There are also a number of prominent radio stations located in Kenya's capital including Citizen radio, Inooro fm, KISS 100, Capital FM, East FM, Kameme FM, Metro FM, and Family FM, among others.

Several multinational media organisations have their regional headquarters in Nairobi. These include the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"), [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN"), [Agence France-Presse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agence_France-Presse "Agence France-Presse"), [Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters "Reuters"), [Deutsche Welle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Welle "Deutsche Welle"), and the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press "Associated Press"). _[Rise and Fall of Idi Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rise\_and\_Fall\_of\_Idi\_Amin "Rise and Fall of Idi Amin")_, also referred to as, _Amin: The Rise and Fall_, is a 1981 biographical film by Sharad Patel. The movie details the controversial actions and atrocities of the once dictator of [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda"), [Idi Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idi_Amin "Idi Amin"), in the time of his violent rise to power in 1971 until he descends in 1979 as the result of Uganda–[Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania") uprising. The movie depicts some of the roles Nairobi as the political hub of Kenya served in opposing the Ugandan dictator, including the coordination between [Tel Aviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Aviv "Tel Aviv") and Nairobi during [operation Entebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Entebbe "Operation Entebbe").

In 2012, a Kenyan [drama film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_film "Drama film") directed by David "Tosh" Gitonga named _[Nairobi Half Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi\_Half\_Life "Nairobi Half Life")_ came to the big screen. The film was selected as the Kenyan entry for the [Best Foreign Language Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Foreign_Language_Film "Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film") at the [85th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/85th_Academy_Awards "85th Academy Awards"), but did not make the final shortlist, and is the first time Kenya has submitted a film in this category.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-Oscars-180)

Nairobi inspired the nicknaming of the character Ágata Jiménez as ['Nairobi'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_(Money_Heist) "Nairobi (Money Heist)")**;** a fictional character in the [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") series _[Money Heist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money\_Heist "Money Heist")_, portrayed by [Alba Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alba_Flores "Alba Flores"). She serves as the quality manager of the group, in charge of printing money in the [Royal Mint of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Mint_of_Spain "Royal Mint of Spain") in parts 1 and 2, and overseeing the melting of gold in the [Bank of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Spain "Bank of Spain") in parts 3 and 4. She is widely considered to be the show's most popular character.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-Alba-181)

**Nairobi** ( [_ny-ROH-bee_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) (_Jiji kuu la Nairobi_, in [Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_language "Swahili language")), is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") and largest city of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), located in the south-central part of the country. As of 2026, it has a population of 5.6 million and a metropolitan population of 15.95 million,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-Africapolis2025-5) making it the [8th most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Africa_by_population "List of cities in Africa by population") in [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa") and the 4th most populous metropolitan area. The city goes beyond its borders and has expanded into neighbouring counties, making it the 4th largest metropolitan area in Africa.

Nicknamed the "Green City under the Sun", Nairobi is uniquely notable for being the only capital city in the world that hosts a [national park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_National_Park "Nairobi National Park") within its boundaries. Its name originates from the [Maasai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maasai_language "Maasai language") phrase _Enkare Nyirobi_, meaning "place of cool waters".

As the national capital, Nairobi is home to the [Kenyan Parliament Buildings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_Buildings_(Kenya) "Parliament Buildings (Kenya)"), the [State House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_House,_Nairobi "State House, Nairobi") and the [Supreme Court Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Kenya "Supreme Court of Kenya"). It is the major financial and economic hub of [East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa "East Africa"), hosting thousands of Kenyan businesses and international companies and organisations, including the [United Nations Environment Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Environment_Programme "United Nations Environment Programme") (UN Environment) and the [United Nations Office at Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Office_at_Nairobi "United Nations Office at Nairobi") (UNON). The [Nairobi Securities Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi_Securities_Exchange "Nairobi Securities Exchange") (NSE) is one of the largest [stock exchanges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_exchange "Stock exchange") in Africa and the second-oldest exchange on the continent. It is Africa's fourth-largest stock exchange by trading volume, capable of processing 10 million trades a day. Nairobi is considered a [global city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_city "Global city") and was ranked as a "Beta World City" by the [Globalisation and World Cities Research Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network "Globalization and World Cities Research Network") as of 2024.

Nairobi was founded in 1898 by colonial authorities in [British East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_East_Africa "British East Africa"), as a rail depot on the [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#Railroad "Uganda")–[Kenya Railway.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Kenya "Rail transport in Kenya") The authorities favoured it as an ideal resting place due to its [high elevation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montane_ecosystems "Montane ecosystems"), [temperate climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_climate "Temperate climate"), and adequate water supply.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-Greenway2-9) The town quickly grew to replace [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa") as the capital of Kenya in 1907.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-10)

After independence in 1963, Nairobi became the capital of the [Republic of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-11) During Kenya's early period, the city became a centre for the [coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee "Coffee"), [tea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea "Tea") and [sisal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisal "Sisal") industries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-13) Successive post-independence governments have built and turned Nairobi into a modern metropolitan city with a diverse population and a growing economy.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-14)

Nairobi was founded in 1898 by colonial authorities in [British East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_East_Africa "British East Africa"), as a rail depot on the [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#Railroad "Uganda")–[Kenya Railway.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Kenya "Rail transport in Kenya") The authorities favoured it as an ideal resting place due to its [high elevation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montane_ecosystems "Montane ecosystems"), [temperate climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_climate "Temperate climate"), and adequate water supply.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-Greenway2-9) The town quickly grew to replace [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa") as the capital of Kenya in 1907.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-10)

After independence in 1963, Nairobi became the capital of the [Republic of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-11) During Kenya's early period, the city became a centre for the [coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee "Coffee"), [tea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea "Tea") and [sisal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisal "Sisal") industries.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-13) Successive post-independence governments have built and turned Nairobi into a modern metropolitan city with a diverse population and a growing economy.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi#cite_note-14)

**Munich**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-3) ([German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language"): _München_[[ˈmʏnçn̩]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/7/78/Muenchentitle.ogg/Muenchentitle.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Muenchentitle.ogg "File:Muenchentitle.ogg"), [Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_language "Bavarian language"): _Minga_[[ˈmɪŋ(ː)ɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA "Help:IPA")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/6/61/Bar-M%C3%BCnchen.ogg/Bar-M%C3%BCnchen.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bar-M%C3%BCnchen.ogg "File:Bar-München.ogg")) is the capital and most populous city of the German state of [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria"). As of 30 November 2024, its population was 1,604,384,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-stadtbevoelkerung-4) making it the [third most-populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Germany_by_population "List of cities in Germany by population") in Germany after [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"). Munich is the largest city in Germany that is not [a state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_of_Germany "States of Germany") of [its own](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-state "City-state"), and it ranks as the 11th-largest city in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU). The metropolitan area has around 3 million inhabitants, and the broader [Munich Metropolitan Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Metropolitan_Region "Munich Metropolitan Region") is home to about 6.2 million people.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-mmr_official_site-5) It is the [third largest metropolitan region by GDP in the EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_EU_metropolitan_regions_by_GDP#2021_ranking_of_top_four_German_metropolitan_regions "List of EU metropolitan regions by GDP"). Munich is located on the river [Isar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isar "Isar") north of the [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps"). It is the seat of the [Upper Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Bavaria "Upper Bavaria") administrative region. With 4,800 people per km 2, Munich is Germany's most densely populated municipality. It is also the second-largest city in the [Bavarian dialect area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_language "Bavarian language") after [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna").

The first record of Munich dates to 1158. The city has played an important role in Bavarian and German history. During the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation "Reformation"), it remained a Catholic stronghold. Munich became the capital of the [Kingdom of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bavaria "Kingdom of Bavaria") in 1806 and developed as a centre for arts, architecture, culture, and science. The [House of Wittelsbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wittelsbach "House of Wittelsbach") ruled until 1918, when the [German revolution of 1918–1919](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German revolution of 1918–1919") ended their reign and saw the short-lived [Bavarian Soviet Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_Soviet_Republic "Bavarian Soviet Republic"). In the 1920s, Munich became a centre of political movements, including the rise of the [Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party "Nazi Party"). The city was known as the "Capital of the Movement". During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Munich was heavily bombed, but much of its historic architecture has since been restored.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-englund-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-zensus-7) After the war, the city's population and economy grew rapidly. Munich hosted the [1972 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics") and the [1974 FIFA World Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_FIFA_World_Cup_final "1974 FIFA World Cup final").

Munich is a major centre for science, technology, finance, innovation, business, and tourism. It has a high standard of living, ranking first in Germany and third worldwide in the 2018 [Mercer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercer_(consulting_firm) "Mercer (consulting firm)") survey.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-mercer-8) It was named the world's most liveable city by [_Monocle_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monocle_(brand) "Monocle (brand)")'s [Quality of Life Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_quality_of_life_indices "City quality of life indices") 2018.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-forbes-9) Munich is the wealthiest city in the EU by GDP per capita among cities with over one million inhabitants[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-10) and is among the most expensive German cities for real estate and rents.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-biimmobilien-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-hausimmobilien-12) In 2023, 30.1% of residents were foreigners, and 19.4% were German citizens with a [migration background](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_background "Migration background") from abroad.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-migr2023-13) Munich's economy is based on [high tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_tech "High tech"), automobiles, the service sector, information technology, biotechnology, engineering, and electronics. Multinational companies such as [BMW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMW "BMW"), [Siemens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siemens "Siemens"), [Allianz SE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allianz_SE "Allianz SE"), and [Munich Re](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Re "Munich Re") are headquartered there. The city has two research universities and many scientific institutions.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-nature-14) Munich is known for its architecture, cultural venues, sports events, exhibitions, and the annual [Oktoberfest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oktoberfest "Oktoberfest"), the world's largest _[Volksfest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volksfest "Volksfest")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-tourismus-15)

Munich was a tiny 10th-century [monastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monasticism "Monasticism") settlement, which was named _zu den Munchen_ ("to the monks"). The Old High German _Munche_ served as the base for the modern German city name _München_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-16)

The river [Isar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isar "Isar") was a prehistoric [trade route](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_route "Trade route") and in the [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") Munich was among the largest [raft ports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft "Raft") in Europe.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-Bernan_Associates_UNESCO-17) Bronze Age settlements up to four millennia old have been discovered.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-18) Evidence of [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celt "Celt") settlements from the [Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age "Iron Age") have been discovered in areas around [Ramersdorf-Perlach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramersdorf-Perlach "Ramersdorf-Perlach").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-19)

The ancient Roman road Via Julia, which connected [Augsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augsburg "Augsburg") and [Salzburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salzburg "Salzburg"), crossed over the Isar south of Munich, at the towns of [Baierbrunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baierbrunn "Baierbrunn") and [Gauting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauting "Gauting").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-20) A Roman settlement north-east of Munich was excavated in the neighborhood of [Denning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denning_(Munich) "Denning (Munich)").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-21)

Starting in the 6th century, the [Baiuvarii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baiuvarii "Baiuvarii") populated the area around what is now modern Munich, such as in [Johanneskirchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johanneskirchen "Johanneskirchen"), [Feldmoching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feldmoching "Feldmoching"), [Bogenhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogenhausen "Bogenhausen") and [Pasing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasing "Pasing").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-23) The first known Christian church was built ca. 815 in Fröttmanning.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-24)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Nuremberg_Chronicle_f_225v_226r.jpg/330px-Nuremberg_Chronicle_f_225v_226r.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nuremberg_Chronicle_f_225v_226r.jpg)

Munich in a 1493 woodcut from [Hartmann Schedel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartmann_Schedel "Hartmann Schedel")'s _[Nuremberg Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg\_Chronicle "Nuremberg Chronicle")_

The first medieval bridges across the river Isar were located in current city areas of Munich and [Landshut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landshut "Landshut").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-Bernan_Associates_UNESCO-17)[Henry the Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_the_Lion "Henry the Lion"), the Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, founded the town of Munich in his territory to control the [salt trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_trade "Salt trade"), after having burned down the town of Föhring and its bridges over the Isar.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-25) Historians date this event at about 1158.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-freed-26):167

Henry built a new toll bridge, customs house and a coin market closer to his home, somewhat upstream, at a settlement around the area of modern old town Munich. This new toll bridge most likely crossed the Isar where the Museuminsel and the modern Ludwigsbrücke are now located.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-27)

[Otto of Freising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_of_Freising "Otto of Freising") protested to his nephew, [Emperor Frederick Barbarossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Barbarossa "Frederick Barbarossa"). However, on 14 June 1158, in [Augsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augsburg "Augsburg"), the conflict was settled in favor of Duke Henry. The _[Augsburg Arbitration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augsburg\_Arbitration "Augsburg Arbitration")_ mentions the name of the location in dispute as _forum apud Munichen_. Although Bishop Otto had lost his bridge, the arbiters ordered Duke Henry to pay a third of his income to the Bishop in Freising as compensation.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-30)

14 June 1158 is considered the official founding day of the city of Munich. Archaeological excavations at Marienhof Square (near [Marienplatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marienplatz "Marienplatz")) in advance of the expansion of the S-Bahn (subway) in 2012 discovered shards of vessels from the 11th century, which prove again that the settlement of Munich must be older than the Augsburg Arbitration of 1158.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-32) The old [St. Peter's Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter's_Church,_Munich "St. Peter's Church, Munich") near Marienplatz is also believed to predate the founding date of the town.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-33)

In 1175, Munich received city status and fortification. In 1180, after Henry the Lion's fall from grace with Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, including his trial and exile, [Otto I Wittelsbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_I_of_Wittelsbach,_Duke_of_Bavaria "Otto I of Wittelsbach, Duke of Bavaria") became Duke of Bavaria, and Munich was handed to the [Bishop of Freising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Munich_and_Freising "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Munich and Freising"). In 1240, Munich was transferred to [Otto II Wittelsbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_II_Wittelsbach,_Duke_of_Bavaria "Otto II Wittelsbach, Duke of Bavaria") and in 1255, when the [Duchy of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Bavaria "Duchy of Bavaria") was split in two, Munich became the ducal residence of [Upper Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Bavaria "Upper Bavaria").

Duke [Louis IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_IV,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor"), a native of Munich, was elected [German king](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_king "German king") in 1314 and crowned as [Holy Roman Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Emperor "Holy Roman Emperor") in 1328.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-muenchen-stadtgeschichte-34) He strengthened the city's position by granting it the salt monopoly with [staple rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stapelrecht "Stapelrecht"), thus assuring it of additional income.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-35)

The growth of Munich was aided by its location on a gravel plain, where the Isar branched into multiple streams that in turn provided drinking water, defensive advantages, and power for many mills and industries within the city.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-36)

In the 15th century, Munich underwent a revival of [Gothic arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_art "Gothic art"): the Old Town Hall was enlarged, and Munich's largest [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") church – the [Frauenkirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Frauenkirche "Munich Frauenkirche") – now a cathedral, was constructed in only 20 years, starting in 1468.

### Capital of reunited Bavaria

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Munich&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Capital of reunited Bavaria")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/Antiquarium%2C_M%C3%BCnchner_Residenz.jpg/250px-Antiquarium%2C_M%C3%BCnchner_Residenz.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Antiquarium,_M%C3%BCnchner_Residenz.jpg)

The Renaissance _Antiquarium_ of the [Munich Residenz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Residenz "Munich Residenz")

When Bavaria was reunited in 1506 after the [War of the Succession of Landshut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Succession_of_Landshut "War of the Succession of Landshut") against the [Duchy of Bavaria-Landshut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Bavaria-Landshut "Duchy of Bavaria-Landshut"), Munich became its capital.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-muenchen-stadtgeschichte-34) During the 16th century Munich became a centre of the [Counter-Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-Reformation "Counter-Reformation").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-muenchen-stadtgeschichte-34) The [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance") movement beset Munich and the Bavarian branch of the [House of Wittelsbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wittelsbach "House of Wittelsbach") under Duke [Albrecht V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_V,_Duke_of_Bavaria "Albert V, Duke of Bavaria") who bolstered their prestige by conjuring up a lineage that reached back to [classical antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_antiquity "Classical antiquity"). In 1568 Albrecht V built the Antiquarium to house the [Wittelsbach collection of Greek and Roman antiquities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staatliche_Antikensammlungen "Staatliche Antikensammlungen") in the [Munich Residenz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residenz,_Munich "Residenz, Munich").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-37) Albrecht V appointed the composer [Orlando di Lasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_di_Lasso "Orlando di Lasso") as director of the court orchestra and tempted numerous Italian musicians to work at the Munich court, establishing Munich as a hub for late [Renaissance music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_music "Renaissance music").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-38) During the rule of [Duke William V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_V,_Duke_of_Bavaria "William V, Duke of Bavaria") Munich began to be called the "German Rome" and William V began presenting Emperor [Charlemagne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlemagne "Charlemagne") as ancestor of the Wittelsbach dynasty.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-39)

Duke William V further cemented the Wittelsbach rule by commissioning the [Jesuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit "Jesuit")[Michaelskirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Michael's_Church,_Munich "St. Michael's Church, Munich"). He had the sermons of his Jesuit court preacher [Jeremias Drexel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremias_Drexel "Jeremias Drexel") translated from Latin into German and published them to a greater audience.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-40) William V was addressed with the epithet "the Pious" and like his contemporary Wittelsbach dukes promoted himself as "father of the land" (_Landesvater_), encouraged pilgrimages and [Marian devotions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veneration_of_Mary_in_the_Catholic_Church "Veneration of Mary in the Catholic Church").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-41) William V had the [Hofbräuhaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hofbr%C3%A4uhaus "Hofbräuhaus") built in 1589.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-muenchen-stadtgeschichte-34) It would become the prototype for [beer halls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_hall "Beer hall") across Munich.

The [Catholic League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_League_(German) "Catholic League (German)") was founded in Munich in 1609. In 1623, during the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years'_War "Thirty Years' War") (1618–1648), Munich became an electoral residence when Duke [Maximilian I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilian_I,_Elector_of_Bavaria "Maximilian I, Elector of Bavaria") was invested with the [electoral dignity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_dignity "Electoral dignity") of the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"), but in 1632 the city was occupied by King [Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavus_Adolphus_of_Sweden "Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-42) In 1634, Swedish and Spanish troops advanced on Munich. Maximilian I published a plague ordinance to halt an epidemic escalation.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-43) The [bubonic plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubonic_plague "Bubonic plague") nevertheless ravaged Munich and the surrounding countryside in 1634 and 1635.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-44) Troops again converged on Munich in 1647 and precautions were taken, so as to avoid another epidemic.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-45) The city remained physically untouched during the war.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-englund-6)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Marcktzumuenchen.png/250px-Marcktzumuenchen.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marcktzumuenchen.png)

[Marienplatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marienplatz "Marienplatz"), c. 1650

During its time as the capital of the [Electorate of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electorate_of_Bavaria "Electorate of Bavaria"), Munich was an important centre of [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque "Baroque") life, but also had to suffer under [Habsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Habsburg "House of Habsburg") occupations in 1704 after Bavaria's defeat in the [War of the Spanish Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Spanish_Succession "War of the Spanish Succession") and again in 1742 during the [War of the Austrian Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Austrian_Succession "War of the Austrian Succession").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-muenchen-stadtgeschichte-34) When Elector [Maximilian III Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilian_III_Joseph "Maximilian III Joseph") died in 1777, the succession empowered the [Palatinate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_palatine "Count palatine") branch within the House of Wittelsbach.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-46) In 1785, Elector [Karl Theodor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Theodore,_Elector_of_Bavaria "Charles Theodore, Elector of Bavaria") invited Count Rumford ([Benjamin Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Thompson "Benjamin Thompson")) to Munich to implement social reforms, including [workhouses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workhouses "Workhouses") for the poor and army restructuring with improved conditions for soldiers.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-47) In the 1790s, Munich became the largest German city to remove its [fortifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortifications "Fortifications"), starting in 1791 under Karl Theodor and Rumford.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-48) After 1793, citizens built new structures outside the former city walls.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-49)

After making an alliance with Napoleonic France, the city became the capital of the new [Kingdom of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bavaria "Kingdom of Bavaria") in 1806 with Elector [Maximilian IV Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilian_I_Joseph_of_Bavaria "Maximilian I Joseph of Bavaria") becoming its first king. The state parliament (the _[Landtag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landtag "Landtag")_) and the new [archdiocese of Munich and Freising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Munich_and_Freising "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Munich and Freising") were also located in the city.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-50)

The establishment of Bavarian state sovereignty made Munich the centre of a modernising kingdom. In 1802, King Maximilian Joseph [secularised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secularised "Secularised") Bavaria, dissolving [monasteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monasteries "Monasteries") and selling church lands to generate state revenue. He also took control of the right to brew beer, granting a monopoly to Munich's wealthiest brewers in exchange for substantial taxes. In 1807, he abolished restrictions on the number of brewery workers, allowing brewers to meet growing demand.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-51)

In October 1810, a beer festival was held on the meadows outside Munich to celebrate the crown prince's wedding to Princess [Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therese_of_Saxe-Hildburghausen "Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen"). The event, featuring parades in regional dress, later evolved into the annual [Oktoberfest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oktoberfest "Oktoberfest"), now held at [Theresienwiese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theresienwiese "Theresienwiese").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-52)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Propylaeen_Muenchen-1.jpg/250px-Propylaeen_Muenchen-1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Propylaeen_Muenchen-1.jpg)

[Neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") buildings erected under [Ludwig I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_I "Ludwig I"), such as the [Propylaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propylaea_(Munich) "Propylaea (Munich)"), earned Munich the nickname 'Athens on the Isar'.

The first Munich railway station was built in 1839, with a line going to [Augsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augsburg "Augsburg") in the west. By 1849 a newer Munich Central Train Station ([München Hauptbahnhof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%BCnchen_Hauptbahnhof "München Hauptbahnhof")) was completed, with a line going to [Landshut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landshut "Landshut") and [Regensburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regensburg "Regensburg") in the north.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-54) In 1825 [Ludwig I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_I_of_Bavaria "Ludwig I of Bavaria") had ascended to the throne and commissioned leading architects such as [Leo von Klenze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_von_Klenze "Leo von Klenze") to design a series of public museums in [neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") style. Between 1856 and 1861 the court gardener [Carl von Effner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_von_Effner "Carl von Effner") landscaped the banks of the river [Isar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isar "Isar") and established the _Maximilian Gardens_. Leo von Klenze supervised the construction of the [Propylaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propylaea_(Munich) "Propylaea (Munich)") between 1854 and 1862.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-55) In 1857 the construction of the [Maximilianeum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilianeum "Maximilianeum") was begun.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-56) The grand building projects of Ludwig I gave Munich the endearment "Athens on the Isar" (German: _Isar-Athen_) and "Monaco di Bavaria".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-57)

By the time [Ludwig II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_II_of_Bavaria "Ludwig II of Bavaria") became king in 1864, he remained mostly aloof from his capital and focused more on his fanciful castles in the Bavarian countryside. In 1876 Munich hosted the first German Art and Industry Exhibition, which showcased the northern [Neo-Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Renaissance "Neo-Renaissance") fashion that came to be the [German Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire")'s predominant style. Munich based artists put on the German National Applied Arts Exhibition in 1888, showcasing [Baroque Revival architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_Revival_architecture "Baroque Revival architecture") and [Rococo Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rococo_Revival "Rococo Revival") designs.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-58)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/M%C3%BCnchen_Jugendstil_1.jpg/250px-M%C3%BCnchen_Jugendstil_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:M%C3%BCnchen_Jugendstil_1.jpg)

[Jugendstil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jugendstil "Jugendstil") style house at Leopoldstr. 77. At the beginning of the 20th century, Munich was a hub for the Jugendstil movement.

The Prince Regent [Luitpold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luitpold,_Prince_Regent_of_Bavaria "Luitpold, Prince Regent of Bavaria")'s reign from 1886 to 1912 was marked by tremendous artistic and cultural activity in Munich.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-59) At the dawn of the 20th century Munich was an epicenter for the [Jugendstil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jugendstil "Jugendstil") movement, combining a liberal magazine culture with progressive [industrial design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_design "Industrial design") and architecture. The German art movement took its name from the Munich magazine _Die Jugend_ (_The Youth_).[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-60) Prominent Munich Jugendstil artists include [Hans Eduard von Berlepsch-Valendas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Eduard_von_Berlepsch-Valendas "Hans Eduard von Berlepsch-Valendas"), [Otto Eckmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Eckmann "Otto Eckmann"),[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-61)[Margarethe von Brauchitsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margarethe_von_Brauchitsch?action=edit&redlink=1 "Margarethe von Brauchitsch (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margarethe%20von%20Brauchitsch "de:Margarethe von Brauchitsch")], [August Endell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Endell "August Endell"), [Hermann Obrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Obrist "Hermann Obrist"), [Wilhelm von Debschitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_von_Debschitz "Wilhelm von Debschitz"),[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-62) and [Richard Riemerschmid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Riemerschmid "Richard Riemerschmid"). In 1905 two large department stores opened in Munich, the Kaufhaus Oberpollinger and the [Warenhaus Hermann Tietz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Tietz "Hermann Tietz"), both having been designed by the architect [Max Littmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Littmann "Max Littmann").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-63) In 1911 the [expressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expressionist "Expressionist") group [Der Blaue Reiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Blaue_Reiter "Der Blaue Reiter") was established in Munich. Its founding members include [Gabriele Münter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriele_M%C3%BCnter "Gabriele Münter").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-64)

### World War I to World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Munich&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: World War I to World War II")]

Following the outbreak of World War I in 1914, life in Munich became very difficult, as the [Allied blockade of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockade_of_Germany_(1914%E2%80%931919) "Blockade of Germany (1914–1919)") led to food and fuel shortages. During a French air raid in 1916, three bombs fell on Munich.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-65)

In 1916, the 'Bayerische Motoren Werke' ([BMW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMW "BMW")) produced its first [aircraft engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_engine "Aircraft engine") in Munich.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-66) The public limited company BMW AG was founded in 1918, with [Camillo Castiglioni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camillo_Castiglioni "Camillo Castiglioni") owning one third of the share capital. In 1922 BMW relocated its headquarters to a factory in Munich.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-67)

After World War I, the city was at the centre of substantial political unrest. In November 1918, on the eve of the German revolution, [Ludwig III of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_III_of_Bavaria "Ludwig III of Bavaria") and his family fled the city. After the murder of the first republican [premier of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ministers-President_of_Bavaria "List of Ministers-President of Bavaria")[Kurt Eisner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Eisner "Kurt Eisner") in February 1919 by [Anton Graf von Arco auf Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_Graf_von_Arco_auf_Valley "Anton Graf von Arco auf Valley"), the [Bavarian Soviet Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_Soviet_Republic "Bavarian Soviet Republic") was proclaimed.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-68) The November 1918 revolution ended the reign of the Wittelsbach in Bavaria.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-City_Halls_and_Civic_Materialism-69) In _[Mein Kampf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mein\_Kampf "Mein Kampf")_[Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") described his political activism in Munich after November 1918 as the "Beginning of My Political Activity". Hitler called the short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic "the rule of the Jews".[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-70)

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Bundesarchiv_Bild_119-1486%2C_Hitler-Putsch%2C_M%C3%BCnchen%2C_Marienplatz.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_119-1486%2C_Hitler-Putsch%2C_M%C3%BCnchen%2C_Marienplatz.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_Bild_119-1486,_Hitler-Putsch,_M%C3%BCnchen,_Marienplatz.jpg)

Unrest during the 1923 [Beer Hall Putsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_Hall_Putsch "Beer Hall Putsch"), a failed [coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_d'%C3%A9tat "Coup d'état") led by [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler"), [Erich Ludendorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Ludendorff "Erich Ludendorff"), and other _[Kampfbund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampfbund "Kampfbund")_ leaders

In 1923 [Gustav von Kahr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_von_Kahr "Gustav von Kahr") was appointed Bavarian prime minister and immediately planned for the expulsion of all Jews who did not hold German citizenship. Chief of Police [Ernst Pöhner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_P%C3%B6hner "Ernst Pöhner") and [Wilhelm Frick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Frick "Wilhelm Frick") openly indulged in antisemitism, while Bavarian judges praised people on the political right as patriotic for their crimes and handed down mild sentences.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-71) In 1923, Adolf Hitler and his supporters, who were concentrated in Munich, staged the [Beer Hall Putsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer_Hall_Putsch "Beer Hall Putsch"), an attempt to overthrow the [Weimar Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weimar_Republic "Weimar Republic") and seize power. The revolt failed, resulting in Hitler's arrest and the temporary crippling of the [Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party "Nazi Party") (NSDAP).[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-72)
