The unofficial city anthem of Munich, recorded in 1929

Munich was chosen as capital for the [Free State of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_State_of_Bavaria "Free State of Bavaria") and acquired increased responsibility for administering the city itself and the surrounding districts. Offices needed to be built for bureaucracy, so a 12-story office building was erected in the southern part of the historic city centre in the late 1920s.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-City_Halls_and_Civic_Materialism-69)

Munich again became important to the Nazis when they took power in Germany in 1933. The party created its first [concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_concentration_camp "Nazi concentration camp") at [Dachau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dachau_concentration_camp "Dachau concentration camp"), 16 km (10 mi) north-west of the city. Because of its importance to the rise of National Socialism, Munich was referred to as the _Hauptstadt der Bewegung_ ("Capital of the Movement").[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-73)

The NSDAP headquarters and the documentation apparatus for controlling all aspects of life were located in Munich. Nazi organizations, such as the [National Socialist Women's League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Socialist_Women's_League "National Socialist Women's League") and the [Gestapo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestapo "Gestapo"), had their offices along [Brienner Straße](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brienner_Stra%C3%9Fe_(Munich) "Brienner Straße (Munich)") and around the [Königsplatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6nigsplatz,_Munich "Königsplatz, Munich"). The party acquired 68 buildings in the area and many _Führerbauten_ ("_Führer_ buildings") were built to reflect a new aesthetic of power.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-74) Construction work for the [Führerbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%BChrerbau "Führerbau") and the party headquarters (known as the [Brown House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_House,_Munich "Brown House, Munich")) started in September 1933.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-75) The _[Haus der Kunst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haus\_der\_Kunst "Haus der Kunst")_ (House of German Art) was the first building to be commissioned by Hitler. The architect [Paul Troost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Troost "Paul Troost") was asked to start work shortly after the Nazis had seized power because "the most German of all German cities" was left with no exhibition building when in 1931 the [Glass Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaspalast_(Munich) "Glaspalast (Munich)") was destroyed in an arson attack.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-76)

The city was the site where the 1938 [Munich Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Agreement "Munich Agreement") was signed between [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany"), the United Kingdom, [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_French_Republic "Third French Republic") and [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-77) On 8 November 1939, shortly after the Second World War had begun, [Georg Elser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Elser "Georg Elser") planted a bomb in the [Bürgerbräukeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%BCrgerbr%C3%A4ukeller "Bürgerbräukeller") in Munich in an attempt to assassinate Adolf Hitler, who held a political party speech. Hitler, however, had left the building minutes before the bomb went off.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-78)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Wardamage2.jpg/250px-Wardamage2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wardamage2.jpg)

View of Munich city centre in 1945 after the devastation of World War II, and in 1989 after reconstruction, featuring the restored [Old Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Town_Hall,_Munich "Old Town Hall, Munich"), [Talburgtor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talburgtor "Talburgtor"), and [Heilig-Geist-Kirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilig-Geist-Kirche,_Munich "Heilig-Geist-Kirche, Munich")

During the war, Munich was the location of multiple [forced labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labour_under_German_rule_during_World_War_II "Forced labour under German rule during World War II") camps, including two _Polenlager_ camps for Polish youth,[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-80) and 40 subcamps of the [Dachau concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dachau_concentration_camp "Dachau concentration camp"), in which men and women of various nationalities were held.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-81) With up to 17,000 prisoners in 1945, the largest subcamp of Dachau was the [Munich-Allach concentration camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich-Allach_concentration_camp "Munich-Allach concentration camp"). By mid 1942 the majority of Jews living in Munich and the suburbs had been deported.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-82)

Munich was the base of the [White Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Rose "White Rose"), a student [resistance movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resistance_movement "Resistance movement"). The core members were arrested and executed after [Sophie Scholl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophie_Scholl "Sophie Scholl") and her brother [Hans Scholl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Scholl "Hans Scholl") were caught distributing leaflets on the campus of the [Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig-Maximilians-Universit%C3%A4t_M%C3%BCnchen "Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München"), calling upon the youth to rise against Hitler.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-83)

Around 50% of city were heavily damaged by the [bombing of Munich in World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Munich_in_World_War_II "Bombing of Munich in World War II"), with 71 air raids over five years. After the war, large reconstruction projects restored most of the historically relevant buildings in the old town, that had suffered damage. US troops captured Munich on 30 April 1945.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-84)

In the aftermath of World War II, Germany was subject to [US Military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Military "US Military") occupation.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-85) Due to Polish annexation of the [former eastern territories of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Former_eastern_territories_of_Germany "Former eastern territories of Germany") and [expulsion of Germans from all over Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_and_expulsion_of_Germans_(1944%E2%80%931950) "Flight and expulsion of Germans (1944–1950)"), Munich operated over a thousand refugee camps for 151,113 people in October 1946.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-86) After US occupation Munich was completely rebuilt following a meticulous plan, which preserved its pre-war street grid, bar a few exceptions owing to then-modern traffic concepts. In 1957, Munich's population surpassed one million. The city continued to play a highly significant role in the [West German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_German "West German") economy, politics and culture, giving rise to its nickname _Heimliche Hauptstadt_ ("secret capital") in the decades after World War II.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-87)

The [Free State of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_State_of_Bavaria "Free State of Bavaria") used the [arms industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_industry "Arms industry") as kernel for its [high tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_tech "High tech") development policy.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-Making_Competitive_Cities-88) Since 1963, Munich has been hosting the [Munich Security Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Security_Conference "Munich Security Conference"), a conference on international [security policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_policy "Security policy") held annually in the [Hotel Bayerischer Hof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotel_Bayerischer_Hof,_Munich "Hotel Bayerischer Hof, Munich").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-89) Munich also became known on the political level due to the strong influence of Bavarian politician [Franz Josef Strauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Josef_Strauss "Franz Josef Strauss") from the 1960s to the 1980s. The [Munich Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Airport "Munich Airport"), which commenced operations in 1992, was named in his honor.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-90)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/View_of_the_Olympic_Stadium_from_Olympic_Tower%2C_Munich_-_2018.jpg/250px-View_of_the_Olympic_Stadium_from_Olympic_Tower%2C_Munich_-_2018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:View_of_the_Olympic_Stadium_from_Olympic_Tower,_Munich_-_2018.jpg)

[Olympiapark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympiapark "Olympiapark") was the main venue for the [1972 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Olympic_Games "1972 Olympic Games") and also hosted the [1974 FIFA World Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_FIFA_World_Cup_final "1974 FIFA World Cup final").

Munich hosted the [1972 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics"). After winning the bid in 1966 the [Mayor of Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Munich "Mayor of Munich"), [Hans-Jochen Vogel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans-Jochen_Vogel "Hans-Jochen Vogel"), accelerated the construction of the [U-Bahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_U-Bahn "Munich U-Bahn") subway and the [S-Bahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_S-Bahn "Munich S-Bahn") metropolitan commuter railway. In May 1967 the construction work began for a new U-Bahn line connecting the city with the [Olympic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympiapark_(Munich) "Olympiapark (Munich)") (_Olympiapark_). The Olympic Park subway station was built near the [BMW Headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMW_Headquarters "BMW Headquarters") and the line was completed in May 1972, three months before the opening of the 1972 Summer Olympics. Shortly before the opening ceremony, Munich also inaugurated a sizable pedestrian priority zone between [Karlsplatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlsplatz_(Stachus) "Karlsplatz (Stachus)") and [Marienplatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marienplatz "Marienplatz").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-91) In 1970 the Munich city council released funds so that the [gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") facade and [Glockenspiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rathaus-Glockenspiel "Rathaus-Glockenspiel") of the [New City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neues_Rathaus_(Munich) "Neues Rathaus (Munich)") (_Neues Rathaus_) could be restored.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-92) During the 1972 Summer Olympics 11 Israeli athletes were murdered by Palestinian terrorists in the [Munich massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_massacre "Munich massacre"), when gunmen from the Palestinian "[Black September](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_September_(group) "Black September (group)")" group took hostage members of the Israeli Olympic team.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-93) In 1974, the [FIFA World Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_FIFA_World_Cup_final "1974 FIFA World Cup final") was held at the [Olympic Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Stadium,_Munich "Olympic Stadium, Munich").

Munich and its [urban sprawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_sprawl "Urban sprawl") emerged as the leading German high tech region during the 1980s and 1990s. The urban economy of Munich became characterized by a dynamic labour market, low unemployment, a growing [service economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service_economy "Service economy") and high per capita income.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-Making_Competitive_Cities-88)

Munich was one of the host cities for the [2006 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_FIFA_World_Cup "2006 FIFA World Cup") and both the [UEFA Euro 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2020 "UEFA Euro 2020") – postponed by a year because of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") – and [UEFA Euro 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2024 "UEFA Euro 2024").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-94)

Munich lies on the elevated plains of [Upper Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Bavaria "Upper Bavaria") in the Northern [Alpine Foreland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foothills "Foothills"), about 50 km north of the [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps") and at about 520 m [above mean sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_mean_sea_level "Above mean sea level"). The rivers [Isar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isar "Isar") and [Würm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W%C3%BCrm_(Amper) "Würm (Amper)") flow through the city.

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Luftbild_M%C3%BCnchen_Innenstadt.jpg/250px-Luftbild_M%C3%BCnchen_Innenstadt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Luftbild_M%C3%BCnchen_Innenstadt.jpg)

Aerial view of Munich city centre (facing southeast)

The northern part of this sandy plateau includes a highly fertile [flint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flint "Flint") area no longer affected by Alpine tectonic processes, while the southern part is covered with [morainic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moraine "Moraine") hills. Between them are [fluvio-glacial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluvio-glacial "Fluvio-glacial") outwash plains around Munich. Where these deposits become thinner, [groundwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundwater "Groundwater") can rise through the gravel surface, causing marsh formation in northern Munich.

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/M%C3%BCnchen_und_die_Alpen_bei_F%C3%B6hn.jpg/250px-M%C3%BCnchen_und_die_Alpen_bei_F%C3%B6hn.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:M%C3%BCnchen_und_die_Alpen_bei_F%C3%B6hn.jpg)

View of Munich with the [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps") in the background

According to the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"), the climate is [oceanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") (_Cfb_) bordering on [humid continental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") (_Dfb_), with features like warm to hot summers and cold winters, but without permanent snow cover.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-95)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-96) The city centre lies between both climates, while the [airport of Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Airport "Munich Airport") has a [humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate"). The warmest month, on average, is July. The coolest is January.

The proximity to the [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps") brings higher volumes of rainfall and consequently greater susceptibility to [flood problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_flooding "Urban flooding"). Studies of [adaptation to climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_adaptation "Climate change adaptation") and extreme events are carried out; one of them is the Isar Plan of the [EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") Adaptation Climate.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-97)

Showers and thunderstorms bring the highest average monthly precipitation in late spring and throughout the summer. The most precipitation occurs in July, on average. Winter tends to have less precipitation, the least in February.

The higher elevation and proximity to the Alps cause the city to have more rain and snow than many other parts of Germany. The Alps affect the city's climate in other ways too; for example, the warm downhill wind from the Alps ([föhn wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%B6hn_wind "Föhn wind")), which can raise temperatures sharply within a few hours even in the winter.

Being at the centre of Europe, Munich is subject to many climatic influences, so that weather conditions there are more variable than in other European cities, especially those further west and south of the Alps.

Munich is near the Alps. Annual variation in temperature can be significant, because there are no large bodies of water nearby. The winter in Munich is generally cold and overcast, and some Munich winters have significant snow. January is the coldest month. While winter averages remain only moderately cold, and relatively mild for an elevated inland location of Munich's latitude, [inversion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inversion_(meteorology) "Inversion (meteorology)") from the nearby Alps causes cold air to sink and result in temperatures below −15°C (5°F). In Munich the summer is usually pleasantly warm, with daytime temperatures averaging 25°C (77°F).

Munich is subject to active [convective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convective "Convective") seasons and sometimes damaging events. The Alpine [thunderstorm system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderstorm "Thunderstorm") moves along the mountain range, or detaches, heading east-north-east over the foothills of the Alps.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-98)

At Munich's official [weather stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_station "Weather station"), the highest and lowest temperatures ever measured are 37.6°C (100°F), on 27 June 2026 in Munich City, and −31.6°C (−24.9°F), on 12 February 1929 in the Botanic Garden of the city.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-99)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-100)

In Munich, the general trend of [global warming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming "Global warming") with a rise of medium yearly temperatures of about 1°C (1.8°F) in Germany between 1900 and 2020 can be observed as well. In November 2016 the city council concluded officially that a further rise in medium temperature, a higher number of heat extremes, a rise in the number of hot days and nights with temperatures higher than 20°C ([tropical nights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_night "Tropical night")), a change in [precipitation patterns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precipitation "Precipitation"), as well as a rise in the number of local instances of heavy rain, is to be expected as part of the ongoing climate change. The city administration decided to support a joint study from its own Referat für Gesundheit und Umwelt (department for health and environmental issues) and the [German Meteorological Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutscher_Wetterdienst "Deutscher Wetterdienst") that will gather data on local weather. The data is supposed to be used to create a plan for action for adapting the city to better deal with climate change as well as an integrated action program for climate protection in Munich. With the help of those programs issues regarding [spatial planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spatial_planning "Spatial planning") and settlement density, the development of buildings and green spaces as well as plans for functioning [ventilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ventilation_(architecture) "Ventilation (architecture)") in a cityscape can be monitored and managed.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-105)

From only 24,000 inhabitants in 1700, the city population doubled about every 30 years. It was 100,000 in 1852, 250,000 in 1883 and 500,000 in 1901. Since then, Munich has become Germany's third-largest city. In 1933, 840,901 inhabitants were counted, and in 1957 over 1 million. Munich has reached 1.5 million in 2022.

In December 2023, Munich had 1.58 million inhabitants; 477,855 foreign nationals resided in the city as of 31 December 2023 with 42.88% of these residents being citizens of EU member states, and 29.66% citizens in European states not in the EU (including Kosovo and Turkey).[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-106) Along with the Turks, the Croats are one of the two largest foreign minorities in the city, which is why some Croats refer to Munich as their "second capital".[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-107) The largest groups of foreign nationals were [Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_people "Turkish people") (38,947), [Croats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croats "Croats") (37,541), [Italians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italians "Italians") (28,142), [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks "Greeks") (24,843), [Bosnians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnians "Bosnians") (24,161), [Ukrainians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainians "Ukrainians") (21,899), and [Austrians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrians "Austrians") (21,944).

About 45% of Munich's residents are not affiliated with any religious group; this ratio represents the fastest growing segment of the population. As in the rest of Germany, the Catholic and Protestant churches have experienced a continuous decline in membership. As of 31 December 2017, 31.8% of the city's inhabitants were Catholic, 11.4% Protestant, 0.3% Jewish (see: [History of the Jews in Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Munich "History of the Jews in Munich")),[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-108) and 3.6% were members of an Orthodox Church ([Eastern Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church") or [Oriental Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriental_Orthodoxy "Oriental Orthodoxy")).[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-109) About 1% adhere to other Christian denominations. There is also a small [Old Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Catholic "Old Catholic") parish and an English-speaking parish of the [Episcopal Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)") in the city. According to Munich Statistical Office, in 2013 about 6.9% of Munich's population was Muslim.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-110) Munich has the largest [Uyghur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") population with about 800 (whole Germany about 1,600) people with Uyghur diaspora. Many of them fled to Munich due to the Chinese government and are exiled in Munich. Munich is also home to [World Uyghur Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Uyghur_Congress "World Uyghur Congress"), which is an [international organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_organisation "International organisation") of exiled Uyghurs.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-111)

## Government and politics

The [Bavarian State Chancellery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_State_Chancellery "Bavarian State Chancellery") serves as the executive office of the [Minister-President of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister-President_of_Bavaria "Minister-President of Bavaria").

As the capital of Bavaria, Munich is an important political centre for both the state and country as a whole. It is the seat of the [Landtag of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landtag_of_Bavaria "Landtag of Bavaria"), the [State Chancellery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayerische_Staatskanzlei "Bayerische Staatskanzlei"), and all state departments. Several national and international authorities are located in Munich, including the [Federal Finance Court of Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Finance_Court_of_Germany "Federal Finance Court of Germany"), the [German Patent Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Patent_Office "German Patent Office") and the [European Patent Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Patent_Office "European Patent Office"). Bavaria has been dominated by the [Christian Social Union in Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Social_Union_in_Bavaria "Christian Social Union in Bavaria") (CSU) on a federal, state, and local level since the establishment of the Federal Republic in 1949.

The current mayor of Munich is [Dominik Krause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause "Dominik Krause") of [the Greens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_90/The_Greens "Alliance 90/The Greens").

The governing coalition after the 2020 election consisted of the Greens and the SPD, as well as the allied Volt and Pink List, which had one seat each. While the Greens had gained the most seats in the city council, the mayor was from the SPD. The parties made an agreement including social and ecological goals and focusing on heightening stipulations for new development in the city. The Red-Green alliance is a reprise of the 1990–2014 coalition, which was interrupted by a six-year CSU-SPD majority from 2014 to 2020.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-p829-114)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-x533-115)

The [Frauenkirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frauenkirche,_Munich "Frauenkirche, Munich"), consecrated in 1494, is a landmark and symbol of Munich.

[![Image 52](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/GraphyArchy_-_Wikipedia_00383.jpg/250px-GraphyArchy_-_Wikipedia_00383.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GraphyArchy_-_Wikipedia_00383.jpg)

[Old Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Town_Hall,_Munich "Old Town Hall, Munich") and [Heiliggeistkirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilig-Geist-Kirche,_Munich "Heilig-Geist-Kirche, Munich") seen from [Viktualienmarkt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktualienmarkt "Viktualienmarkt")

At the centre of the old town is the [Marienplatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marienplatz "Marienplatz") with the [Old Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Town_Hall,_Munich "Old Town Hall, Munich") and the [New Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Town_Hall,_Munich "New Town Hall, Munich"). Its tower contains the [Rathaus-Glockenspiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rathaus-Glockenspiel "Rathaus-Glockenspiel"). The [Peterskirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter's_Church,_Munich "St. Peter's Church, Munich") is the oldest church of the inner city. Nearby St. Peter, the Gothic hall-church [Heiliggeistkirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heiliggeistkirche_(Munich) "Heiliggeistkirche (Munich)") was converted to baroque style from 1724 onwards and looks down upon the [Viktualienmarkt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktualienmarkt "Viktualienmarkt"). Three gates of the demolished medieval fortification survive; these are the [Isartor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isartor "Isartor"), the [Sendlinger Tor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendlinger_Tor "Sendlinger Tor"), and the [Karlstor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlstor "Karlstor"). The Karlstor leads up to the [Stachus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlsplatz_(Stachus) "Karlsplatz (Stachus)"), a square dominated by the [Justizpalast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justizpalast_(Munich) "Justizpalast (Munich)") (Palace of Justice).

The [Frauenkirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Frauenkirche "Munich Frauenkirche") serves as the cathedral for the [Catholic Archdiocese of Munich and Freising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Munich_and_Freising "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Munich and Freising"). The nearby [Michaelskirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Michael's_Church,_Munich "St. Michael's Church, Munich") is the largest [renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance "Renaissance") church north of the Alps, while the [Theatinerkirche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatine_Church,_Munich "Theatine Church, Munich") is a [basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica "Basilica") in Italianate high baroque, which had a major influence on southern German [baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque "Baroque") architecture. Its dome dominates the [Odeonsplatz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odeonsplatz "Odeonsplatz").

### Palaces and castles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Munich&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Palaces and castles")]

Schloss Nymphenburg ([Nymphenburg Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nymphenburg_Palace "Nymphenburg Palace"), construction started 1664) is a museum open to the public for tours.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-Zen_2020_i476-117)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-Lonely_Planet_2010_b951-118)

The smaller Schloss Fürstenried ([Fürstenried Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%BCrstenried_Palace "Fürstenried Palace"), construction 1715–1717) is used by the [Archdiocese of Munich and Freising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archdiocese_of_Munich_and_Freising "Archdiocese of Munich and Freising") as a conference location.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-muenchen.de_2022_v258-119)

Schloss Blutenburg ([Blutenburg Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blutenburg_Castle "Blutenburg Castle")) opened as a children's library in 2024,[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-Hordych_2024_l233-120) but visitors may tour the late-Gothic Blutenburg Castle Church built on the same grounds.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-muenchen.de_2022_i705-121)

The large [Munich Residenz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Residenz "Munich Residenz") complex on the edge of Munich's Old Town now ranks among Europe's most significant museums of interior decoration. Within the Residenz is the splendid [Cuvilliés Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuvilli%C3%A9s_Theatre "Cuvilliés Theatre") and next door is the [National Theatre Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Theatre_Munich "National Theatre Munich"). Among the mansions that still exist in Munich are the [Palais Porcia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Porcia "Palais Porcia"), the [Palais Preysing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Preysing "Palais Preysing"), the [Palais Holnstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Holnstein "Palais Holnstein") and the [Prinz-Carl-Palais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prinz-Carl-Palais "Prinz-Carl-Palais"). All mansions are situated close to the Residenz, so is the [Alter Hof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alter_Hof "Alter Hof"), the first residence of the [House of Wittelsbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wittelsbach "House of Wittelsbach").

### Modernist architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Munich&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Modernist architecture")]

Despite Munich being the breeding ground for German [Jugendstil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jugendstil "Jugendstil"), starting with the architect [Martin Dülfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_D%C3%BClfer "Martin Dülfer"), Munich Jugendstil style was quickly submerged as historic trash. While the modernist architect [Theodor Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodor_Fischer "Theodor Fischer") was based in Munich, his influence on Munich underwhelmed. Prior to 1914 the city of Munich was under-industrialized. During the [Weimar Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weimar_Republic "Weimar Republic"), the Munich establishment was hostile to [modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernism "Modernism"). The TUM professor [German Bestelmeyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Bestelmeyer "German Bestelmeyer") favored a conservative style, and [Jacobus Oud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobus_Oud "Jacobus Oud") was rejected for the post of city building chief. Modernist exceptions include a series of post offices by [Robert Vorhoelzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Vorhoelzer "Robert Vorhoelzer") built in the late 1920s and early 1930s. Examples of [avant-garde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde "Avant-garde") temporary constructions include the _Wohnmaschine_ (_Housing Machine_) by [Robert Vorhoelzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Vorhoelzer "Robert Vorhoelzer"), as well as the _Flachdachhaus_ (_Flat Roof House_) by [Fritz Norkauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Norkauer?action=edit&redlink=1 "Fritz Norkauer (page does not exist)"). [Paul Schultze-Naumburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Schultze-Naumburg "Paul Schultze-Naumburg"), and the [Kampfbund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampfbund "Kampfbund") enjoyed particular popularity.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-122)

### High rise buildings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Munich&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: High rise buildings")]

Several high-rise buildings are clustered at the northern edge of Munich in the skyline, like the [HVB Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypo-Haus "Hypo-Haus"), the [Arabella High-Rise Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabella_High-Rise_Building "Arabella High-Rise Building"), the [Highlight Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highlight_Towers "Highlight Towers"), [Uptown Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uptown_Munich "Uptown Munich"), Münchner Tor and the [BMW Headquarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMW_Headquarters "BMW Headquarters") next to the [Olympic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympiapark_(Munich) "Olympiapark (Munich)"). Further high-rise buildings are located in the [Werksviertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werksviertel?action=edit&redlink=1 "Werksviertel (page does not exist)")[[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werksviertel "de:Werksviertel")] in [Berg am Laim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berg_am_Laim "Berg am Laim").

### Long-term residential development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Munich&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Long-term residential development")]

Munich is subject to a long-term residential development plan that is established by the city administration of Munich. The LaSie ("Langfristige Siedlungsentwicklung") was passed in 2011 in response to the acute housing crisis. LaSie is aligned with the strategic development plan passed for Munich in 1998 ("Perspektive München"). LaSie defines three priorities for the construction of residential housing in Munich. Existing [housing estates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_estate "Housing estate"), post-war low-density developments, and the suburban area are subject to [densification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Densification "Densification") ("Nachverdichtung"). Non-residential industrial areas are subject to conservation and will be turned into residential and mixed-use areas. On greenfield sites in the Munich periphery medium and large-scale housing estates are to be built so as to extend Munich's urban center.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-123)

_[Englischer Garten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Englischer\_Garten "Englischer Garten")_ with Munich skyline

[Friedrich Ludwig von Sckell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Ludwig_von_Sckell "Friedrich Ludwig von Sckell") became famous for designing the [Englischer Garten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Englischer_Garten "Englischer Garten") between 1789 and 1807. Besides planning the first public garden in Europe, Sckell also redesigned Baroque gardens as landscape gardens, including the parks of [Nymphenburg Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nymphenburg_Palace "Nymphenburg Palace") and the [Botanischer Garten München-Nymphenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botanischer_Garten_M%C3%BCnchen-Nymphenburg "Botanischer Garten München-Nymphenburg").[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-124)

Other large green spaces are the [Olympiapark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympiapark,_Munich "Olympiapark, Munich"), the [Westpark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westpark_(Munich) "Westpark (Munich)") and the [Ostpark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostpark_(Munich) "Ostpark (Munich)"). The city's oldest park is the [Hofgarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hofgarten_(Munich) "Hofgarten (Munich)"), near the Residenz, dating back to the 16th century. The site of the largest beer garden in town, the former royal Hirschgarten, was founded in 1780.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-125)

German is spoken and understood in and around Munich. While the German language has many dialects, so-called "[Standard German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_German "Standard German")" or "High German" is learned in schools and spoken among Germans, Austrians and in some parts of Switzerland. A speaker of a [Low German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_German "Low German") dialect in Hamburg may find it difficult to understand the dialect of a Bavarian mountaineer.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-126) The [Bavarian dialects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_language "Bavarian language") are recognized as regional languages and continue to be spoken alongside Standard German.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-127)
