### Munich Central Train Station

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Munich&action=edit&section=81 "Edit section: Munich Central Train Station")]

[![Image 77](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/%C3%96BB_Nightjet_train_departing_M%C3%BCnchen_Hbf.jpg/250px-%C3%96BB_Nightjet_train_departing_M%C3%BCnchen_Hbf.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%C3%96BB_Nightjet_train_departing_M%C3%BCnchen_Hbf.jpg)

Austrian [Nightjet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightjet "Nightjet") train in München Hauptbahnhof

Munich Central Train Station (_München Hauptbahnhof_) is the central railway station located in the city centre and is the long-distance station in Munich.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-221)

Munich Central Train Station serves about 450,000 passengers a day, which puts it on par with other large stations in Germany. Munich Central Train Station alongside [München Ost railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%BCnchen_Ost_railway_station "München Ost railway station") are two of the 21 stations in Germany classified by [Deutsche Bahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Bahn "Deutsche Bahn") as a [category 1 station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_railway_station_categories "German railway station categories").

The central mainline station is a [terminal station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_station "Terminal station") with 32 [platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_platform "Railway platform"). The subterranean [S-Bahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_S-Bahn "Munich S-Bahn") with 2 platforms and [U-Bahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_U-Bahn "Munich U-Bahn") stations with 6 platforms are through stations.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[Intercity-Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercity-Express "Intercity-Express") (ICE) and [EuroCity-Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EuroCity-Express "EuroCity-Express") (ECE; Munich–[Bregenz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bregenz "Bregenz")–[Zurich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zurich "Zurich")) trains – and starting in 2026 also [TGV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TGV "TGV") trains (Munich–Paris)[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-222) – stop at Munich Central Train Station. [InterCity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/InterCity "InterCity") (IC) and [EuroCity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EuroCity "EuroCity") (EC) trains to destinations east of Munich also stop at the München Ost railway station. Munich is connected to [Nuremberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg "Nuremberg") via [Ingolstadt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingolstadt "Ingolstadt") by the [Nuremberg–Munich high-speed railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg%E2%80%93Munich_high-speed_railway "Nuremberg–Munich high-speed railway") and [Berlin–Munich high-speed railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin%E2%80%93Munich_high-speed_railway "Berlin–Munich high-speed railway").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The old air raid shelter next to platform 11 of Munich Central Train Station was an important distribution point for [guest workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guest_worker "Guest worker") (_Gastarbeiter_) between 1960 and 1973. At peak more than 1,000 guest workers arrived per day, in total 1.8 million guest workers passed through Munich Central Train Station.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-223)

Munich [motorway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobahn "Autobahn") network

Munich is an integral part of the [Autobahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobahn "Autobahn") network of southern Germany. Motorways from [Stuttgart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuttgart "Stuttgart") (W), [Nuremberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg "Nuremberg"), [Frankfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfurt_am_Main "Frankfurt am Main") and Berlin (N), [Deggendorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deggendorf "Deggendorf") and [Passau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passau "Passau") (E), [Salzburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salzburg "Salzburg") and [Innsbruck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innsbruck "Innsbruck") (SE), [Garmisch Partenkirchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garmisch-Partenkirchen "Garmisch-Partenkirchen") (S) and [Lindau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindau "Lindau") (SW) terminate at Munich, allowing direct access to the different parts of Germany, Austria and Italy.

Traffic is often very heavy in and around Munich. [Traffic congestion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_congestion "Traffic congestion") are commonplace at the beginning and end of major Bavarian holidays. There are few "green waves" or [roundabouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundabout "Roundabout"), and an abundance of construction sites.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Munich has introduced an [environmental zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_and_Environmental_Zone "Traffic and Environmental Zone") and was among the first German cities to require a [green sticker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_sticker "Green sticker") for vehicles, these are a requirement when entering the city or driving in the wider surrounding area.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-224)

#### Munich International Airport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Munich&action=edit&section=84 "Edit section: Munich International Airport")]

[![Image 79](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Flughafen_turm.png/250px-Flughafen_turm.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flughafen_turm.png)

[Munich International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Airport "Munich Airport") (MUC)

[Franz Josef Strauss International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Airport "Munich Airport") ([IATA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Air_Transport_Association "International Air Transport Association"): MUC, [ICAO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Civil_Aviation_Organization "International Civil Aviation Organization"): EDDM) is the second-largest airport in Germany and seventh-largest in Europe after [London Heathrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Heathrow_Airport "London Heathrow Airport"), [Paris Charles de Gaulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle_Airport "Charles de Gaulle Airport"), [Frankfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfurt_International_Airport "Frankfurt International Airport"), [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Airport_Schiphol "Amsterdam Airport Schiphol"), [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barajas_Airport "Barajas Airport") and [Istanbul Atatürk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atat%C3%BCrk_International_Airport "Atatürk International Airport"). It is used by about 46 million passengers a year, and lies some 30 km (19 mi) north east of the city centre. It replaced the smaller [Munich-Riem Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich-Riem_Airport "Munich-Riem Airport") in 1992. The airport can be reached by suburban train lines from the city. From the [main railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%BCnchen_Hauptbahnhof "München Hauptbahnhof") the journey takes 40–45 minutes. A [magnetic levitation train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maglev_(transport) "Maglev (transport)") (called [Transrapid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transrapid "Transrapid")), which was to have run at speeds of up to 400 km/h (249 mph) from the central station to the airport in a travel time of 10 minutes, had been approved,[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-225) but was cancelled in March 2008 because of cost escalation and after heavy protests.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-226)[Lufthansa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lufthansa "Lufthansa") opened its second hub at the airport when Terminal 2 was opened in 2003.

In 2008, the Bavarian state government granted a licence to expand Oberpfaffenhofen Air Station located west of Munich, for commercial use. These plans were opposed by many residents in the Oberpfaffenhofen area as well as other branches of local government, including the city of Munich, which took the case to court.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-227) However, in October 2009, the permit allowing up to 9725 business flights per year to depart from or land at Oberpfaffenhofen was confirmed by a regional judge.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-228)

Despite being 110 km (68 mi) from Munich, [Memmingen Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memmingen_Airport "Memmingen Airport") has been advertised as Airport Munich West. After 2005, passenger traffic of nearby [Augsburg Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augsburg_Airport "Augsburg Airport") was relocated to Munich Airport, leaving the Augsburg region of Bavaria without an air passenger airport within close reach.

**Munich**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-3) ([German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language"): _München_[[ˈmʏnçn̩]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/7/78/Muenchentitle.ogg/Muenchentitle.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Muenchentitle.ogg "File:Muenchentitle.ogg"), [Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_language "Bavarian language"): _Minga_[[ˈmɪŋ(ː)ɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA "Help:IPA")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/6/61/Bar-M%C3%BCnchen.ogg/Bar-M%C3%BCnchen.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bar-M%C3%BCnchen.ogg "File:Bar-München.ogg")) is the capital and most populous city of the German state of [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria"). As of 30 November 2024, its population was 1,604,384,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-stadtbevoelkerung-4) making it the [third most-populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Germany_by_population "List of cities in Germany by population") in Germany after [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"). Munich is the largest city in Germany that is not [a state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_of_Germany "States of Germany") of [its own](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-state "City-state"), and it ranks as the 11th-largest city in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU). The metropolitan area has around 3 million inhabitants, and the broader [Munich Metropolitan Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Metropolitan_Region "Munich Metropolitan Region") is home to about 6.2 million people.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-mmr_official_site-5) It is the [third largest metropolitan region by GDP in the EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_EU_metropolitan_regions_by_GDP#2021_ranking_of_top_four_German_metropolitan_regions "List of EU metropolitan regions by GDP"). Munich is located on the river [Isar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isar "Isar") north of the [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps"). It is the seat of the [Upper Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Bavaria "Upper Bavaria") administrative region. With 4,800 people per km 2, Munich is Germany's most densely populated municipality. It is also the second-largest city in the [Bavarian dialect area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_language "Bavarian language") after [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna").

The first record of Munich dates to 1158. The city has played an important role in Bavarian and German history. During the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation "Reformation"), it remained a Catholic stronghold. Munich became the capital of the [Kingdom of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bavaria "Kingdom of Bavaria") in 1806 and developed as a centre for arts, architecture, culture, and science. The [House of Wittelsbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wittelsbach "House of Wittelsbach") ruled until 1918, when the [German revolution of 1918–1919](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German revolution of 1918–1919") ended their reign and saw the short-lived [Bavarian Soviet Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_Soviet_Republic "Bavarian Soviet Republic"). In the 1920s, Munich became a centre of political movements, including the rise of the [Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party "Nazi Party"). The city was known as the "Capital of the Movement". During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Munich was heavily bombed, but much of its historic architecture has since been restored.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-englund-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-zensus-7) After the war, the city's population and economy grew rapidly. **Munich**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-3) ([German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language"): _München_[[ˈmʏnçn̩]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/7/78/Muenchentitle.ogg/Muenchentitle.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Muenchentitle.ogg "File:Muenchentitle.ogg"), [Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_language "Bavarian language"): _Minga_[[ˈmɪŋ(ː)ɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA "Help:IPA")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/6/61/Bar-M%C3%BCnchen.ogg/Bar-M%C3%BCnchen.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bar-M%C3%BCnchen.ogg "File:Bar-München.ogg")) is the capital and most populous city of the German state of [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria"). As of 30 November 2024, its population was 1,604,384,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-stadtbevoelkerung-4) making it the [third most-populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Germany_by_population "List of cities in Germany by population") in Germany after [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"). Munich is the largest city in Germany that is not [a state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_of_Germany "States of Germany") of [its own](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-state "City-state"), and it ranks as the 11th-largest city in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU). The metropolitan area has around 3 million inhabitants, and the broader [Munich Metropolitan Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Metropolitan_Region "Munich Metropolitan Region") is home to about 6.2 million people.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-mmr_official_site-5) It is the [third largest metropolitan region by GDP in the EU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_EU_metropolitan_regions_by_GDP#2021_ranking_of_top_four_German_metropolitan_regions "List of EU metropolitan regions by GDP"). Munich is located on the river [Isar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isar "Isar") north of the [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps"). It is the seat of the [Upper Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Bavaria "Upper Bavaria") administrative region. With 4,800 people per km 2, Munich is Germany's most densely populated municipality. It is also the second-largest city in the [Bavarian dialect area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_language "Bavarian language") after [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna").

The first record of Munich dates to 1158. The city has played an important role in Bavarian and German history. During the [Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation "Reformation"), it remained a Catholic stronghold. Munich became the capital of the [Kingdom of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bavaria "Kingdom of Bavaria") in 1806 and developed as a centre for arts, architecture, culture, and science. The [House of Wittelsbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Wittelsbach "House of Wittelsbach") ruled until 1918, when the [German revolution of 1918–1919](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_revolution_of_1918%E2%80%931919 "German revolution of 1918–1919") ended their reign and saw the short-lived [Bavarian Soviet Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavarian_Soviet_Republic "Bavarian Soviet Republic"). In the 1920s, Munich became a centre of political movements, including the rise of the [Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party "Nazi Party"). The city was known as the "Capital of the Movement". During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Munich was heavily bombed, but much of its historic architecture has since been restored.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-englund-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-zensus-7) After the war, the city's population and economy grew rapidly. 4) in [Africa](link_45) and the 4th most populous metropolitan area. The city goes beyond its borders and has expanded into neighbouring counties, making it the 4th largest metropolitan area in Africa.

Nicknamed the "Green City under the Sun", Nairobi is uniquely notable for being the only capital city in the world that hosts a [national park](link_11) within its boundaries. Its name originates from the [Maasai](link_46) phrase _Enkare Nyirobi_, meaning "place of cool waters".

As the national capital, Nairobi is home to the [Kenyan Parliament Buildings](link_47), the [State House](link_48) and the [Supreme Court Building](link_49). It is the major financial and economic hub of [East Africa](link_37), hosting thousands of Kenyan businesses and international companies and organisations, including the [United Nations Environment Programme](link_50) (UN Environment) and the [United Nations Office at Nairobi](link_51) (UNON). The [Nairobi Securities Exchange](link_52) (NSE) is one of the largest [stock exchanges](link_53) in Africa and the second-oldest exchange on the continent. It is Africa's fourth-largest stock exchange by trading volume, capable of processing 10 million trades a day. Nairobi is considered a [global city](link_54) and was ranked as a "Beta World City" by the [Globalisation and World Cities Research Network](link_55) as of 2024.

Munich is the largest city in Germany that is not [a state](link_18) of [its own](link_72), and it ranks as the 11th-largest city in the [European Union](link_73) (EU). The metropolitan area has around 3 million inhabitants, and the broader [Munich Metropolitan Region](link_74) is home to about 6.2 million people.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich#cite_note-mmr_official_site-5) It is the [third largest metropolitan region by GDP in the EU](link_75). Munich is located on the river [Isar](link_76) north of the [Alps](link_77). It is the seat of the [Upper Bavarian](link_20) administrative region. With 4,800 people per km 2, Munich is Germany's most densely populated municipality. It is also the second-largest city in the [Bavarian dialect area](link_3) after [Vienna](link_78).

The first record of Munich dates to 1158. The city has played an important role in Bavarian and German history. During the [Reformation](link_79), it remained a Catholic stronghold. Munich became the capital of the [Kingdom of Bavaria](link_80) in 1806 and developed as a centre for arts, architecture, culture, and science. **Dominik Krause** (born 3 August 1990 in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-1)) is a German politician of the [Alliance 90/The Greens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_90/The_Greens "Alliance 90/The Greens") party. He has served as [mayor of Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_Munich "List of mayors of Munich") since May 2026, having previously served as Second Mayor of Munich from October 2023 until April 2026.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:0-2)

In the [2026 Munich mayoral election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Bavarian_local_elections#Mayoral_results "2026 Bavarian local elections"), Krause won the [runoff election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runoff_election "Runoff election") against the incumbent mayor [Dieter Reiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dieter_Reiter "Dieter Reiter"). He took office on 1 May 2026.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:2-3)

Krause grew up in the Munich district of [Obermenzing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obermenzing "Obermenzing").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-4) After graduating from the Städtisches Louise-Schroeder-Gymnasium in 2009, he did his [Zivildienst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zivildienst "Zivildienst") at a [Montessori school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montessori_education "Montessori education") in Großhadern. He then studied applied and engineering physics at the [Technical University of Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_University_of_Munich "Technical University of Munich"), graduating with a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:0-2)

In 2024 he became engaged to his long-time partner, physician Sebastian Müller.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-5) According to Krause, the couple met as teenagers at a dance class.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-6) They live in the Munich neighborhood of Obergiesing-Fasangarten.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-7)

From 2012 to 2014, Krause served as spokesperson of [Green Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%BCne_Jugend "Grüne Jugend") in Munich.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-8) In 2014 he was elected to the [City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Council "City Council") and served as [parliamentary group leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_group_leader "Parliamentary group leader") from 2022 to 2023. In 2019 and 2020 he also chaired the Greens in Munich. Since October 2023 he has served as Second Mayor.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:1-9)

Krause has been a member of München ist bunt! e.V. since 2012, where he advocates against [racism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism "Racism").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:1-9) Since 2016 he has served on the organization's board.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-10)

Krause was a member of the advisory board of the Eine-Welt-Haus; he resigned at the end of 2017 in protest against the membership assembly's decision to make rooms available for an event connected to the anti-Israeli [BDS campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boycott,_Divestment_and_Sanctions "Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-11) Krause is also a member of the [German-Israeli Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German-Israeli_Society "German-Israeli Society") and is known for his close ties to [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-12)

Shortly after taking office, he attracted national attention with his remark that the [Oktoberfest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oktoberfest "Oktoberfest") was the "world's largest open [drug scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_scene "Drug scene")".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-14) In the Instagram interview where he made the remark, he was not advocating drug use at the Oktoberfest, but rather calling for a more relaxed approach to cannabis following its legalization. He clarified that in his view both alcohol and cannabis were perfectly fine, but that both should be consumed within an appropriate context.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-15)

As Second Mayor, he chairs the supervisory boards of several city-owned companies, including Deutsche Theater Betriebs-GmbH, [Gasteig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gasteig "Gasteig") München GmbH, Internationale Münchner Filmwochen GmbH, [Münchner Volkstheater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%BCnchner_Volkstheater "Münchner Volkstheater") GmbH, and [Pasinger Fabrik Kultur- und Bürgerzentrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasinger_Fabrik "Pasinger Fabrik") GmbH. He also serves as a supervisory board member of [SWM München](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadtwerke_M%C3%BCnchen "Stadtwerke München") GmbH, SWM Service GmbH, and Bayerngas GmbH.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-16)

In December 2024, Munich's Greens elected Krause as their mayoral candidate for the March 2026 election with 99.3% of the vote.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-17) He became the first Alliance 90/The Greens candidate to reach a mayoral runoff in Munich. He received 29.5% in the first round and faced incumbent Dieter Reiter of the SPD in the runoff on March 22, 2026, which he won with 56.4%.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:2-3)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-19)

**Dominik Krause** (born 3 August 1990 in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-1)) is a German politician of the [Alliance 90/The Greens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_90/The_Greens "Alliance 90/The Greens") party. He has served as [mayor of Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_Munich "List of mayors of Munich") since May 2026, having previously served as Second Mayor of Munich from October 2023 until April 2026.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:0-2)

In the [2026 Munich mayoral election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Bavarian_local_elections#Mayoral_results "2026 Bavarian local elections"), Krause won the [runoff election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runoff_election "Runoff election") against the incumbent mayor [Dieter Reiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dieter_Reiter "Dieter Reiter"). He took office on 1 May 2026.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:2-3)

Krause grew up in the Munich district of [Obermenzing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obermenzing "Obermenzing").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-4) After graduating from the Städtisches Louise-Schroeder-Gymnasium in 2009, he did his [Zivildienst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zivildienst "Zivildienst") at a [Montessori school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montessori_education "Montessori education") in Großhadern. He then studied applied and engineering physics at the [Technical University of Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technical_University_of_Munich "Technical University of Munich"), graduating with a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:0-2)

In 2024 he became engaged to his long-time partner, physician Sebastian Müller.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-5) According to Krause, the couple met as teenagers at a dance class.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-6) They live in the Munich neighborhood of Obergiesing-Fasangarten.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-7)

From 2012 to 2014, Krause served as spokesperson of [Green Youth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%BCne_Jugend "Grüne Jugend") in Munich.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-8) In 2014 he was elected to the [City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Council "City Council") and served as [parliamentary group leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_group_leader "Parliamentary group leader") from 2022 to 2023. In 2019 and 2020 he also chaired the Greens in Munich. Since October 2023 he has served as Second Mayor.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:1-9)

Krause has been a member of München ist bunt! e.V. since 2012, where he advocates against [racism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism "Racism").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:1-9) Since 2016 he has served on the organization's board.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-10)

Krause was a member of the advisory board of the Eine-Welt-Haus; he resigned at the end of 2017 in protest against the membership assembly's decision to make rooms available for an event connected to the anti-Israeli [BDS campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boycott,_Divestment_and_Sanctions "Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-11) Krause is also a member of the [German-Israeli Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German-Israeli_Society "German-Israeli Society") and is known for his close ties to [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-12)

Shortly after taking office, he attracted national attention with his remark that the [Oktoberfest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oktoberfest "Oktoberfest") was the "world's largest open [drug scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_scene "Drug scene")".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-14) In the Instagram interview where he made the remark, he was not advocating drug use at the Oktoberfest, but rather calling for a more relaxed approach to cannabis following its legalization. He clarified that in his view both alcohol and cannabis were perfectly fine, but that both should be consumed within an appropriate context.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-15)

As Second Mayor, he chairs the supervisory boards of several city-owned companies, including Deutsche Theater Betriebs-GmbH, [Gasteig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gasteig "Gasteig") München GmbH, Internationale Münchner Filmwochen GmbH, [Münchner Volkstheater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%BCnchner_Volkstheater "Münchner Volkstheater") GmbH, and [Pasinger Fabrik Kultur- und Bürgerzentrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasinger_Fabrik "Pasinger Fabrik") GmbH. He also serves as a supervisory board member of [SWM München](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadtwerke_M%C3%BCnchen "Stadtwerke München") GmbH, SWM Service GmbH, and Bayerngas GmbH.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-16)

In December 2024, Munich's Greens elected Krause as their mayoral candidate for the March 2026 election with 99.3% of the vote.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-17) He became the first Alliance 90/The Greens candidate to reach a mayoral runoff in Munich. He received 29.5% in the first round and faced incumbent Dieter Reiter of the SPD in the runoff on March 22, 2026, which he won with 56.4%.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-:2-3)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominik_Krause#cite_note-19)

The **Protectorate of Uganda** was a [protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate") of the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") from 1894 to 1962. In 1893 the [Imperial British East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_East_Africa_Company "Imperial British East Africa Company") transferred its administration rights of territory consisting mainly of the [Kingdom of Buganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buganda "Buganda") to the [British government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom").

In 1894 the Uganda Protectorate was established, and the territory was extended beyond the borders of Buganda to an area that roughly corresponds to that of present-day [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda").

In the mid-1880s, the Kingdom of Buganda was divided between four religious factions – Adherents of Uganda's Native Religion, [Catholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholics "Catholics"), [Protestants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestants "Protestants") and [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") – each vying for political control.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2) In 1888, [Mwanga II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwanga_II_of_Buganda "Mwanga II of Buganda") was ousted in a coup led by the [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") faction, who installed [Kalema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalema_of_Buganda "Kalema of Buganda") as leader. The following year, a Protestant and Catholic coalition formed to remove Kalema and return Mwanga II to power. This coalition secured an alliance with the [Imperial British East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_East_Africa_Company "Imperial British East Africa Company") (IBEAC), and succeeded in ousting Kalema and reinstating Mwanga in 1890.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2)

The IBEAC sent [Frederick Lugard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Lugard "Frederick Lugard") to Uganda in 1890 as its chief representative and to help maintain the peace between the competing factions. In 1891, Mwanga concluded a treaty with Lugard whereby Mwanga would place his land and tributary states under the protection of the IBEAC.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-3)

In 1892, having subdued the Muslim faction, the Protestants and Catholics resumed their struggle for supremacy which led to civil war.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2) That same year, the British government extended their support for the IBEAC to remain in Uganda until 1893. Despite strong opposition to getting involved in Uganda, the government felt that withdrawal of British influence would lead to war and the threat of a fellow European power encroaching on Britain's sphere of influence in East Africa it shared with Germany in 1890.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2)

On 31 March 1893, the IBEAC formally ended its involvement in Uganda. Missionaries, led by [Alfred Tucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Tucker "Alfred Tucker"), lobbied the British government to take over the administration of Uganda in place of the IBEAC, arguing that British withdrawal would lead to a continuance of the civil war between the different religious factions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2) Shortly after, [Sir Gerald Portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Gerald_Portal "Sir Gerald Portal"), a representative of the British government on the ground in Uganda, proposed a plan of double chieftainships – whereby every chieftainship would have one Protestant and one Catholic chief. On 19 April 1893, the British government and the chiefs of Uganda signed a treaty giving effect to this plan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2)

On 18 June 1894, the British government declared that [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Republic_of_Uganda "Second Republic of Uganda") would come under British protection as a [Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate").

The [Uganda Agreement of 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Agreement_of_1900 "Uganda Agreement of 1900") solidified the power of the largely Protestant 'Bakungu' client-chiefs, led by Kagwa. London sent only a few officials to administer the country, relying primarily on the 'Bakungu' chiefs. For decades they were preferred because of their political skills, their Christianity, their friendly relations with the British, their ability to collect taxes, and the proximity of [Entebbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entebbe "Entebbe") (the Ugandan colonial capital) to the Buganda capital. By the 1920s, the British administrators were more confident and had less need for military or administrative support. Colonial officials taxed cash crops produced by the peasants. There was popular discontent among the [Baganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baganda "Baganda") rank-and-file, which weakened the position of their leaders. In 1912, Kagwa moved to solidify 'Bakungu' power by proposing a second 'Lukiko' for Buganda with himself as president and the 'Bakungu' as a sort of hereditary aristocracy. British officials vetoed the idea when they discovered widespread popular opposition. Instead, British officials began some reforms and attempted to make the 'Lukiko' a genuine representative assembly.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-4)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/The_White_Elephant%2C_Punch_103.png/250px-The_White_Elephant%2C_Punch_103.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_White_Elephant,_Punch_103.png)

_[Punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch\_(magazine) "Punch (magazine)")_ cartoon depicting Uganda personified as a [White elephant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_elephant "White elephant") which the [East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa_Company "East Africa Company") is attempting to sell to Britain (1892)

Although momentous change occurred during the colonial era in Uganda, some characteristics of late-nineteenth-century African society survived to reemerge at the time of independence. The status of [Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate") had significantly different consequences for Uganda than had the region been made a colony like neighbouring [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), insofar as Uganda retained a degree of self-government that would have otherwise been limited under a full colonial administration.

Colonial rule, however, affected local economic systems dramatically, in part because the first concern of the British was financial. Quelling the 1897 Sudanese mutiny (see [Uganda before 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_before_1900 "Uganda before 1900")) under the leadership of protectorate commissioner [George Wilson CB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wilson_(Chief_Colonial_Secretary_of_Uganda) "George Wilson (Chief Colonial Secretary of Uganda)") had been costly—units of the [British Indian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Indian_Army "British Indian Army") had been transported to Uganda at considerable expense. The new commissioner of Uganda in 1900, [Sir Harry H. Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Johnston "Harry Johnston"), had orders to establish an efficient administration and to levy taxes as quickly as possible. Johnston approached the chiefs in [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") with offers of jobs in the colonial administration in return for their collaboration.

The chiefs were more interested in preserving Uganda as a self-governing entity, continuing the royal line of [Kabakas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaka_of_Buganda "Kabaka of Buganda"), and securing private land tenure for themselves and their supporters. Hard bargaining ensued, but the chiefs ended up with everything they wanted, including one-half of all the land in Buganda. The half left to the British as "Crown Land" was later found to be largely swamp and scrub.

Johnston's [Uganda Agreement of 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Agreement_of_1900 "Uganda Agreement of 1900") imposed a tax on huts and guns, designated the chiefs as tax collectors, and testified to the continued alliance of British and Baganda interests. The British signed much less generous treaties with the other kingdoms ([Toro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toro_(kingdom) "Toro (kingdom)") in 1900, [Ankole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankole "Ankole") in 1901, and [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro") in 1933) without the provision of large-scale private land tenure. The smaller chiefdoms of [Busoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busoga "Busoga") were ignored.

### Buganda administrators

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Protectorate_of_Uganda&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Buganda administrators")]

The Baganda immediately offered their services to the British as administrators over their recently conquered neighbours, an offer which was attractive to the economy-minded colonial administration. Baganda agents fanned out as local tax collectors and labour organizers in areas such as [Kigezi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kigezi "Kigezi"), [Mbale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mbale "Mbale"), and, significantly, Bunyoro. This sub-imperialism and Ganda cultural chauvinism was resented by the people being administered.

Wherever they went, Baganda insisted on the exclusive use of their language, [Luganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luganda "Luganda"), and they planted [bananas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana "Banana") as the only proper food worth eating. They regarded their traditional dress—long cotton gowns called [kanzus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanzu "Kanzu")—as civilized; all else was barbarian. They also encouraged and engaged in mission work, attempting to convert locals to their form of Christianity or Islam. In some areas, the resulting backlash aided the efforts of religious rivals — for example, Catholics won converts in areas where oppressive rule was identified with a Protestant [Muganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muganda "Muganda") chief.

The people of [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro") were particularly aggrieved, having fought the Baganda and the British; having a substantial section of their heartland annexed to Buganda as the "lost counties", and finally having "arrogant" Baganda administrators issuing orders, collecting taxes, and forcing unpaid labour. In 1907 the Banyoro rose in a rebellion called _[nyangire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyangire?action=edit&redlink=1 "Nyangire (page does not exist)")_, or "refusing", and succeeded in having the Baganda subimperial agents withdrawn.

Meanwhile, in 1901 the completion of the [Uganda Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Railway "Uganda Railway") from the coast at [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa") to the [Lake Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria "Lake Victoria") port of [Kisumu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kisumu "Kisumu") moved colonial authorities to encourage the growth of cash crops to help pay the railway's operating costs. Another result of the railway construction was the 1902 decision to transfer the eastern section of the Uganda Protectorate to the [Kenya Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Colony "Kenya Colony"), then called the [East Africa Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa_Protectorate "East Africa Protectorate"), to keep the entire line under one local colonial administration. Because the railway experienced cost overruns in Kenya, the British decided to justify its exceptional expense and pay its operating costs by introducing large-scale European settlement in a vast tract of land that became a centre of cash-crop agriculture known as the "[White Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Highlands "White Highlands")". A major part of the territory eventually left out of the "East Africa Protectorate" was the [Uganda Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Scheme "Uganda Scheme"), in which the British Empire offered to create a Jewish nation-state. The offer was made to the [Zionist movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Zionist_Organization "World Zionist Organization") which rejected it, refusing to accept anything other than the ancient [Land of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_of_Israel "Land of Israel").

In many areas of Uganda, by contrast, agricultural production was placed in the hands of Africans, if they responded to the opportunity. Cotton was the crop of choice, largely because of pressure by the [British Cotton Growing Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Cotton_Growing_Association "British Cotton Growing Association"), textile manufacturers who urged the colonies to provide raw materials for British mills. This was done by cash cropping the land. Even the [CMS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Mission_Society "Church Mission Society") joined the effort by launching the [Uganda Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Company?action=edit&redlink=1 "Uganda Company (page does not exist)") (managed by a former missionary) to promote cotton planting and to buy and transport the produce.

Buganda, with its strategic location on the lakeside, reaped the benefits of cotton growing. The advantages of this crop were quickly recognized by the Baganda chiefs who had newly acquired freehold estates, which came to be known as [mailo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mailo "Mailo") because they were measured in square miles. In 1905 the initial baled cotton export was valued at £200; in 1906, £1,000; in 1907; £11,000; and in 1908, £52,000. By 1915 the value of cotton exports had climbed to £369,000, and Britain was able to end its subsidy of colonial administration in Uganda, while in Kenya the white settlers required continuing subsidies by the home government.

The income generated by cotton sales made the Uganda kingdom relatively prosperous, compared with the rest of colonial Uganda, although before [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") cotton was also being grown in the eastern regions of [Busoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busoga "Busoga"), [Lango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lango_sub-region "Lango sub-region"), and [Teso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teso_sub-region "Teso sub-region"). Many Baganda spent their new earnings on imported clothing, bicycles, metal roofing, and even cars. They also invested in their children's education. The Christian missions emphasized literacy skills, and African converts quickly learned to read and write. By 1911 two popular journals, _Ebifa_ (News) and _Munno_ (Your Friend), were published monthly in Luganda.

Heavily supported by African funds, new schools were soon turning out graduating classes at Mengo High School, St. Mary's Kisubi, Namilyango, Gayaza, and [King's College Budo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College_Budo "King's College Budo") — all in Buganda. The chief minister of the Buganda kingdom, Sir [Apollo Kaggwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_Kaggwa "Apollo Kaggwa"), personally awarded a bicycle to the top graduate at [King's College Budo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_College_Budo "King's College Budo"), together with the promise of a government job. The schools, in fact, had inherited the educational function formerly performed in the [Kabaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaka_of_Uganda?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kabaka of Uganda (page does not exist)")'s palace, where generations of young pages had been trained to become chiefs. Now the qualifications sought were literacy and skills, including typing and English translation.

Two important principles of precolonial political life carried over into the colonial era: clientage, whereby ambitious younger officeholders attached themselves to older high-ranking chiefs, and generational conflict, which resulted when the younger generation sought to expel their elders from office in order to replace them. After World War I, the younger aspirants to high office in Buganda became impatient with the seemingly perpetual tenure of Sir Apollo and his contemporaries, who lacked many of the skills that members of the younger generation had acquired through schooling. Calling themselves the [Young Baganda Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Baganda_Association "Young Baganda Association"), members of the new generation attached themselves to the young Kabaka, [Daudi Chwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daudi_Chwa "Daudi Chwa"), who was the figurehead ruler of Buganda under indirect rule. But Kabaka Daudi never gained real political power, and after a short and frustrating reign, he died at the relatively young age of forty-three.

### First World War era military forces

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Protectorate_of_Uganda&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: First World War era military forces")]

Early on in the Protectorate's history of occupation the British colonial government had recognised the need for a local defence force.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-5) In 1895 the British colonial armed force in the Protectorate was the Uganda Rifles, who were formed as an internal security force (i.e. keeping the peace in tribal areas rather than defending against external aggression).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-7) In the late nineteenth century the local defence force was largely composed of Sudanese troops brought in by the British, these troops were commanded by a mix of British and Sudanese officers, local tribes were not that evident in this force defending the interests of the [Imperial British East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_East_Africa_Company "Imperial British East Africa Company"). Unfortunately the Sudanese grew resentful of their conditions of service and the Uganda Rifles mutinied in 1897.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Uganda_Army_History-8) On 1 January 1902[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-9) the somewhat irregular armed force in Uganda was reformed (with far fewer Sudanese and more local tribes in its ranks)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Uganda_Army_History-8) and re-titled the 4th Battalion the [King's African Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_African_Rifles "King's African Rifles") (KAR). It was with this defensive structure that was in place at the outbreak of hostilities in 1914, although there had been cuts in the KAR in 1911 stretching the force structure of the regiment even further.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-10) By the end of the Great War the Ugandan contingent in the KAR had grown considerably and they had become an effective fighting force built out of Ugandans rather than outsiders and had enjoyed success against the German forces in East Africa.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-12) The Protectorate also developed an emergency response for the intelligence collection on German activities and performing political-military liaison with allies in East Africa; according to UK National Archive records this organisation (known as the [Uganda Intelligence Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Intelligence_Department "Uganda Intelligence Department"))[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-13) was about 20 strong and included European officers and African soldiers.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-14)

Most of this recruitment was done from the northern part of the protectorate especially the Acholi sub-region. The British colonial administration had also fought with the Lamogi clan of the Acholi people in what that culminated in to the Lamogi Rebellion.

![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/11/Uganda_Protectorate_British_administration.png/330px-Uganda_Protectorate_British_administration.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

Subdivisions under the Ugandan Protectorate (1926 borders). (Click area to go to article.) The areas in red and blue hues had centralized kingdoms prior to British arrival, while the colonialists introduced centralized rule on the Baganda model to areas in yellow. Areas in khaki never had centralized kingdoms.

Far more promising as a source of political support were the British colonial officers, who welcomed the typing and translation skills of school graduates and advanced the careers of their favourites. The contest was decided after World War I, when an influx of British ex-military officers, now serving as district commissioners, began to feel that self-government was an obstacle to good government. Specifically, they accused Sir Apollo and his generation of inefficiency, abuse of power, and failure to keep adequate financial accounts—charges that were not hard to document.

Sir Apollo resigned in 1926, at about the same time that a host of elderly Baganda chiefs were replaced by a new generation of officeholders. The Buganda treasury was also audited that year for the first time. Although it was not a nationalist organization, the Young Baganda Association claimed to represent popular African dissatisfaction with the old order. As soon as the younger Baganda had replaced the older generation in office, however, their objections to privilege accompanying power ceased. The pattern persisted in Ugandan politics up to and after independence.

The commoners, who had been labouring on the cotton estates of the chiefs before World War I, did not remain servile. As time passed, they bought small parcels of land from their erstwhile landlords. This land fragmentation was aided by the British, who in 1927 forced the chiefs to limit severely the rents and obligatory labour they could demand from their tenants. Thus the oligarchy of landed chiefs who had emerged with the Uganda Agreement of 1900 declined in importance, and agricultural production shifted to independent [smallholders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallholders "Smallholders"), who grew cotton, and later coffee, for the export market.

Unlike [Tanganyika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanganyika_(territory) "Tanganyika (territory)"), which was devastated during the prolonged fighting between Britain and Germany in the [East African Campaign of World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Campaign_of_World_War_I "East African Campaign of World War I"), Uganda prospered from wartime agricultural production. After the population losses from disease during the era of conquest and at the turn of the century (particularly the devastating [sleeping sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleeping_sickness "Sleeping sickness") epidemic of 1900–1906), Uganda's population was growing again. Even the 1930s depression seemed to affect smallholder cash farmers in Uganda less severely than it did the white settler producers in Kenya. Ugandans simply grew their own food until rising prices made export crops attractive again.

Two issues continued to create grievance through the 1930s and 1940s. The colonial government strictly regulated the buying and processing of cash crops, setting prices and reserving the role of intermediary for Asians, who were thought to be more efficient. The British and Asians firmly repelled African attempts to break into cotton ginning. In addition, on the Asian-owned sugar plantations established in the 1920s, labour for sugar-cane and other cash crops was increasingly provided by migrants from peripheral areas of Uganda and even from outside Uganda.

In 1949, discontented Baganda rioted and burned down the houses of pro-government chiefs. The rioters had three demands: the right to bypass government price controls on the export sales of cotton, the removal of the Asian monopoly over cotton ginning, and the right to have their own representatives in local government replace chiefs appointed by the British. They were critical as well of the young Kabaka, [Frederick Walugembe Mutesa II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutesa_II "Mutesa II") (also known as "King Freddie" or "Kabaka Freddie"), for his inattention to the needs of his people. The British governor, [Sir John Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hathorn_Hall "John Hathorn Hall"), regarded the riots as the work of communist-inspired agitators and rejected the suggested reforms.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/BEA-KUT_1958_MiNr0094I_pm_B002.jpg/250px-BEA-KUT_1958_MiNr0094I_pm_B002.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BEA-KUT_1958_MiNr0094I_pm_B002.jpg)

Stamp of British East Africa with a portrait of [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II")

Far from leading the people into confrontation, Uganda's would-be agitators were slow to respond to popular discontent. Nevertheless, the [Uganda African Farmers Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_African_Farmers_Union?action=edit&redlink=1 "Uganda African Farmers Union (page does not exist)"), founded by [I.K. Musazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.K._Musazi "I.K. Musazi") in 1947, was blamed for the riots and was banned by the British. Musazi's [Uganda National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_National_Congress "Uganda National Congress") replaced the farmers union in 1952 when it was set up with [Abu Mayanja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Mayanja "Abu Mayanja") as its first Secretary General, but because the Congress remained a casual discussion group more than an organized political party, it stagnated and came to an end just two years after its inception.

Meanwhile, the British began to move ahead of the Ugandans in preparing for independence. The effects of Britain's postwar withdrawal from [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), the march of nationalism in [West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Africa "West Africa"), and a more liberal philosophy in the [Colonial Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Office "Colonial Office") geared toward future self-rule all began to be felt in Uganda. The embodiment of these issues arrived in 1952 in the person of a new and energetic reformist governor, [Sir Andrew Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Cohen_(statesman) "Andrew Cohen (statesman)") (formerly undersecretary for African affairs in the Colonial Office).

Cohen set about preparing Uganda for independence. On the economic side, he removed obstacles to African cotton ginning, rescinded price discrimination against African-grown coffee, encouraged cooperatives, and established the [Uganda Development Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Development_Corporation "Uganda Development Corporation") to promote and finance new projects. On the political side, he reorganized the [Legislative Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Legislative_Council "Uganda Legislative Council"), which had consisted of an unrepresentative selection of interest groups heavily favouring the European community, to include African representatives elected from districts throughout Uganda. This system became a prototype for the future [Parliament of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Uganda "Parliament of Uganda").

## Power politics in Buganda

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Protectorate_of_Uganda&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Power politics in Buganda")]

The prospect of elections caused a sudden proliferation of new political parties. This development alarmed the old-guard leaders within the Ugandan kingdoms, because they realized that the centre of power would be at the national level. The spark that ignited wider opposition to Governor Cohen's reforms was a 1953 speech in London in which the secretary of state for colonies referred to the possibility of a federation of the three East African territories (Kenya, Uganda, and Tanganyika), similar to that established in [Rhodesia and Nyasaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland "Rhodesia and Nyasaland").

Many Ugandans were aware of the [Central African Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_African_Federation "Central African Federation") of [Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia "Rhodesia") and [Nyasaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyasaland "Nyasaland") (later [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"), [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia"), and [Malawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malawi "Malawi")) and its domination by white settler interests. Ugandans deeply feared the prospect of an East African federation dominated by the settlers of Kenya, which was then in the midst of the bitter [Mau Mau uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_uprising "Mau Mau uprising"). They had vigorously resisted a similar suggestion by the 1930 [Hilton Young Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilton_Young_Commission "Hilton Young Commission"). Confidence in Cohen vanished just as the Governor was preparing to urge Buganda to recognize that its special status would have to be sacrificed in the interests of a new and larger nation-state.

Kabaka Mutesa II, who had been regarded by his subjects as uninterested in their welfare, now refused to cooperate with Cohen's plan for an integrated Buganda. Instead, he demanded that Buganda be separated from the rest of the protectorate and transferred to Foreign Office jurisdiction. Cohen's response to this crisis was to deport the Kabaka to a comfortable exile in London. His forced departure made the Kabaka an instant martyr in the eyes of the Baganda, whose latent separatism and anticolonial sentiments set off a storm of protest. Cohen's action had backfired, and he could find no one among the Baganda prepared or able to mobilize support for his schemes. After two frustrating years of unrelenting Ganda hostility and obstruction, Cohen was forced to reinstate [Kabaka Mutesa II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaka_Mutesa_II "Kabaka Mutesa II").

The negotiations leading to the Kabaka's return had an outcome similar to the negotiations of Commissioner Johnston in 1900; although appearing to satisfy the British, they were a resounding victory for the Baganda. Cohen secured the Kabaka's agreement not to oppose independence within the larger Ugandan framework. Not only was the Kabaka reinstated in return, but for the first time since 1889, the monarch was given the power to appoint and dismiss his chiefs (Buganda government officials) instead of acting as a mere figurehead while they conducted the affairs of government.

The Kabaka's new power was cloaked in the misleading claim that he would be only a "constitutional monarch", while in fact he was a leading player in deciding how Uganda would be governed. A new grouping of Baganda calling themselves "the King's Friends" rallied to the Kabaka's defence. They were conservative, fiercely loyal to Buganda as a kingdom, and willing to entertain the prospect of participation in an independent Uganda only if it were headed by the Kabaka as head of state. Baganda politicians who did not share this vision or who were opposed to the "King's Friends" found themselves branded as the "King's Enemies", which meant political and social ostracism.

The major exception to this rule were the Roman Catholic Baganda who had formed their own party, the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(Uganda) "Democratic Party (Uganda)") (DP), led by [Benedicto Kiwanuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedicto_Kiwanuka "Benedicto Kiwanuka"). Many Catholics had felt excluded from the Protestant-dominated establishment in Buganda ever since Lugard's Maxim had turned the tide in 1892. The Kabaka had to be Protestant, and he was invested in a coronation ceremony modelled on that of British monarchs (who are invested by the Church of England's Archbishop of Canterbury) that took place at the main Protestant church. Religion and politics were equally inseparable in the other kingdoms throughout Uganda. The DP had Catholic as well as other adherents and was probably the best organized of all the parties preparing for elections. It had printing presses and the backing of the popular newspaper, Munno, which was published at the St. Mary's Kisubi mission.

Elsewhere in Uganda, the emergence of the Kabaka as a political force provoked immediate hostility. Political parties and local interest groups were riddled with divisions and rivalries, but they shared one concern: they were determined not to be dominated by Buganda. In 1960 a political organizer from Lango, [Milton Obote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Obote "Milton Obote"), seized the initiative and formed a new party, the [Uganda People's Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_People's_Congress "Uganda People's Congress") (UPC), as a coalition of all those outside the Roman Catholic-dominated DP who opposed Buganda hegemony.

The steps Cohen had initiated to bring about the independence of a unified Ugandan state had led to a polarization between factions from Buganda and those opposed to its domination. Buganda's population in 1959 was 2 million, out of Uganda's total of 6 million. Even discounting the many non-Baganda resident in Buganda, there were at least 1 million people who owed allegiance to the Kabaka — too many to be overlooked or shunted aside, but too few to dominate the country as a whole.

At the [London Conference of 1960](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Conference_of_1960?action=edit&redlink=1 "London Conference of 1960 (page does not exist)"), it was obvious that Buganda autonomy and a strong unitary government were incompatible, but no compromise emerged, and the decision on the form of government was postponed. The British announced that elections would be held in March 1961 for "responsible government", the next-to-last stage of preparation before the formal granting of independence. It was assumed that those winning the election would gain valuable experience in office, preparing them for the probable responsibility of governing after independence.

In Buganda the "King's Friends" urged a total boycott of the election because their attempts to secure promises of future autonomy had been rebuffed. Consequently, when the voters went to the polls throughout Uganda to elect eighty-two [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Uganda "National Assembly of Uganda") members, in Buganda only the Roman Catholic supporters of the DP braved severe public pressure and voted, capturing twenty of Buganda's twenty-one allotted seats. This artificial situation gave the DP a majority of seats, although they had a minority of 416,000 votes nationwide versus 495,000 for the UPC. Benedicto Kiwanuka became the new chief minister of Uganda.

Shocked by the results, the Baganda separatists, who formed a political party called [Kabaka Yekka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaka_Yekka "Kabaka Yekka"), had second thoughts about the wisdom of their election boycott. They quickly welcomed the recommendations of a British commission that proposed a future federal form of government. According to these recommendations, Buganda would enjoy a measure of internal autonomy if it participated fully in the national government.

For its part, the UPC was equally anxious to eject its DP rivals from government before they became entrenched. Obote reached an understanding with Kabaka Freddie and the KY, accepting Buganda's special federal relationship and even a provision by which the kabaka could appoint Buganda's representatives to the National Assembly, in return for a strategic alliance to defeat the DP. The Kabaka was also promised the largely ceremonial position of Head of state of Uganda, which was of great symbolic importance to the Baganda.

This marriage of convenience between the UPC and the KY made inevitable the defeat of the DP interim administration. In the aftermath of the April 1962 final election leading up to independence, Uganda's national assembly consisted of forty-three UPC members, twenty-four KY members, and twenty-four DP members. The new UPC-KY coalition led Uganda into independence in October 1962, with Obote as [Prime Minister of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Uganda "Prime Minister of Uganda"), and the Kabaka becoming [President of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Uganda "President of Uganda") a year later.
