The **Protectorate of Uganda** was a [protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate") of the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") from 1894 to 1962. In 1893 the [Imperial British East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_East_Africa_Company "Imperial British East Africa Company") transferred its administration rights of territory consisting mainly of the [Kingdom of Buganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buganda "Buganda") to the [British government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom").

In 1894 the Uganda Protectorate was established, and the territory was extended beyond the borders of Buganda to an area that roughly corresponds to that of present-day [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda").

In the mid-1880s, the Kingdom of Buganda was divided between four religious factions – Adherents of Uganda's Native Religion, [Catholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholics "Catholics"), [Protestants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestants "Protestants") and [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") – each vying for political control.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2) In 1888, [Mwanga II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwanga_II_of_Buganda "Mwanga II of Buganda") was ousted in a coup led by the [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") faction, who installed [Kalema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalema_of_Buganda "Kalema of Buganda") as leader. The following year, a Protestant and Catholic coalition formed to remove Kalema and return Mwanga II to power. This coalition secured an alliance with the [Imperial British East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_East_Africa_Company "Imperial British East Africa Company") (IBEAC), and succeeded in ousting Kalema and reinstating Mwanga in 1890.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2)

The IBEAC sent [Frederick Lugard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Lugard "Frederick Lugard") to Uganda in 1890 as its chief representative and to help maintain the peace between the competing factions. In 1891, Mwanga concluded a treaty with Lugard whereby Mwanga would place his land and tributary states under the protection of the IBEAC.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-3)

In 1892, having subdued the Muslim faction, the Protestants and Catholics resumed their struggle for supremacy which led to civil war.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2) That same year, the British government extended their support for the IBEAC to remain in Uganda until 1893. Despite strong opposition to getting involved in Uganda, the government felt that withdrawal of British influence would lead to war and the threat of a fellow European power encroaching on Britain's sphere of influence in East Africa it shared with Germany in 1890.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2)

On 31 March 1893, the IBEAC formally ended its involvement in Uganda. Missionaries, led by [Alfred Tucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Tucker "Alfred Tucker"), lobbied the British government to take over the administration of Uganda in place of the IBEAC, arguing that British withdrawal would lead to a continuance of the civil war between the different religious factions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2) Shortly after, [Sir Gerald Portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Gerald_Portal "Sir Gerald Portal"), a representative of the British government on the ground in Uganda, proposed a plan of double chieftainships – whereby every chieftainship would have one Protestant and one Catholic chief. On 19 April 1893, the British government and the chiefs of Uganda signed a treaty giving effect to this plan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2)

On 18 June 1894, the British government declared that [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Republic_of_Uganda "Second Republic of Uganda") would come under British protection as a [Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate").

The [Uganda Agreement of 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Agreement_of_1900 "Uganda Agreement of 1900") solidified the power of the largely Protestant 'Bakungu' client-chiefs, led by Kagwa. London sent only a few officials to administer the country, relying primarily on the 'Bakungu' chiefs. For decades they were preferred because of their political skills, their Christianity, their friendly relations with the British, their ability to collect taxes, and the proximity of [Entebbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entebbe "Entebbe") (the Ugandan colonial capital) to the Buganda capital. By the 1920s, the British administrators were more confident and had less need for military or administrative support. Colonial officials taxed cash crops produced by the peasants. There was popular discontent among the [Baganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baganda "Baganda") rank-and-file, which weakened the position of their leaders. In 1912, Kagwa moved to solidify 'Bakungu' power by proposing a second 'Lukiko' for Buganda with himself as president and the 'Bakungu' as a sort of hereditary aristocracy. British officials vetoed the idea when they discovered widespread popular opposition. Instead, British officials began some reforms and attempted to make the 'Lukiko' a genuine representative assembly.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-4)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/The_White_Elephant%2C_Punch_103.png/250px-The_White_Elephant%2C_Punch_103.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_White_Elephant,_Punch_103.png)

_[Punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch\_(magazine) "Punch (magazine)")_ cartoon depicting Uganda personified as a [White elephant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_elephant "White elephant") which the [East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa_Company "East Africa Company") is attempting to sell to Britain (1892)

Although momentous change occurred during the colonial era in Uganda, some characteristics of late-nineteenth-century African society survived to reemerge at the time of independence. The status of [Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate") had significantly different consequences for Uganda than had the region been made a colony like neighbouring [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), insofar as Uganda retained a degree of self-government that would have otherwise been limited under a full colonial administration.

Colonial rule, however, affected local economic systems dramatically, in part because the first concern of the British was financial. Quelling the 1897 Sudanese mutiny (see [Uganda before 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_before_1900 "Uganda before 1900")) under the leadership of protectorate commissioner [George Wilson CB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wilson_(Chief_Colonial_Secretary_of_Uganda) "George Wilson (Chief Colonial Secretary of Uganda)") had been costly—units of the [British Indian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Indian_Army "British Indian Army") had been transported to Uganda at considerable expense. The new commissioner of Uganda in 1900, [Sir Harry H. Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Johnston "Harry Johnston"), had orders to establish an efficient administration and to levy taxes as quickly as possible. Johnston approached the chiefs in [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") with offers of jobs in the colonial administration in return for their collaboration.

The chiefs were more interested in preserving Uganda as a self-governing entity, continuing the royal line of [Kabakas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaka_of_Buganda "Kabaka of Buganda"), and securing private land tenure for themselves and their supporters. Hard bargaining ensued, but the chiefs ended up with everything they wanted, including one-half of all the land in Buganda. The half left to the British as "Crown Land" was later found to be largely swamp and scrub.

Johnston's [Uganda Agreement of 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Agreement_of_1900 "Uganda Agreement of 1900") imposed a tax on huts and guns, designated the chiefs as tax collectors, and testified to the continued alliance of British and Baganda interests. The British signed much less generous treaties with the other kingdoms ([Toro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toro_(kingdom) "Toro (kingdom)") in 1900, [Ankole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankole "Ankole") in 1901, and [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro") in 1933) without the provision of large-scale private land tenure. The smaller chiefdoms of [Busoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busoga "Busoga") were ignored.

### Buganda administrators

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Protectorate_of_Uganda&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Buganda administrators")]

The Baganda immediately offered their services to the British as administrators over their recently conquered neighbours, an offer which was attractive to the economy-minded colonial administration. They also encouraged and engaged in mission work, attempting to convert locals to their form of Christianity or Islam. In some areas, the resulting backlash aided the efforts of religious rivals — for example, Catholics won converts in areas where oppressive rule was identified with a Protestant [Muganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muganda "Muganda") chief.

The people of [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro") were particularly aggrieved, having fought the Baganda and the British; having a substantial section of their heartland annexed to Buganda as the "lost counties", and finally having "arrogant" Baganda administrators issuing orders, collecting taxes, and forcing unpaid labour. In 1907 the Banyoro rose in a rebellion called _[nyangire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyangire?action=edit&redlink=1 "Nyangire (page does not exist)")_, or "refusing", and succeeded in having the Baganda subimperial agents withdrawn.

Another result of the railway construction was the 1902 decision to transfer the eastern section of the Uganda Protectorate to the [Kenya Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Colony "Kenya Colony"), then called the [East Africa Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa_Protectorate "East Africa Protectorate"), to keep the entire line under one local colonial administration. A major part of the territory eventually left out of the "East Africa Protectorate" was the [Uganda Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Scheme "Uganda Scheme"), in which the British Empire offered to create a Jewish nation-state. The **Protectorate of Uganda** was a [protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate") of the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") from 1894 to 1962. In 1893 the [Imperial British East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_East_Africa_Company "Imperial British East Africa Company") transferred its administration rights of territory consisting mainly of the [Kingdom of Buganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buganda "Buganda") to the [British government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom").

In 1894 the Uganda Protectorate was established, and the territory was extended beyond the borders of Buganda to an area that roughly corresponds to that of present-day [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda").

In the mid-1880s, the Kingdom of Buganda was divided between four religious factions – Adherents of Uganda's Native Religion, [Catholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholics "Catholics"), [Protestants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestants "Protestants") and [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") – each vying for political control.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2) In 1888, [Mwanga II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwanga_II_of_Buganda "Mwanga II of Buganda") was ousted in a coup led by the [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") faction, who installed [Kalema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalema_of_Buganda "Kalema of Buganda") as leader. The following year, a Protestant and Catholic coalition formed to remove Kalema and return Mwanga II to power. This coalition secured an alliance with the [Imperial British East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_East_Africa_Company "Imperial British East Africa Company") (IBEAC), and succeeded in ousting Kalema and reinstating Mwanga in 1890.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2)

The IBEAC sent [Frederick Lugard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Lugard "Frederick Lugard") to Uganda in 1890 as its chief representative and to help maintain the peace between the competing factions. In 1891, Mwanga concluded a treaty with Lugard whereby Mwanga would place his land and tributary states under the protection of the IBEAC.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-3)

In 1892, having subdued the Muslim faction, the Protestants and Catholics resumed their struggle for supremacy which led to civil war.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2) That same year, the British government extended their support for the IBEAC to remain in Uganda until 1893. Despite strong opposition to getting involved in Uganda, the government felt that withdrawal of British influence would lead to war and the threat of a fellow European power encroaching on Britain's sphere of influence in East Africa it shared with Germany in 1890.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2)

On 31 March 1893, the IBEAC formally ended its involvement in Uganda. Missionaries, led by [Alfred Tucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Tucker "Alfred Tucker"), lobbied the British government to take over the administration of Uganda in place of the IBEAC, arguing that British withdrawal would lead to a continuance of the civil war between the different religious factions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2) Shortly after, [Sir Gerald Portal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Gerald_Portal "Sir Gerald Portal"), a representative of the British government on the ground in Uganda, proposed a plan of double chieftainships – whereby every chieftainship would have one Protestant and one Catholic chief. On 19 April 1893, the British government and the chiefs of Uganda signed a treaty giving effect to this plan.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-Bishop_Alfred_Tucker_and_the_Establishment_of_a_British_Protectorate_in_Uganda_1890-94-2)

On 18 June 1894, the British government declared that [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Republic_of_Uganda "Second Republic of Uganda") would come under British protection as a [Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate").

The [Uganda Agreement of 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Agreement_of_1900 "Uganda Agreement of 1900") solidified the power of the largely Protestant 'Bakungu' client-chiefs, led by Kagwa. London sent only a few officials to administer the country, relying primarily on the 'Bakungu' chiefs. For decades they were preferred because of their political skills, their Christianity, their friendly relations with the British, their ability to collect taxes, and the proximity of [Entebbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entebbe "Entebbe") (the Ugandan colonial capital) to the Buganda capital. By the 1920s, the British administrators were more confident and had less need for military or administrative support. Colonial officials taxed cash crops produced by the peasants. There was popular discontent among the [Baganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baganda "Baganda") rank-and-file, which weakened the position of their leaders. In 1912, Kagwa moved to solidify 'Bakungu' power by proposing a second 'Lukiko' for Buganda with himself as president and the 'Bakungu' as a sort of hereditary aristocracy. British officials vetoed the idea when they discovered widespread popular opposition. Instead, British officials began some reforms and attempted to make the 'Lukiko' a genuine representative assembly.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda#cite_note-4)

_[Punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch\_(magazine) "Punch (magazine)")_ cartoon depicting Uganda personified as a [White elephant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_elephant "White elephant") which the [East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa_Company "East Africa Company") is attempting to sell to Britain (1892)

Although momentous change occurred during the colonial era in Uganda, some characteristics of late-nineteenth-century African society survived to reemerge at the time of independence. The status of [Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate") had significantly different consequences for Uganda than had the region been made a colony like neighbouring [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), insofar as Uganda retained a degree of self-government that would have otherwise been limited under a full colonial administration.

Colonial rule, however, affected local economic systems dramatically, in part because the first concern of the British was financial. The new commissioner of Uganda in 1900, [Sir Harry H. Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Johnston "Harry Johnston"), had orders to establish an efficient administration and to levy taxes as quickly as possible. Johnston approached the chiefs in [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") with offers of jobs in the colonial administration in return for their collaboration.

The chiefs were more interested in preserving Uganda as a self-governing entity, continuing the royal line of [Kabakas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaka_of_Buganda "Kabaka of Buganda"), and securing private land tenure for themselves and their supporters. Hard bargaining ensued, but the chiefs ended up with everything they wanted, including one-half of all the land in Buganda. The half left to the British as "Crown Land" was later found to be largely swamp and scrub.

Johnston's [Uganda Agreement of 1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Agreement_of_1900 "Uganda Agreement of 1900") imposed a tax on huts and guns, designated the chiefs as tax collectors, and testified to the continued alliance of British and Baganda interests. The British signed much less generous treaties with the other kingdoms ([Toro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toro_(kingdom) "Toro (kingdom)") in 1900, [Ankole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankole "Ankole") in 1901, and [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro") in 1933) without the provision of large-scale private land tenure. The smaller chiefdoms of [Busoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busoga "Busoga") were ignored.

**Joshua Kiprui Cheptegei** (born 12 September 1996) is a Ugandan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). He is the current world record holder for the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"), and once held the world-best time over the [15 kilometres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15K_run "15K run") distance.

Cheptegei is the reigning [Olympic champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics") in the 10000 m and three-time [World champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") in the 10,000 m. Cheptegei also won a gold medal in the 5000 m and 10,000 m at the [2018 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2018_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2018 Commonwealth Games") and at the [2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"). At the [2024 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"), Cheptegei won gold in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres"), becoming the Olympic champion and setting a new [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") in the process.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-5)

Cheptegei is the tenth man in history to hold the 5000 m and 10,000 m world records concurrently, both set in 2020.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-7)

Cheptegei was born on 12 September 1996 in Kapsewui, [Kapchorwa District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapchorwa_District "Kapchorwa District"), Uganda.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-CWG-2) In primary school, he first played football and tried out [long jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_jump "Long jump") and [triple jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_jump "Triple jump"), but he switched to running when he discovered his talent in distance running.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-CWG-2)

Cheptegei studied procurement and logistics management in Uganda and is employed by the [Uganda National Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_National_Police "Uganda National Police").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-8) His coach is Addy Ruiter. In the timeframe from March to May 2020, he reduced his weekly training sessions from 12 to 8.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-FAZ202008-9)

### 2015–2019: Career beginnings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joshua_Cheptegei&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2015–2019: Career beginnings")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5%2C000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps%2C_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_%2829090428856%29.jpg/330px-Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5%2C000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps%2C_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_%2829090428856%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5,000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps,_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_(29090428856).jpg)

Cheptegei (L in yellow) races the 5000 m at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), where he finished eighth.

Cheptegei competed in the 10,000 metres at the [2015 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), finishing ninth.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-Beijing2015-10) He ran at the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") in the 5000 metres and 10,000 metres, finishing eighth and sixth. respectively.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-Rio2016-5-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-Rio2016-10-12) He is a silver medallist in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") at the [2017 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics") in London.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-13) Cheptegei was the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and 10,000 metres champion at the [2018 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Commonwealth_Games "2018 Commonwealth Games").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-14)

Cheptegei is a four-time winner of the [Zevenheuvelenloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zevenheuvelenloop "Zevenheuvelenloop") 15 km road race in [Nijmegen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nijmegen "Nijmegen"), Netherlands. In 2018, he set the world record for a 15 km road race.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-15) Abrar Osman finished second with 42:34 and the 2017 5000 m world champion Muktar Edris placed third with 42:56.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-16) On 19 February 2022, the record was broken by Cheptegei's compatriot [Jacob Kiplimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo "Jacob Kiplimo"), who ran a 15 km split of 40:43 min at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-17)

Cheptegei was the winner of the senior men's race at the 2019 [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in [Aarhus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aarhus "Aarhus"), Denmark. He won in 31:40 on the 10.24 km course. Ugandan teammate Jacob Kiplimo finished second in 31:44, while Thomas Ayeko placed seventh and Joseph Ayeko tenth; Uganda won the team first-place title.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-18)

### 2019–2020: World records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joshua_Cheptegei&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2019–2020: World records")]

On 1 December 2019, Cheptegei set a new [10 km road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run") record in [Valencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia "Valencia"), Spain. His time of 26:38 improved on the previous world record, set by [Leonard Komon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Komon "Leonard Komon") in 2010, by 6 seconds.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-19) This mark has since been lowered to 26:24, the world record being held, as of October 2020, by [Rhonex Kipruto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhonex_Kipruto "Rhonex Kipruto") of Kenya, who also incidentally set it in Valencia just six weeks later, on 12 January 2020.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-20)

On 16 February 2020, he set a new [5 km road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5K_run "5K run") world record in [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco") with a time of 12:51. The previous ratified record was 13:22, set by Robert Keter on 9 November 2019 in [Lille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille "Lille"), France, and the previous fastest time ever recorded over the distance was 13:00 set by [Sammy Kipketer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kipketer "Sammy Kipketer") on 26 March 2000 in [Carlsbad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlsbad,_California "Carlsbad, California"), USA. This record stood for nearly two years until broken by [Berihu Aregawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berihu_Aregawi "Berihu Aregawi"), who ran 12:49 at the Cursa dels Nassos meet in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona") on 31 December 2021.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-21)

On 13 August 2020, a day before the [Herculis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculis "Herculis") meet of the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Diamond_League "2020 Diamond League") in Monaco, Cheptegei announced that he aimed to return to the track and run his first official race in the season with a world record time in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"), which would be more than 20 seconds faster than his personal best on a track.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-22) At the meet on the next day, with the help of expert pace-making from Roy Hoornweg, Stephen Kissa, and [Matthew Ramsden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Ramsden "Matthew Ramsden"), he set a [new world record in the 5000 metres with a time of 12:35.36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres_world_record_progression "5000 metres world record progression"), which broke [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s 16-year-old record—the longest duration in the history of the event—by almost 2 seconds.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-24) His splits were 2:31.87; 5:03.77; 7:35.14 and 10:05.46. Kenenisa congratulated Cheptegei from Addis Ababa.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-FAZ202008-9)

On 7 October 2020, in Valencia, he set a [world-record time of 26:11.00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres_world_record_progression "10,000 metres world record progression") in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"), which improved on [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s 15-year-old record by more than 6 seconds.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-25)

### 2021–present: Olympic medals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joshua_Cheptegei&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2021–present: Olympic medals")]

Cheptegei won gold in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and silver in the 10,000 metres at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-26)

At the [2022 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships"), Cheptegei won the 10,000 metres[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-27) and placed ninth in the 5000 metres.

At the [2023 World Athletics Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2023 World Athletics Cross Country Championships"), Cheptegei placed third to his countryman [Jacob Kiplimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo "Jacob Kiplimo") and Ethiopian [Berihu Aregawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berihu_Aregawi "Berihu Aregawi").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-28) Cheptegei successfully defended his 10,000 metres title at the [2023 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Championships "2023 World Athletics Championships").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-29) Later that year, he made his marathon debut at the [Valencia Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_Marathon "Valencia Marathon"), running 2:08:59 to place 37th.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-30)

At the [2024 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics") in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), Cheptegei won gold in the [10,000 metres final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres"), in a new [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") of 26:43.14.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-31) The former Olympic record was [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s 27:01.17 set at the [2008 Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-32) Shortly after winning gold in the 10000 meter event, Cheptegei announced on Instagram that he would not be defending his 5000-metre gold medal from Tokyo, citing failure to recover from the race.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-33) Cheptegei also hinted that he will not pursue another Olympic Games on the track, and instead focus more on road racing in the future.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-34) In September 2026, Cheptegei placed third in the half marathon at the [2026 World Athletics Road Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships "2026 World Athletics Road Running Championships") in Copenhagen, Demark, in a new personal best time of 58:26.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-35)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| [Field Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Marshal "Field Marshal") Dedan Kĩmathi Waciũri |
| --- |
| [![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Dedan_Kimathi_Waciuri_-_Veteran_Mau_Mau_Leader_in_Kenya.jpg/250px-Dedan_Kimathi_Waciuri_-_Veteran_Mau_Mau_Leader_in_Kenya.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dedan_Kimathi_Waciuri_-_Veteran_Mau_Mau_Leader_in_Kenya.jpg) |
| Born | Kĩmathi wa Waciũri 31 October 1920 [Nyeri District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyeri_District "Nyeri District"), [Central Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Province_(Kenya) "Central Province (Kenya)"), Kenya |
| Died | 18 February 1957 (aged 36) [Kamiti Maximum Security Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamiti_Maximum_Security_Prison "Kamiti Maximum Security Prison"), [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"), [British Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Kenya "British Kenya") |
| Cause of death | [Execution by hanging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_by_hanging "Execution by hanging") |
| Resting place | [Kamiti Maximum Security Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamiti_Maximum_Security_Prison "Kamiti Maximum Security Prison") (Alleged) |
| Occupations | Teacher, soldier |
| Organization | [Kenya Land and Freedom Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Land_and_Freedom_Army "Kenya Land and Freedom Army") |
| Known for | Leader of the [Kenya Land and Freedom Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Land_and_Freedom_Army "Kenya Land and Freedom Army") |
| Spouse | Mũkami Kĩmathi |

**Dedan Kĩmathi Waciũri** (born Kĩmathi Waciũri; 31 October 1920 – 18 February 1957) was the leader of the [Kenya Land and Freedom Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Land_and_Freedom_Army "Kenya Land and Freedom Army") during the [Mau Mau Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_Uprising "Mau Mau Uprising") (1952–1960) against the British colonial rule in Kenya in the 1950s. He was captured by the British in 1956 and executed in 1957. Kenya gained independence in 1963.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-KM-1) Kĩmathi is credited with leading efforts to create formal military structures within the Mau Mau, and convening a war council in 1953. He, along with Baimungi M'marete, [Musa Mwariama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_Mwariama "Musa Mwariama"), [Kubu Kubu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kubu_Kubu "Kubu Kubu"), [General China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waruhiu_Itote "Waruhiu Itote") and [Mũthoni Kīrīma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muthoni_Kirima "Muthoni Kirima"), was one of the Field Marshals.

Kenyan nationalists view him as a freedom fighter in the Kenyan struggle for independence, while the British colonial authorities labelled Kĩmathi as a terrorist, and according to historian David Anderson "did all they could to besmirch his reputation."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-3) Despite being viewed negatively by Kenya's first two presidents, [Jomo Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomo_Kenyatta "Jomo Kenyatta") and [Daniel arap Moi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_arap_Moi "Daniel arap Moi"), Kĩmathi and his fellow Mau Mau rebels were officially recognised as heroes in the struggle for Kenyan independence under the [Mwai Kibaki administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwai_Kibaki "Mwai Kibaki"), culminating in the unveiling of a Kĩmathi statue in 2007.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-4) This was reinforced by the passage of a new Constitution in 2010 calling for recognition of national heroes.

Kimathi belonged to the Ambu Clan, one of the nine clans that make the Kikuyu, Kenyas largest ethnic group, which is concentrated mainly in the central part of the East African Country[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-5).

Kĩmathi was born on 31st October 1920 in Thege village near [Nyeri County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyeri_County "Nyeri County") in central Kenya, where his father, valuing education, sent him to school.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-6) He entered elementary school at the age of fifteen and went to join the church of Scotland mission secondary school in the region but later dropped out.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-7) Kĩmathi excelled and his skills in writing and speech were noted. Anderson writes however that Kĩmathi was fiercely competitive, bullying, and frequently disciplined by teachers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2) Kĩmathi traveled to Nairobi in the late 1930s and joined the British army in 1940 but, according to Anderson, was discharged after one month, allegedly for drunkenness and violence.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2) He moved from job to job, from swineherd to primary school teacher, from which he was reportedly dismissed after accusations of violence against his pupils.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2)

Around 1947 or 1948, while working in [Ol Kalou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ol_Kalou "Ol Kalou"), Kĩmathi came into contact with members of the [Kenya African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_African_Union "Kenya African Union") (KAU). By 1950 he had become secretary to the KAU branch at Ol Kalou, which was controlled by militant supporters of the [Mau Mau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_uprising "Mau Mau uprising") cause.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2) The Mau Mau began as the [Kenya Land and Freedom Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Land_and_Freedom_Army "Kenya Land and Freedom Army") (KLFA), a militant [Kikuyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kikuyu_people "Kikuyu people"), [Embu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embu_people "Embu people") and [Meru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ameru_people "Ameru people") army which sought to reclaim land, which the British settlers had gradually stripped away from them. Later the term MAU MAU came to mean "Mzungu Arudi Ulaya, mwafrika apate uhuru" a swahili phrase which means - Let the foreigner go back to Europe so the African can gain independence.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-8) As the group's influence and membership widened it became a major threat to the colonial government.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Upon taking the [oath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oath "Oath") of the Mau Mau, Kĩmathi in 1951 joined the [Forty Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forty_Group "Forty Group"), the militant wing of the defunct [Kikuyu Central Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kikuyu_Central_Association "Kikuyu Central Association"). As branch secretary, Kĩmathi presided over oath-taking. He believed in compelling fellow Kikuyu by way of oath to bring solidarity to the independence movement. To achieve this he administered beatings and carried a double-barrelled shotgun.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.288-9) His activities with the group made him a target of the colonial government, and he was briefly arrested that same year but escaped with the help of local police. This marked the beginning of his involvement in the uprising, and he formed the Kenya Defence Council to co-ordinate all forest fighters in 1953.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Capture and execution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dedan_Kimathi&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Capture and execution")]

[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Museo_Nacional_de_Nairobi_11.jpg/250px-Museo_Nacional_de_Nairobi_11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Museo_Nacional_de_Nairobi_11.jpg)

Uniform worn by Dedan Kimathi when he was killed. Collection of the [National Museum of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museums_of_Kenya "National Museums of Kenya").

Kĩmathi's fight for an independent Kenya came to an end in 1956. On 21 October of that year, [Ian Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Henderson_(police_officer) "Ian Henderson (police officer)"), a British colonial police officer who had been on an "obsessive hunt" for Kĩmathi managed to trap him in his hide-out in the forest.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.288-9) Kĩmathi was shot in the leg and captured by a Tribal Policeman called Ndirangu Mau.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-10) His capture marked the beginning of the end of the forest war; the image of Kĩmathi being carried away on a stretcher was printed in leaflets by the British (over 120,000 were distributed), to demoralise the Mau Mau and their supporters.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-Ohio-11)

Kĩmathi was charged under the Emergency Regulations with unlawful possession of a .38 Webley Scott revolver and six rounds of ammunition.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-IH-obit-12)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-Ohio-11) He was tried before Chief Justice O’Connor with three African assessors. O’Connor found him guilty and sentenced him to death while he lay in a hospital bed at the General Hospital in Nyeri.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-Ohio-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-IH-obit-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-13) His appeal was dismissed, and the sentence was upheld.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-Ohio-11)

The day before his execution, Kimathi wrote a letter to a Father Marino asking him to get his son an education: "He is far from many of your schools, but I trust that something must be done to see that he starts earlier under your care." He also wrote about his wife, Mũkami saying "She is detained at Kamĩtĩ Prison and I suggest that she will be released some time. I would like her to be comforted by sisters e.g. Sister Modester, etc. for she too feels lonely. And if by any possibility she can be near the mission as near Mathari so that she may be so close to the sisters and to the church."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-14)

He asked to see his wife, and the morning of the execution Mũkami was allowed to see Kĩmathi. The two chatted for close to two hours. He told her that "I have no doubt in my mind that the British are determined to execute me. I have committed no crime. My only crime is that I am a Kenyan revolutionary who led a liberation army... Now If I must leave you and my family I have nothing to regret about. My blood will water the tree of Independence."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-15)

In the early morning of 18 February 1957 he was executed by British soldiers by [hanging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging "Hanging") at the [Kamĩtĩ Maximum Security Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamiti_Maximum_Security_Prison "Kamiti Maximum Security Prison").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-16) He was buried in an [unmarked grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unmarked_grave "Unmarked grave"), and his burial site remained unknown for 62 years until 25 October 2019 when the Dedan Kĩmathi Foundation[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-17) reported that the grave-site had been identified at the Kamĩtĩ Prison grounds.

Kĩmathi was married to Mũkami Kĩmathi.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-18) The government constructed a three-bedroomed house for Mukami at her farm in [Kinangop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinangop_Constituency "Kinangop Constituency"), [Nyandarua County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyandarua_County "Nyandarua County") in 2009 and provided her with a double cabin pickup for private use in 2012.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-20) In 2010, Kĩmathi's widow requested that the search for her husband's body be renewed so she could give him a proper burial.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-21) Mũkami Kĩmathi died on 4 May 2023 at the age of 96 and was buried in Njabini Kinangop.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-22)

### Official registration of the Mau Mau

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dedan_Kimathi&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Official registration of the Mau Mau")]

On 11 November 2003, the Kibaki government formally registered the Mau Mau movement, disregarding the colonial-era legislation that had outlawed the organisation and branded its members "terrorists". In his remarks during the handing over of the certificate, Vice President [Moody Awori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Awori "Moody Awori") regretted that it had taken 40 years for the group to be officially registered despite the sacrifices the Mau Mau had made for Kenya's independence.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-23)

### The Dedan Kimathi statue

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dedan_Kimathi&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: The Dedan Kimathi statue")]

[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Nairobi%2C_Kenya_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Nairobi%2C_Kenya_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Nairobi,_Kenya_(cropped).jpg)

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Lascar_Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Waciuri_%284540820430%29.jpg/250px-Lascar_Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Waciuri_%284540820430%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lascar_Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Waciuri_(4540820430).jpg)

Dedan Kimathi statue in Nairobi

The Kibaki government erected a 2.1 metre bronze statue titled Freedom Fighter Dedan Kimathi on a graphite plinth, in central [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"). The statue is at the junction of Kimathi Street and Mama Ngina Street. Kimathi, clad in military regalia, holds a rifle in the right hand and a dagger in the left, the last weapons he held in his struggle. The foundation stone for the statue was laid by Vice President Awori on 11 December 2006[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-24) and the completed statue unveiled by President Kibaki on 18 February 2007 coinciding with the 50th anniversary of the day he was executed. In his remarks, Kibaki paid homage to Kimathi as a man who not only paid the ultimate price for Kenya's liberation but also inspired others to fight against oppression.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-25)

The statue attracted praise from Kenyans as a long overdue recognition of the Mau Mau for their part in the struggle for independence. This was in marked contrast to the post-colonial norm of the [Jomo Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomo_Kenyatta "Jomo Kenyatta") and [Daniel Arap Moi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Arap_Moi "Daniel Arap Moi") governments' regard of the Mau Mau as terrorists.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-26)

On 12 September 2015, the British government unveiled a Mau Mau memorial statue in Nairobi's [Uhuru Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uhuru_Park "Uhuru Park") that it funded "as a symbol of reconciliation between the British government, the Mau Mau, and all those who suffered". This followed a June 2013 decision by Britain to compensate more than 5,000 Kenyans tortured and abused during the Mau Mau insurgency.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-27)

Kĩmathi was held in high regard by [anti-apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_resistance_to_apartheid "Internal resistance to apartheid") leader [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela"). In July 1990, five months after his release from 27 years of imprisonment by South Africa's apartheid regime, Mandela visited Nairobi and requested to see Kimathi's grave and meet his widow Mũkami. Mandela's request was an embarrassing moment for the Moi administration, which had largely ignored Kĩmathi like Jomo Kenyatta's government before it. It was an awkward moment searching for her in the village where she and her family lived forgotten in poverty. Mandela's request was not met. During a public address at the [Kasarani Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasarani_Stadium "Kasarani Stadium") in Nairobi before he left the country, Mandela stated his admiration for Kimathi, [Musa Mwariama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_Mwariama "Musa Mwariama"), [Waruhiu Itote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waruhiu_Itote "Waruhiu Itote"), [Kubu Kubu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kubu_Kubu "Kubu Kubu") and other Mau Mau leaders who inspired his own struggle against injustice. It was only 15 years later in 2005, during his second visit to Kenya, that Mandela finally managed to meet Mukami as well as two of Kimathi's children.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-newafricanmagazine.com-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-29)

Mandela's respect for Kimathi by the early 1960s is also alluded to in _My Moment with a Legend_ by [Ronnie Kasrils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Kasrils "Ronnie Kasrils"), the former intelligence chief of the ANC's armed wing [Umkhonto We Sizwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UMkhonto_weSizwe "UMkhonto weSizwe") (MK) and defence minister in Mandela's government.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-newafricanmagazine.com-28)

### Places named after Kĩmathi

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dedan_Kimathi&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Places named after Kĩmathi")]

*   Dedan Kĩmathi University of Technology (Nyeri Country)
*   Dedan Kĩmathi Stadium, Nyeri, Kenya (formerly known as Kamukunji Grounds)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-30)
*   Kĩmathi Street, Nairobi, Kenya – One of the main roads in Nairobi's Central Business District and where there is a statue in his honor
*   Dedan Kĩmathii Road, [Lusaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusaka "Lusaka"), Zambia - Situated on this road is the Intercity Bus Terminus and ZCAS University.

| Born | Kĩmathi wa Waciũri 31 October 1920 [Nyeri District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyeri_District "Nyeri District"), [Central Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Province_(Kenya) "Central Province (Kenya)"), Kenya |
| Died | 18 February 1957 (aged 36) [Kamiti Maximum Security Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamiti_Maximum_Security_Prison "Kamiti Maximum Security Prison"), [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"), [British Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Kenya "British Kenya") |
| Cause of death | [Execution by hanging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Execution_by_hanging "Execution by hanging") |
| Resting place | [Kamiti Maximum Security Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamiti_Maximum_Security_Prison "Kamiti Maximum Security Prison") (Alleged) |
| Occupations | Teacher, soldier |
| Organization | [Kenya Land and Freedom Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Land_and_Freedom_Army "Kenya Land and Freedom Army") |

| Spouse | Mũkami Kĩmathi |

**Dedan Kĩmathi Waciũri** (born Kĩmathi Waciũri; 31 October 1920 – 18 February 1957) was the leader of the [Kenya Land and Freedom Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Land_and_Freedom_Army "Kenya Land and Freedom Army") during the [Mau Mau Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_Uprising "Mau Mau Uprising") (1952–1960) against the British colonial rule in Kenya in the 1950s. He was captured by the British in 1956 and executed in 1957. Kenya gained independence in 1963.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-KM-1) Kĩmathi is credited with leading efforts to create formal military structures within the Mau Mau, and convening a war council in 1953. He, along with Baimungi M'marete, [Musa Mwariama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_Mwariama "Musa Mwariama"), [Kubu Kubu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kubu_Kubu "Kubu Kubu"), [General China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waruhiu_Itote "Waruhiu Itote") and [Mũthoni Kīrīma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muthoni_Kirima "Muthoni Kirima"), was one of the Field Marshals.

Kenyan nationalists view him as a freedom fighter in the Kenyan struggle for independence, while the British colonial authorities labelled Kĩmathi as a terrorist, and according to historian David Anderson "did all they could to besmirch his reputation."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-3) Despite being viewed negatively by Kenya's first two presidents, [Jomo Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomo_Kenyatta "Jomo Kenyatta") and [Daniel arap Moi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_arap_Moi "Daniel arap Moi"), Kĩmathi and his fellow Mau Mau rebels were officially recognised as heroes in the struggle for Kenyan independence under the [Mwai Kibaki administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwai_Kibaki "Mwai Kibaki"), culminating in the unveiling of a Kĩmathi statue in 2007.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-4) This was reinforced by the passage of a new Constitution in 2010 calling for recognition of national heroes.

Kimathi belonged to the Ambu Clan, one of the nine clans that make the Kikuyu, Kenyas largest ethnic group, which is concentrated mainly in the central part of the East African Country[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-5).

Kĩmathi was born on 31st October 1920 in Thege village near [Nyeri County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyeri_County "Nyeri County") in central Kenya, where his father, valuing education, sent him to school.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-6) He entered elementary school at the age of fifteen and went to join the church of Scotland mission secondary school in the region but later dropped out.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-7) Kĩmathi excelled and his skills in writing and speech were noted. Anderson writes however that Kĩmathi was fiercely competitive, bullying, and frequently disciplined by teachers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2) Kĩmathi traveled to Nairobi in the late 1930s and joined the British army in 1940 but, according to Anderson, was discharged after one month, allegedly for drunkenness and violence.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2) He moved from job to job, from swineherd to primary school teacher, from which he was reportedly dismissed after accusations of violence against his pupils.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2)

Around 1947 or 1948, while working in [Ol Kalou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ol_Kalou "Ol Kalou"), Kĩmathi came into contact with members of the [Kenya African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_African_Union "Kenya African Union") (KAU). By 1950 he had become secretary to the KAU branch at Ol Kalou, which was controlled by militant supporters of the [Mau Mau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_uprising "Mau Mau uprising") cause.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2) The Mau Mau began as the [Kenya Land and Freedom Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Land_and_Freedom_Army "Kenya Land and Freedom Army") (KLFA), a militant [Kikuyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kikuyu_people "Kikuyu people"), [Embu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embu_people "Embu people") and [Meru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ameru_people "Ameru people") army which sought to reclaim land, which the British settlers had gradually stripped away from them. Later the term MAU MAU came to mean "Mzungu Arudi Ulaya, mwafrika apate uhuru" a swahili phrase which means - Let the foreigner go back to Europe so the African can gain independence.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-8) As the group's influence and membership widened it became a major threat to the colonial government.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Upon taking the [oath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oath "Oath") of the Mau Mau, Kĩmathi in 1951 joined the [Forty Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forty_Group "Forty Group"), the militant wing of the defunct [Kikuyu Central Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kikuyu_Central_Association "Kikuyu Central Association"). As branch secretary, Kĩmathi presided over oath-taking. He believed in compelling fellow Kikuyu by way of oath to bring solidarity to the independence movement. To achieve this he administered beatings and carried a double-barrelled shotgun.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.288-9) His activities with the group made him a target of the colonial government, and he was briefly arrested that same year but escaped with the help of local police. This marked the beginning of his involvement in the uprising, and he formed the Kenya Defence Council to co-ordinate all forest fighters in 1953.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Capture and execution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dedan_Kimathi&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Capture and execution")]

[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Museo_Nacional_de_Nairobi_11.jpg/250px-Museo_Nacional_de_Nairobi_11.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Museo_Nacional_de_Nairobi_11.jpg)

Uniform worn by Dedan Kimathi when he was killed. Collection of the [National Museum of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museums_of_Kenya "National Museums of Kenya").

Kĩmathi's fight for an independent Kenya came to an end in 1956. On 21 October of that year, [Ian Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Henderson_(police_officer) "Ian Henderson (police officer)"), a British colonial police officer who had been on an "obsessive hunt" for Kĩmathi managed to trap him in his hide-out in the forest.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.288-9) Kĩmathi was shot in the leg and captured by a Tribal Policeman called Ndirangu Mau.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-10) His capture marked the beginning of the end of the forest war; the image of Kĩmathi being carried away on a stretcher was printed in leaflets by the British (over 120,000 were distributed), to demoralise the Mau Mau and their supporters.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-Ohio-11)

Kĩmathi was charged under the Emergency Regulations with unlawful possession of a .38 Webley Scott revolver and six rounds of ammunition.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-IH-obit-12)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-Ohio-11) He was tried before Chief Justice O’Connor with three African assessors. O’Connor found him guilty and sentenced him to death while he lay in a hospital bed at the General Hospital in Nyeri.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-Ohio-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-IH-obit-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-13) His appeal was dismissed, and the sentence was upheld.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-Ohio-11)

The day before his execution, Kimathi wrote a letter to a Father Marino asking him to get his son an education: "He is far from many of your schools, but I trust that something must be done to see that he starts earlier under your care." He also wrote about his wife, Mũkami saying "She is detained at Kamĩtĩ Prison and I suggest that she will be released some time. I would like her to be comforted by sisters e.g. Sister Modester, etc. for she too feels lonely. And if by any possibility she can be near the mission as near Mathari so that she may be so close to the sisters and to the church."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-14)

He asked to see his wife, and the morning of the execution Mũkami was allowed to see Kĩmathi. The two chatted for close to two hours. He told her that "I have no doubt in my mind that the British are determined to execute me. I have committed no crime. My only crime is that I am a Kenyan revolutionary who led a liberation army... Now If I must leave you and my family I have nothing to regret about. My blood will water the tree of Independence."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-15)

In the early morning of 18 February 1957 he was executed by British soldiers by [hanging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging "Hanging") at the [Kamĩtĩ Maximum Security Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamiti_Maximum_Security_Prison "Kamiti Maximum Security Prison").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-16) He was buried in an [unmarked grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unmarked_grave "Unmarked grave"), and his burial site remained unknown for 62 years until 25 October 2019 when the Dedan Kĩmathi Foundation[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-17) reported that the grave-site had been identified at the Kamĩtĩ Prison grounds.

Kĩmathi was married to Mũkami Kĩmathi.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-18) The government constructed a three-bedroomed house for Mukami at her farm in [Kinangop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinangop_Constituency "Kinangop Constituency"), [Nyandarua County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyandarua_County "Nyandarua County") in 2009 and provided her with a double cabin pickup for private use in 2012.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-20) In 2010, Kĩmathi's widow requested that the search for her husband's body be renewed so she could give him a proper burial.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-21) Mũkami Kĩmathi died on 4 May 2023 at the age of 96 and was buried in Njabini Kinangop.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-22)

### Official registration of the Mau Mau

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dedan_Kimathi&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Official registration of the Mau Mau")]

On 11 November 2003, the Kibaki government formally registered the Mau Mau movement, disregarding the colonial-era legislation that had outlawed the organisation and branded its members "terrorists". In his remarks during the handing over of the certificate, Vice President [Moody Awori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moody_Awori "Moody Awori") regretted that it had taken 40 years for the group to be officially registered despite the sacrifices the Mau Mau had made for Kenya's independence.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-23)

### The Dedan Kimathi statue

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dedan_Kimathi&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: The Dedan Kimathi statue")]

[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Nairobi%2C_Kenya_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Nairobi%2C_Kenya_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Nairobi,_Kenya_(cropped).jpg)

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Lascar_Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Waciuri_%284540820430%29.jpg/250px-Lascar_Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Waciuri_%284540820430%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lascar_Statue_of_Dedan_Kimathi_Waciuri_(4540820430).jpg)

Dedan Kimathi statue in Nairobi

The Kibaki government erected a 2.1 metre bronze statue titled Freedom Fighter Dedan Kimathi on a graphite plinth, in central [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"). The statue is at the junction of Kimathi Street and Mama Ngina Street. Kimathi, clad in military regalia, holds a rifle in the right hand and a dagger in the left, the last weapons he held in his struggle. The foundation stone for the statue was laid by Vice President Awori on 11 December 2006[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-24) and the completed statue unveiled by President Kibaki on 18 February 2007 coinciding with the 50th anniversary of the day he was executed. In his remarks, Kibaki paid homage to Kimathi as a man who not only paid the ultimate price for Kenya's liberation but also inspired others to fight against oppression.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-25)

The statue attracted praise from Kenyans as a long overdue recognition of the Mau Mau for their part in the struggle for independence. This was in marked contrast to the post-colonial norm of the [Jomo Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomo_Kenyatta "Jomo Kenyatta") and [Daniel Arap Moi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Arap_Moi "Daniel Arap Moi") governments' regard of the Mau Mau as terrorists.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-26)

On 12 September 2015, the British government unveiled a Mau Mau memorial statue in Nairobi's [Uhuru Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uhuru_Park "Uhuru Park") that it funded "as a symbol of reconciliation between the British government, the Mau Mau, and all those who suffered". This followed a June 2013 decision by Britain to compensate more than 5,000 Kenyans tortured and abused during the Mau Mau insurgency.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-27)

Kĩmathi was held in high regard by [anti-apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_resistance_to_apartheid "Internal resistance to apartheid") leader [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela"). In July 1990, five months after his release from 27 years of imprisonment by South Africa's apartheid regime, Mandela visited Nairobi and requested to see Kimathi's grave and meet his widow Mũkami. Mandela's request was an embarrassing moment for the Moi administration, which had largely ignored Kĩmathi like Jomo Kenyatta's government before it. It was an awkward moment searching for her in the village where she and her family lived forgotten in poverty. Mandela's request was not met. During a public address at the [Kasarani Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasarani_Stadium "Kasarani Stadium") in Nairobi before he left the country, Mandela stated his admiration for Kimathi, [Musa Mwariama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_Mwariama "Musa Mwariama"), [Waruhiu Itote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waruhiu_Itote "Waruhiu Itote"), [Kubu Kubu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kubu_Kubu "Kubu Kubu") and other Mau Mau leaders who inspired his own struggle against injustice. It was only 15 years later in 2005, during his second visit to Kenya, that Mandela finally managed to meet Mukami as well as two of Kimathi's children.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-newafricanmagazine.com-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-29)

**Dedan Kĩmathi Waciũri** (born Kĩmathi Waciũri; 31 October 1920 – 18 February 1957) was the leader of the [Kenya Land and Freedom Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Land_and_Freedom_Army "Kenya Land and Freedom Army") during the [Mau Mau Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_Uprising "Mau Mau Uprising") (1952–1960) against the British colonial rule in Kenya in the 1950s. He was captured by the British in 1956 and executed in 1957. Kenya gained independence in 1963.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-KM-1) Kĩmathi is credited with leading efforts to create formal military structures within the Mau Mau, and convening a war council in 1953. He, along with Baimungi M'marete, [Musa Mwariama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_Mwariama "Musa Mwariama"), [Kubu Kubu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kubu_Kubu "Kubu Kubu"), [General China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waruhiu_Itote "Waruhiu Itote") and [Mũthoni Kīrīma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muthoni_Kirima "Muthoni Kirima"), was one of the Field Marshals.

Kenyan nationalists view him as a freedom fighter in the Kenyan struggle for independence, while the British colonial authorities labelled Kĩmathi as a terrorist, and according to historian David Anderson "did all they could to besmirch his reputation."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-3) Despite being viewed negatively by Kenya's first two presidents, [Jomo Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomo_Kenyatta "Jomo Kenyatta") and [Daniel arap Moi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_arap_Moi "Daniel arap Moi"), Kĩmathi and his fellow Mau Mau rebels were officially recognised as heroes in the struggle for Kenyan independence under the [Mwai Kibaki administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwai_Kibaki "Mwai Kibaki"), culminating in the unveiling of a Kĩmathi statue in 2007.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-4) This was reinforced by the passage of a new Constitution in 2010 calling for recognition of national heroes.

Kimathi belonged to the Ambu Clan, one of the nine clans that make the Kikuyu, Kenyas largest ethnic group, which is concentrated mainly in the central part of the East African Country[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-5).

Kĩmathi was born on 31st October 1920 in Thege village near [Nyeri County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyeri_County "Nyeri County") in central Kenya, where his father, valuing education, sent him to school.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-6) He entered elementary school at the age of fifteen and went to join the church of Scotland mission secondary school in the region but later dropped out.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-7) Kĩmathi excelled and his skills in writing and speech were noted. Anderson writes however that Kĩmathi was fiercely competitive, bullying, and frequently disciplined by teachers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2) Kĩmathi traveled to Nairobi in the late 1930s and joined the British army in 1940 but, according to Anderson, was discharged after one month, allegedly for drunkenness and violence.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2) He moved from job to job, from swineherd to primary school teacher, from which he was reportedly dismissed after accusations of violence against his pupils.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2)

Around 1947 or 1948, while working in [Ol Kalou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ol_Kalou "Ol Kalou"), Kĩmathi came into contact with members of the [Kenya African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_African_Union "Kenya African Union") (KAU). By 1950 he had become secretary to the KAU branch at Ol Kalou, which was controlled by militant supporters of the [Mau Mau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mau_Mau_uprising "Mau Mau uprising") cause.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.287-2) The Mau Mau began as the [Kenya Land and Freedom Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Land_and_Freedom_Army "Kenya Land and Freedom Army") (KLFA), a militant [Kikuyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kikuyu_people "Kikuyu people"), [Embu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embu_people "Embu people") and [Meru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ameru_people "Ameru people") army which sought to reclaim land, which the British settlers had gradually stripped away from them. Later the term MAU MAU came to mean "Mzungu Arudi Ulaya, mwafrika apate uhuru" a swahili phrase which means - Let the foreigner go back to Europe so the African can gain independence.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-8) As the group's influence and membership widened it became a major threat to the colonial government.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Upon taking the [oath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oath "Oath") of the Mau Mau, Kĩmathi in 1951 joined the [Forty Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forty_Group "Forty Group"), the militant wing of the defunct [Kikuyu Central Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kikuyu_Central_Association "Kikuyu Central Association"). As branch secretary, Kĩmathi presided over oath-taking. He believed in compelling fellow Kikuyu by way of oath to bring solidarity to the independence movement. To achieve this he administered beatings and carried a double-barrelled shotgun.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-David_Anderson_2005_p.288-9) His activities with the group made him a target of the colonial government, and he was briefly arrested that same year but escaped with the help of local police. This marked the beginning of his involvement in the uprising, and he formed the Kenya Defence Council to co-ordinate all forest fighters in 1953.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The statue attracted praise from Kenyans as a long overdue recognition of the Mau Mau for their part in the struggle for independence. This was in marked contrast to the post-colonial norm of the [Jomo Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jomo_Kenyatta "Jomo Kenyatta") and [Daniel Arap Moi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Arap_Moi "Daniel Arap Moi") governments' regard of the Mau Mau as terrorists.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-26)

On 12 September 2015, the British government unveiled a Mau Mau memorial statue in Nairobi's [Uhuru Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uhuru_Park "Uhuru Park") that it funded "as a symbol of reconciliation between the British government, the Mau Mau, and all those who suffered". This followed a June 2013 decision by Britain to compensate more than 5,000 Kenyans tortured and abused during the Mau Mau insurgency.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-27)

Kĩmathi was held in high regard by [anti-apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_resistance_to_apartheid "Internal resistance to apartheid") leader [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela"). In July 1990, five months after his release from 27 years of imprisonment by South Africa's apartheid regime, Mandela visited Nairobi and requested to see Kimathi's grave and meet his widow Mũkami. Mandela's request was an embarrassing moment for the Moi administration, which had largely ignored Kĩmathi like Jomo Kenyatta's government before it. It was an awkward moment searching for her in the village where she and her family lived forgotten in poverty. Mandela's request was not met. During a public address at the [Kasarani Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasarani_Stadium "Kasarani Stadium") in Nairobi before he left the country, Mandela stated his admiration for Kimathi, [Musa Mwariama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musa_Mwariama "Musa Mwariama"), [Waruhiu Itote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waruhiu_Itote "Waruhiu Itote"), [Kubu Kubu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kubu_Kubu "Kubu Kubu") and other Mau Mau leaders who inspired his own struggle against injustice. It was only 15 years later in 2005, during his second visit to Kenya, that Mandela finally managed to meet Mukami as well as two of Kimathi's children.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-newafricanmagazine.com-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedan_Kimathi#cite_note-29)
