**Martha Karambu Koome** (born 3 June 1960) is a Kenyan advocate who is currently serving as the [chief justice of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_Kenya "Chief Justice of Kenya") and is the first woman to occupy the post.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martha_Koome&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Koome was born on 3 June 1960 in Kithiu village, [Meru District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meru_County "Meru County"), Kenya. She attended Our Lady Consolata Mugoiri Girls High School in [Murang'a County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murang'a_County "Murang'a County").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-4) She holds an LL.B. from the [University of Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi "University of Nairobi"), which she received in 1986. Koome enrolled at [Kenya School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_School_of_Law "Kenya School of Law") the following year. She completed her master's degree (LL.M) in public international law at the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") in 2010.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-5)

Koome began her legal career as a legal associate at Mathenge and Muchemi Advocates, and later started a law firm, working as a managing partner until 2003. She was elected as a council member of the [Law Society of Kenya (LSK)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_Society_of_Kenya "Law Society of Kenya") in 1993–1996.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-6)

During her tenure at the [Law Society of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_Society_of_Kenya "Law Society of Kenya"), she took a leading role in constitutional and legal reforms and was part of the constitutional review process as a delegate at the [Bomas of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomas_of_Kenya "Bomas of Kenya") where she partially chaired the thematic area on the Bill of Rights. Koome also served as the inaugural treasurer of the [East Africa Law Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa_Law_Society "East Africa Law Society") between 1994 and 1996. She has also served as chairperson of FIDA, one of the leading human rights organizations in the country.

Koome has distinguished herself as a defender of human and gender rights. She was one of the lawyers who actively participated in the clamor for the repeal of section 2A of the [Constitution of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Kenya "Constitution of Kenya") and for the independence of the judiciary. She is an acclaimed expert in [family law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_law "Family law") and she takes a keen interest in the welfare of children. She was a runner-up in the 2020 [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") person of the year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-7) In 1995 she was appointed by the [African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union "African Union") meeting of heads of states as a commissioner to the African Committee on the Rights and welfare of children. She has also served as the chairperson of the National Council on the Administration of Justice special taskforce on children matters where she helped steer the review of the Children's Act.

Koome was appointed Judge of the [Court of Appeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Appeal_of_Kenya "Court of Appeal of Kenya") in January 2012. Prior to her appointment to the Court of Appeal, she served as a judge of the [High Court of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_(Kenya) "High Court (Kenya)") for over eight years.

In the same year she was appointed as Court of Appeal judge, she was also elected the chairperson of the [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") Magistrates and Judges Association. In 2016 she was among 13 female candidates shortlisted by the Judicial Service Commission for the deputy chief justice position,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-8) which would later be occupied by [Justice Philomena Mwilu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philomena_Mwilu "Philomena Mwilu").

Koome was among 13 candidates who applied for appointment to replace [David Maraga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Maraga "David Maraga") when he retired in January 2021.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-9) She was shortlisted for the position, and attended her public interview on 14 April 2021. Koome is a renowned human rights and gender advocate. She participated in the campaign for the repeal of section 2A of the Kenyan constitution which converted Kenya into a multi-party state. This essential repeal introduced term limits on the presidency.

Koome is also a protector of women and children's rights. She was the African Union Commissioner to the African committee on the rights and welfare of children.[](https://nation.africa/kenya/people/martha-koome--3818198)

When the JSC invited memoranda on her suitability for nomination, the president of the [Law Society of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_Society_of_Kenya "Law Society of Kenya") submitted a complaint[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-lsk-10) accusing her of being an unfair arbiter, by ruling some specific court cases based on [nepotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotism "Nepotism"), favouritism and improper motive by ruling in favour of the executive arm of the Kenyan government for improper motive and sometimes based on ethnicity.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-lsk-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-13) Later, she instructed her lawyers to issue a demand to the LSK president to retract the law society's allegations against her within seven days, threatening to sue him over defamation arising from the complaints he submitted to the JSC.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-14) In May 2021, the president of the LSK, Nelson Havi, told off Koome and demanded she be transparent and accountable for her actions in the mentioned memoranda, by vowing not to apologize for the evidence-backed memoranda.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-15)

[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Martha_Koome.jpg/250px-Martha_Koome.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Martha_Koome.jpg)

Martha Koome at the Supreme Court of Kenya

Koome's suitability was also challenged by Khelef Khalifa who questioned the manner in which she took part in a Court of Appeal sitting that reversed a judgment of the High Court that had declared that all returning officers who had been retained by the IEBC to manage the repeat presidential election on 26 October 2017 had been unlawfully appointed.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-17) Once arguments in the case were concluded, the High Court scheduled the judgment for delivery on 25 October 2017, the eve of the repeat presidential election. On the eve of this judgment, the government declared 25 October a public holiday, meaning courts would not be operational and judges would not be in a position to render any judgments. Chief Justice David Maraga issued special authority to the Judicial Review Division of the High Court in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") to sit during the public holiday so that the judges could dispense with the scheduled judgment. No such authority was given for the Court of Appeal, whose registries remained closed. Once the High Court delivered the judgment holding that the returning officers were in office illegally, the IEBC somehow managed to file an appeal at the Court of Appeal which was closed due to the public holiday, and Koome appeared alongside two other judges of the Court of Appeal to handle the matter. All three judges were not serving in the Court of Appeal in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") at the time, and the chief justice had not given authority for the court to sit on a public holiday. The three judges had ostensibly been called to sit by the then president of the Court of Appeal, Justice [Paul Kihara Kariuki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kihara_Kariuki "Paul Kihara Kariuki").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-18) The judges stayed the High Court Judgment, thereby giving the IEBC the green light to run the repeat presidential poll the following day.

When questioned about her role in this case during the interviews, she indicated that she had to comply with the directives of the president of the Court of Appeal who summoned her to sit, and that the sitting was important because it saved the country from a constitutional crisis,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-19) alluding to the apparent lack of a provision in Kenya's laws for the extension of the term of the president where a repeat presidential election is not held within 60 days as demanded by the Constitution.

At the conclusion of the interviews, the JSC announced her nomination for the position, setting her up to be the 1st female, 15th chief justice, and the third chief justice after the [2010 constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Kenya "Constitution of Kenya").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-20)

Her name was subsequently transmitted to the president, who sent it to Parliament[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-21) for vetting and approval before her formal appointment. The Justice & Legal Affairs Committee of the National Assembly conducted her vetting hearing on 13 May[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-22) and recommended that the full house should approve her nomination.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-23) The report of the committee was tabled before the full house on 19 May for discussion. The full house voted to approve her nomination on 19 May 2021[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-24) paving the way for her appointment as the chief justice.

Within hours of Parliament's approval vote, President [Uhuru Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uhuru_Kenyatta "Uhuru Kenyatta") appointed her on 19 May 2021, as the chief justice of the Republic of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-25) She took her oath of office at State House, [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"), on 21 May 2021.

She assumed office on Monday, 24 May 2021, in an Assumption of Office ceremony at the Supreme Court Building during which Deputy Chief Justice [Philomena Mwilu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philomena_Mwilu "Philomena Mwilu") handed over the instruments of power to the new chief justice.

On Monday 5 February 2024, Hon. Martha Koome presided over the launch and commissioning of the Nairobi Land Justice Working Group which is tasked with Expediting Land Justice through a People Centered Approach.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-28)

Koome is married to Koome Kiragu and has three children.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-29)

**Martha Karambu Koome** (born 3 June 1960) is a Kenyan advocate who is currently serving as the [chief justice of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_Kenya "Chief Justice of Kenya") and is the first woman to occupy the post.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Martha_Koome&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Koome was born on 3 June 1960 in Kithiu village, [Meru District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meru_County "Meru County"), Kenya. She attended Our Lady Consolata Mugoiri Girls High School in [Murang'a County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murang'a_County "Murang'a County").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-4) She holds an LL.B. from the [University of Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi "University of Nairobi"), which she received in 1986. Koome enrolled at [Kenya School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_School_of_Law "Kenya School of Law") the following year. She completed her master's degree (LL.M) in public international law at the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") in 2010.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-5)

Koome began her legal career as a legal associate at Mathenge and Muchemi Advocates, and later started a law firm, working as a managing partner until 2003. She was elected as a council member of the [Law Society of Kenya (LSK)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_Society_of_Kenya "Law Society of Kenya") in 1993–1996.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-6)

During her tenure at the [Law Society of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_Society_of_Kenya "Law Society of Kenya"), she took a leading role in constitutional and legal reforms and was part of the constitutional review process as a delegate at the [Bomas of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomas_of_Kenya "Bomas of Kenya") where she partially chaired the thematic area on the Bill of Rights. Koome also served as the inaugural treasurer of the [East Africa Law Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa_Law_Society "East Africa Law Society") between 1994 and 1996. She has also served as chairperson of FIDA, one of the leading human rights organizations in the country.

Koome has distinguished herself as a defender of human and gender rights. She was one of the lawyers who actively participated in the clamor for the repeal of section 2A of the [Constitution of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Kenya "Constitution of Kenya") and for the independence of the judiciary. She is an acclaimed expert in [family law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_law "Family law") and she takes a keen interest in the welfare of children. She was a runner-up in the 2020 [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") person of the year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-7) In 1995 she was appointed by the [African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union "African Union") meeting of heads of states as a commissioner to the African Committee on the Rights and welfare of children. She has also served as the chairperson of the National Council on the Administration of Justice special taskforce on children matters where she helped steer the review of the Children's Act.

Koome was appointed Judge of the [Court of Appeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Appeal_of_Kenya "Court of Appeal of Kenya") in January 2012. Prior to her appointment to the Court of Appeal, she served as a judge of the [High Court of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_(Kenya) "High Court (Kenya)") for over eight years.

In the same year she was appointed as Court of Appeal judge, she was also elected the chairperson of the [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") Magistrates and Judges Association. In 2016 she was among 13 female candidates shortlisted by the Judicial Service Commission for the deputy chief justice position,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-8) which would later be occupied by [Justice Philomena Mwilu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philomena_Mwilu "Philomena Mwilu").

Koome was among 13 candidates who applied for appointment to replace [David Maraga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Maraga "David Maraga") when he retired in January 2021.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-9) She was shortlisted for the position, and attended her public interview on 14 April 2021. Koome is a renowned human rights and gender advocate. She participated in the campaign for the repeal of section 2A of the Kenyan constitution which converted Kenya into a multi-party state. This essential repeal introduced term limits on the presidency.

Koome is also a protector of women and children's rights. She was the African Union Commissioner to the African committee on the rights and welfare of children.[](https://nation.africa/kenya/people/martha-koome--3818198)

When the JSC invited memoranda on her suitability for nomination, the president of the [Law Society of Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_Society_of_Kenya "Law Society of Kenya") submitted a complaint[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-lsk-10) accusing her of being an unfair arbiter, by ruling some specific court cases based on [nepotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotism "Nepotism"), favouritism and improper motive by ruling in favour of the executive arm of the Kenyan government for improper motive and sometimes based on ethnicity.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-lsk-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-13) Later, she instructed her lawyers to issue a demand to the LSK president to retract the law society's allegations against her within seven days, threatening to sue him over defamation arising from the complaints he submitted to the JSC.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-14) In May 2021, the president of the LSK, Nelson Havi, told off Koome and demanded she be transparent and accountable for her actions in the mentioned memoranda, by vowing not to apologize for the evidence-backed memoranda.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-15)

[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/Martha_Koome.jpg/250px-Martha_Koome.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Martha_Koome.jpg)

Martha Koome at the Supreme Court of Kenya

Koome's suitability was also challenged by Khelef Khalifa who questioned the manner in which she took part in a Court of Appeal sitting that reversed a judgment of the High Court that had declared that all returning officers who had been retained by the IEBC to manage the repeat presidential election on 26 October 2017 had been unlawfully appointed.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-17) Once arguments in the case were concluded, the High Court scheduled the judgment for delivery on 25 October 2017, the eve of the repeat presidential election. On the eve of this judgment, the government declared 25 October a public holiday, meaning courts would not be operational and judges would not be in a position to render any judgments. Chief Justice David Maraga issued special authority to the Judicial Review Division of the High Court in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") to sit during the public holiday so that the judges could dispense with the scheduled judgment. No such authority was given for the Court of Appeal, whose registries remained closed. Once the High Court delivered the judgment holding that the returning officers were in office illegally, the IEBC somehow managed to file an appeal at the Court of Appeal which was closed due to the public holiday, and Koome appeared alongside two other judges of the Court of Appeal to handle the matter. All three judges were not serving in the Court of Appeal in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") at the time, and the chief justice had not given authority for the court to sit on a public holiday. The three judges had ostensibly been called to sit by the then president of the Court of Appeal, Justice [Paul Kihara Kariuki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Kihara_Kariuki "Paul Kihara Kariuki").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-18) The judges stayed the High Court Judgment, thereby giving the IEBC the green light to run the repeat presidential poll the following day.

When questioned about her role in this case during the interviews, she indicated that she had to comply with the directives of the president of the Court of Appeal who summoned her to sit, and that the sitting was important because it saved the country from a constitutional crisis,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-19) alluding to the apparent lack of a provision in Kenya's laws for the extension of the term of the president where a repeat presidential election is not held within 60 days as demanded by the Constitution.

At the conclusion of the interviews, the JSC announced her nomination for the position, setting her up to be the 1st female, 15th chief justice, and the third chief justice after the [2010 constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Kenya "Constitution of Kenya").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-20)

Her name was subsequently transmitted to the president, who sent it to Parliament[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-21) for vetting and approval before her formal appointment. The Justice & Legal Affairs Committee of the National Assembly conducted her vetting hearing on 13 May[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-22) and recommended that the full house should approve her nomination.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-23) The report of the committee was tabled before the full house on 19 May for discussion. The full house voted to approve her nomination on 19 May 2021[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-24) paving the way for her appointment as the chief justice.

Within hours of Parliament's approval vote, President [Uhuru Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uhuru_Kenyatta "Uhuru Kenyatta") appointed her on 19 May 2021, as the chief justice of the Republic of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-25) She took her oath of office at State House, [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi"), on 21 May 2021.

She assumed office on Monday, 24 May 2021, in an Assumption of Office ceremony at the Supreme Court Building during which Deputy Chief Justice [Philomena Mwilu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philomena_Mwilu "Philomena Mwilu") handed over the instruments of power to the new chief justice.

On Monday 5 February 2024, Hon. Martha Koome presided over the launch and commissioning of the Nairobi Land Justice Working Group which is tasked with Expediting Land Justice through a People Centered Approach.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-28)

Koome is married to Koome Kiragu and has three children.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Koome#cite_note-29)

The **10,000 metres** or the **10,000-metre run** is a common [long-distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running") track running event. The event is part of the [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_(sport) "Athletics (sport)") programme at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") and the [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships"), and is common at championship-level events. The race consists of 25 laps around an Olympic-sized 400 m track. It is less commonly held at track and field meetings due to its duration. The 10,000-metre track race is usually distinguished from its [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") counterpart, the [10K run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run"), by referring to the distance in metres rather than kilometres.

The 10,000 metres is the longest standard track event, approximately equivalent to 6 miles 376 yards or 32,808 feet 5 inches.

[![Image 88](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9d/Taisto_M%C3%A4ki_sets_10%2C000_m_world_record.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taisto_M%C3%A4ki_sets_10,000_m_world_record.jpeg)

[Taisto Mäki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taisto_M%C3%A4ki "Taisto Mäki") from [Finland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland "Finland") breaks the 30-minute barrier in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki") on 17 September 1939.

Added to the Olympic programme in 1912, athletes from Finland, nicknamed the "[Flying Finns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_Finn "Flying Finn")", dominated the event until the late 1940s. In the 1960s, African runners began to come to the fore.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres#cite_note-1) In 1988, the women's competition debuted in the Olympic Games.

Official records are kept for outdoor 10,000-metre track events. The world record for men is held by [Joshua Cheptegei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei "Joshua Cheptegei") of [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") in 26:11.00, set in [Valencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia "Valencia"), Spain on 7 October 2020. For women, the world record is held by [Beatrice Chebet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_Chebet "Beatrice Chebet") of [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), in 28:54.14, set in Eugene, Oregon, on 25 May 2024.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres#cite_note-2)

The 10,000 metres demands exceptional levels of aerobic endurance, and elite athletes typically train in excess of 160 km (100 miles) a week.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres#cite_note-3)

## 6 miles

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=10,000_metres&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: 6 miles")]

10,000 metres is the slightly longer metric derivative of the 6-mile (9,656.1-metre) run, an event common in countries when they were using the [imperial measurement system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_units "Imperial units"). 6 miles was used in the [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the Commonwealth Games") until 1966 and was a [championship in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_Outdoor_Track_and_Field_Championships "USA Outdoor Track and Field Championships") in non-Olympic years from 1953 to 1973. It is 24 laps around a 1⁄4-mile (402 m; 440 yd; 1,320 ft) track.

**Uganda**,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-13) officially the **Republic of Uganda**,[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-14) is a [landlocked country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landlocked_country "Landlocked country") in [East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa "East Africa"). It is bordered to the east by [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), to the north by [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan"), to the west by the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), to the south-west by [Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda"), and to the south by [Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania"). The southern part includes a substantial portion of [Lake Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria "Lake Victoria"), shared with Kenya and Tanzania. Uganda is in the [African Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Great_Lakes "African Great Lakes") region, lies within the [Nile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile "Nile") basin, and has a varied [equatorial climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equatorial_climate "Equatorial climate"). As of 2024, it had a population of 45.9 million, of whom 1.8 million live in the capital and largest city, [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-census24-9)

Uganda is named after the [Buganda kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buganda "Buganda"), which encompasses a large portion of the south, including Kampala, and whose language [Luganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luganda "Luganda") is widely spoken; the official language is English, while [Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili "Swahili") is the second official language. The region was populated by people of various ethnicities before Bantu and Nilotic groups arrived around 3,000 years ago. These new inhabitants established influential kingdoms such as the [Empire of Kitara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Kitara "Empire of Kitara"). The arrival of [Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs") traders in the 1830s and British explorers in the late 19th century marked the beginning of foreign influence. The British established the [Protectorate of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda "Protectorate of Uganda") in 1894, setting the stage for future political dynamics.

Uganda gained independence in 1962, with [Milton Obote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Obote "Milton Obote") as the first prime minister. The 1966 [Mengo Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mengo_Crisis "Mengo Crisis") marked a significant conflict with the Buganda kingdom, as well as the country's conversion from a [parliamentary system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_system "Parliamentary system") to a [presidential system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_system "Presidential system"). Obote was overthrown in a [military coup in 1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Ugandan_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1971 Ugandan coup d'état") by [Idi Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idi_Amin "Idi Amin"), who subsequently ruled the country under a brutal dictatorship until he was overthrown in 1979 during the [Uganda–Tanzania War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda%E2%80%93Tanzania_War "Uganda–Tanzania War").

Obote returned to power following the controversial [1980 Ugandan general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Ugandan_general_election "1980 Ugandan general election"), prompting a [six-year guerrilla war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugandan_Bush_War "Ugandan Bush War"), ending with the victory of [Yoweri Museveni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoweri_Museveni "Yoweri Museveni")'s [National Resistance Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Resistance_Movement "National Resistance Movement") in 1986. While Museveni's rule resulted in stability and economic growth, political oppression and human rights abuses continued. The abolition of presidential term limits as well as allegations of electoral fraud and repression have raised concerns about Uganda's democratic future. Museveni was elected president in the [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Ugandan_general_election "2011 Ugandan general election"), [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Ugandan_general_election "2016 Ugandan general election"), [2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Ugandan_general_election "2021 Ugandan general election"), and [2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Ugandan_general_election "2026 Ugandan general election") general elections. Human rights issues, corruption, and regional conflicts, such as involvement in the Congo Wars and the struggle against the [Lord's Resistance Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord's_Resistance_Army "Lord's Resistance Army") (LRA), continue to challenge Uganda. Despite this, it has made progress in education and health, improving literacy and reducing HIV infection, though challenges in maternal health and gender inequality persist.

Geographically, Uganda is diverse, with volcanic hills, mountains, and lakes, including [Lake Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria "Lake Victoria"), the world's second-largest freshwater lake. The country has significant natural resources, including fertile agricultural land and untapped [oil reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_reserve "Oil reserve"), contributing to its economic development. The service sector dominates the economy, surpassing agriculture. Uganda's rich [biodiversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity"), with national parks and wildlife reserves, attracts tourism, a vital sector for the economy. Uganda is a member of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"), the [Commonwealth of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations"), the [African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union "African Union"), [G77](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_77 "Group of 77"), the [East African Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Community "East African Community"), and the [Organisation of Islamic Cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_Islamic_Cooperation "Organisation of Islamic Cooperation").

## History

### Precolonial Uganda

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Drawing_showing_a_caesarean_operation_taking_place_in_Uganda_Wellcome_M0001058.jpg/250px-Drawing_showing_a_caesarean_operation_taking_place_in_Uganda_Wellcome_M0001058.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Drawing_showing_a_caesarean_operation_taking_place_in_Uganda_Wellcome_M0001058.jpg)

A [caesarean section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesarean_section "Caesarean section") performed by indigenous healers in Kahura, in the kingdom of [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-How_this_African_kingdom_performed_its_cesarean_section_in_1879-15) present-day Uganda, as observed by medical missionary [Robert William Felkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_William_Felkin "Robert William Felkin") in 1879[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-16)

Much of Uganda was inhabited by [Central Sudanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Sudanic_languages "Central Sudanic languages")- and [Kuliak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuliak_languages "Kuliak languages")-speaking farmers and herders until 3,000 years ago, when [Bantu speakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_languages "Bantu languages") arrived in the south and [Nilotic speakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilotic_languages "Nilotic languages") arrived in the northeast. By 1500 AD, they had all been assimilated into [Bantu-speaking cultures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_peoples "Bantu peoples") south of [Mount Elgon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Elgon "Mount Elgon"), the [Nile River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile_River "Nile River"), and [Lake Kyoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Kyoga "Lake Kyoga").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-17) According to [oral tradition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_tradition "Oral tradition") and archaeological studies, the [Empire of Kitara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Kitara "Empire of Kitara") covered an important part of the [Great Lakes Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_of_Africa "Great Lakes of Africa"), from the northern lakes [Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Albert_(Africa) "Lake Albert (Africa)") and Kyoga to the southern lakes [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria "Lake Victoria") and [Tanganyika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tanganyika "Lake Tanganyika").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-18) Kitara is claimed as the antecedent of the [Tooro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooro_Kingdom "Tooro Kingdom"), [Ankole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankole "Ankole"), and [Busoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busoga "Busoga") kingdoms.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Mwambutsya-19) Some [Luo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luo_people#Uganda "Luo people") invaded Kitara and assimilated with the Bantu society there, establishing the Biito dynasty of the current [Omukama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omukama_of_Bunyoro "Omukama of Bunyoro") (ruler) of [Bunyoro-Kitara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-babito-20)

[Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab "Arab") traders moved into the land from the Indian Ocean coast of East Africa in the 1830s for trade and commerce.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-21) In the late 1860s, [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro") in Mid-Western Uganda found itself threatened from the north by Egyptian-sponsored agents.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-22) Unlike the Arab traders from the East African coast who sought trade, these agents were promoting foreign conquest. In 1869, [Khedive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khedive "Khedive")[Ismail Pasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismail_of_Egypt "Ismail of Egypt") of Egypt, seeking to annex the territories north of the borders of [Lake Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria "Lake Victoria") and east of [Lake Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Albert_(Africa) "Lake Albert (Africa)") and "south of [Gondokoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondokoro "Gondokoro")",[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Baker_1879-23) sent a British explorer, [Samuel Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Baker "Samuel Baker"), on a military expedition to the frontiers of Northern Uganda, with the objective of suppressing the slave-trade there and opening the way to commerce and "civilization".

The Banyoro resisted Baker, who had to fight a desperate battle to secure his retreat. Baker regarded the resistance as an act of treachery, and he denounced the Banyoro in a book (_Ismailia – A Narrative Of The Expedition To Central Africa For The Suppression Of Slave Trade, Organised By Ismail, Khadive Of Egypt_ (1874))[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Baker_1879-23) that was widely read in Britain. Later, the British arrived in Uganda with a predisposition against the kingdom of [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro-Kitara "Bunyoro-Kitara") and sided with the kingdom of [Buganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buganda "Buganda"). This eventually cost Bunyoro half of its territory, which was given to Buganda as a reward from the British. Two of the numerous "lost counties" were [restored to Bunyoro after independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Ugandan_lost_counties_referendum "1964 Ugandan lost counties referendum").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-24)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-25)

In the 1860s, while Arabs sought influence from the north, British explorers searching for the source of the [Nile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile "Nile")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Stanley-26) arrived in Uganda. They were followed by British Anglican missionaries who arrived in the kingdom of Buganda in 1877 and French Catholic missionaries in 1879. This situation gave rise to the death of the [Uganda Martyrs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Martyrs "Uganda Martyrs") in 1885—after the conversion of [Muteesa I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muteesa_I_of_Buganda "Muteesa I of Buganda") and much of his court, and the succession of his [anti-Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Christian_sentiment "Anti-Christian sentiment") son [Mwanga.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mwanga_II_of_Buganda "Mwanga II of Buganda")[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Background-27) The British government chartered the [Imperial British East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_East_Africa_Company "Imperial British East Africa Company") (IBEAC) to negotiate trade agreements in the region beginning in 1888.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Snakes-28)

From 1886, there was a series of religious wars in Buganda, initially between Muslims and Christians and then, from 1890, between "ba-Ingleza" Protestants and "ba-Fransa" Catholics. These factions were named after the imperial powers with which they were aligned.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-29)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-30) Because of civil unrest and financial burdens, IBEAC claimed that it was unable to "maintain their occupation" in the region.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-31) The British government sought to protect its interests along the Nile trade route and established the Uganda Protectorate in 1894.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Snakes-28):3–4[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-32)

### Uganda Protectorate (1894–1962)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Flag_of_the_Uganda_Protectorate.svg/250px-Flag_of_the_Uganda_Protectorate.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_Uganda_Protectorate.svg)

The flag of the [Protectorate of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda "Protectorate of Uganda")

The [Protectorate of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate_of_Uganda "Protectorate of Uganda") was a [protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate") of the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") from 1894 to 1962. In 1893, the [Imperial British East Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_East_Africa_Company "Imperial British East Africa Company") transferred its administration rights of territory consisting mainly of the Kingdom of [Buganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buganda "Buganda") to the British government. The IBEAC relinquished its control over Uganda after Ugandan internal religious wars had driven it into bankruptcy.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-33)

In 1894, the Uganda Protectorate was established, and the territory was extended beyond the borders of Buganda by signing more treaties with the other kingdoms ([Toro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toro_(kingdom) "Toro (kingdom)") in 1900,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-34)[Ankole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankole "Ankole") in 1901, and [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro") in 1933[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-35)) to an area that roughly corresponds to that of present-day Uganda.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-36)

The status of [protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate") meant that Uganda retained a degree of self-government that would have otherwise been limited under a full colonial administration, compared to neighbouring [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), which had been made a colony.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-37)

In the 1890s, 32,000 labourers from British India were [recruited to East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_diaspora_in_East_Africa "Indian diaspora in East Africa") under indentured labour contracts to construct the [Uganda Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Railway "Uganda Railway").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-38) Most of the surviving Indians returned home, but 6,724 decided to remain in East Africa after the line's completion.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-39) Subsequently, some became traders and took control of cotton ginning and sartorial retail.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-40)

From 1900 to 1920, a [sleeping sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_trypanosomiasis "African trypanosomiasis") epidemic in the southern part of Uganda, along the north shores of Lake Victoria, killed more than 250,000 people.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-41)

### Independence (1962–1965)

Uganda gained independence from the UK on 9 October 1962 with [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II "Queen Elizabeth II") as head of state and [Queen of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_of_Uganda "Queen of Uganda"). In 1963, Uganda replaced the Queen as head of state with a ceremonial president, elected from among the country’s [traditional kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_monarchies_in_Uganda "Traditional monarchies in Uganda"), whilst maintaining its membership in the Commonwealth of Nations.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-42) The position of [governor-general of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_governors_of_Uganda "List of governors of Uganda") (who served as representative of the Queen) was abolished in October 1963, one year after independence, although the country would not officially proclaim itself a republic until the 1966 crisis.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-43)

The first post-independence election, held in 1962, was won by an alliance between the [Uganda People's Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_People's_Congress "Uganda People's Congress") (UPC) and [Kabaka Yekka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaka_Yekka "Kabaka Yekka") (KY). UPC and KY formed the first post-independence government with [Milton Obote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Obote "Milton Obote") as executive prime minister, with the Buganda Kabaka (King) [Edward Muteesa II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutesa_II_of_Buganda "Mutesa II of Buganda") holding the largely ceremonial position of president.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-44)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-45)

### Buganda crisis (1962–1966)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Owen_Falls_Dam_construction.jpg/250px-Owen_Falls_Dam_construction.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Owen_Falls_Dam_construction.jpg)

Construction of the [Owen Falls Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nalubaale_Hydroelectric_Power_Station "Nalubaale Hydroelectric Power Station") in [Jinja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinja_District "Jinja District")

Uganda's immediate post-independence years were dominated by the relationship between the central government and the largest regional kingdom, [Buganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buganda "Buganda").[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-46)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/Kabaka_Muwenda_Mutebi_II_ne_Nnaabagereka_Sylvia_Nagginda.jpg/250px-Kabaka_Muwenda_Mutebi_II_ne_Nnaabagereka_Sylvia_Nagginda.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kabaka_Muwenda_Mutebi_II_ne_Nnaabagereka_Sylvia_Nagginda.jpg)

[Kabaka Muwenda Mutebi II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muwenda_Mutebi_II_of_Buganda "Muwenda Mutebi II of Buganda") and his wife [Sylvia Nagginda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_Nagginda "Sylvia Nagginda")

The issue of how to manage the largest monarchy within the framework of a unitary state had been a problem since the British creation of the Protectorate of Uganda. Colonial governors had failed to come up with a formula that worked. This was further complicated by Buganda's nonchalant attitude to its relationship with the central government. Buganda never sought independence but rather appeared to be comfortable with a loose arrangement that guaranteed them privileges above the other subjects within the protectorate or a special status when the British left. This was evidenced in part by hostilities between the British colonial authorities and Buganda prior to independence.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-47)

Within Buganda, there were divisions between those who wanted the [Kabaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaka_of_Buganda "Kabaka of Buganda") to remain a dominant monarch and those who wanted to join with the rest of Uganda to create a modern secular state. The split resulted in the creation of two dominant Buganda based parties – the Kabaka Yekka (Kabaka Only) KY, and the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(Uganda) "Democratic Party (Uganda)") (DP) that had roots in the Catholic Church. The bitterness between these two parties was extremely intense especially as the first elections for the post-Colonial parliament approached. The Kabaka particularly disliked the DP leader, [Benedicto Kiwanuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedicto_Kiwanuka "Benedicto Kiwanuka").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-48)

Outside Buganda, a soft-spoken politician from Northern Uganda, [Milton Obote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Obote "Milton Obote"), had forged an alliance of non-Buganda politicians to form the Uganda People's Congress (UPC). The UPC at its heart was dominated by politicians who wanted to rectify what they saw as the regional inequality that favoured Buganda's special status. This drew in substantial support from outside Buganda. The party, however, remained a loose alliance of interests, but Obote showed great skill at negotiating them into a common ground based on a federal formula.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-kasozi-49)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Uganda_Printers_Kampala_1950s.jpg/250px-Uganda_Printers_Kampala_1950s.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uganda_Printers_Kampala_1950s.jpg)

The Uganda printers building on Kampala Road, Kampala, Uganda

At Independence, the Buganda question remained unresolved. Uganda was one of the few colonial territories that achieved independence without a dominant political party with a clear majority in parliament. In the pre-Independence elections, the UPC ran no candidates in Buganda and won 37 of the 61 directly elected seats (outside Buganda). The DP won 24 seats outside Buganda. The "special status" granted to Buganda meant that the 21 Buganda seats were elected by proportional representation reflecting the elections to the Buganda parliament – the Lukikko. KY won all 21 seats.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-50)

The UPC reached a peak at the end of 1964 when the leader of the DP in parliament, [Basil Kiiza Bataringaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_Kiiza_Bataringaya "Basil Kiiza Bataringaya"), crossed the parliamentary floor with five other MPs, leaving DP with only nine seats. The DP MPs were not particularly happy that the hostility of their leader, Benedicto Kiwanuka, towards the Kabaka was hindering their chances of compromise with KY.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-51) The trickle of defections turned into a flood when 10 KY members crossed the floor when they realised the formal coalition with the UPC was no longer viable. Obote's charismatic speeches across the country were sweeping all before him, and the UPC was winning almost every local election held and increasing its control over all district councils and legislatures outside Buganda.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-52) The response from the Kabaka was mute – probably content in his ceremonial role and symbolism in his part of the country. However, there were also major divisions within his palace that made it difficult for him to act effectively against Obote. By the time Uganda had become independent, Buganda "was a divided house with contending social and political forces".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-kasozi-49):63

There were problems brewing inside the UPC. As its ranks swelled, the ethnic, religious, regional, and personal interests began to shake the party. The party's apparent strength was eroded in a complex sequence of factional conflicts in its central and regional structures. And by 1966, the UPC was tearing itself apart. The conflicts were further intensified by the newcomers who had crossed the parliamentary floor from DP and KY.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-kasozi-49):71

The UPC delegates arrived in [Gulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulu "Gulu") in 1964 for their delegates conference. The battle over the Secretary-General of the party was a bitter contest between the new moderate's candidate – [Grace Ibingira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Ibingira "Grace Ibingira") and the radical John Kakonge. Ibingira subsequently became the symbol of the opposition to Obote within the UPC. For those outside the UPC (including KY supporters), this was a sign that Obote was vulnerable.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-kasozi-49):70

The collapse of the UPC-KY alliance openly revealed the dissatisfaction Obote and others had about Buganda's "special status". In 1964, the government responded to demands from some parts of the vast Buganda Kingdom that they were not the Kabaka's subjects. Prior to colonial rule, Buganda had been rivalled by the neighbouring [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro") kingdom. Buganda had conquered parts of Bunyoro and the British colonialists had formalised this in the Buganda Agreements. Known as the "lost counties", the people in these areas wished to revert to being part of Bunyoro. Obote decided to allow a referendum, which angered the Kabaka and most of the rest of Buganda. The residents of the counties voted to return to Bunyoro despite the Kabaka's attempts to influence the vote.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-53) Having lost the referendum, KY opposed the bill to pass the counties to Bunyoro, thus ending the alliance with the UPC.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The UPC, which had previously been a national party, began to break along tribal lines when Ibingira challenged Obote in the UPC. The "North/South" ethnic divide that had been evident in economic and social spheres now entrenched itself in politics. Obote surrounded himself with mainly northern politicians, while Ibingira's supporters who were subsequently arrested and jailed with him, were mainly from the South. In time, the two factions acquired ethnic labels – "Bantu" (the mainly Southern Ibingira faction) and "Nilotic" (the mainly Northern Obote faction). The perception that the government was at war with the Bantu was further enhanced when Obote arrested and imprisoned the mainly Bantu ministers who backed Ibingira.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Otunnu-54)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/SA18157-Crowned_Crane_-_%C5%BBuraw_Kr%C3%B3lewski.jpg/250px-SA18157-Crowned_Crane_-_%C5%BBuraw_Kr%C3%B3lewski.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SA18157-Crowned_Crane_-_%C5%BBuraw_Kr%C3%B3lewski.jpg)

A [Grey Crowned Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey_crowned_crane "Grey crowned crane") – a symbol of Uganda

These labels brought into the mix two very powerful influences. First Buganda – the people of Buganda are Bantu and therefore naturally aligned to the Ibingira faction. The Ibingira faction further advanced this alliance by accusing Obote of wanting to overthrow the Kabaka.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Otunnu-54) They were now aligned to opposing Obote. Second – the security forces – the British colonialists had recruited the army and police almost exclusively from Northern Uganda due to their perceived suitability for these roles. At independence, the army and police was dominated by northern tribes – mainly Nilotic. They would now feel more affiliated to Obote, and he took full advantage of this to consolidate his power. In April 1966, Obote passed out eight hundred new army recruits at [Moroto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moroto_Town "Moroto Town"), of whom seventy per cent came from the Northern Region.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-kasozi-49):83

At the time, there was a tendency to perceive central government and security forces as dominated by "northerners," particularly the Acholi who through the UPC had significant access to government positions at the national level.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-LRA-MR-55) In northern Uganda there were also varied degrees of anti-Buganda feelings, particularly over the kingdom's "special status" before and after independence, and all the economic and social benefits that came with this status. "Obote brought significant numbers of northerners into the central state, both through the civil service and military, and created a patronage machine in Northern Uganda".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-LRA-MR-55)

However, both "Bantu" and "Nilotic" labels represent significant ambiguities. The Bantu category for example includes both Buganda and Bunyoro – historically bitter rivals. The Nilotic label includes the Lugbara, Acholi, and Langi, all of whom have bitter rivalries that were to define Uganda's military politics later. Despite these ambiguities, these events unwittingly brought to fore the northerner/southerner political divide which to some extent still influences Ugandan politics.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The UPC fragmentation continued as opponents sensed Obote's vulnerability. At local level where the UPC dominated most councils discontent began to challenge incumbent council leaders. Even in Obote's home district, attempts were made to oust the head of the local district council in 1966. A more worrying fact for the UPC was that the next national elections loomed in 1967 – and without the support of KY (who were now likely to back the DP), and the growing factionalism in the UPC, there was the real possibility that the UPC would be out of power in months.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Obote went after KY with a new act of parliament in early 1966 that blocked any attempt by KY to expand outside Buganda. KY appeared to respond in parliament through one of their few remaining MPs, the terminally ill Daudi Ochieng. Ochieng was an irony – although from Northern Uganda, he had risen high in the ranks of KY and become a close confidant to the Kabaka who had gifted him with large land titles in Buganda. In Obote's absence from Parliament, Ochieng laid bare the illegal plundering of ivory and gold from the Congo that had been orchestrated by Obote's army chief of staff, Colonel [Idi Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idi_Amin "Idi Amin"). He further alleged that Obote, Onama and Neykon had all benefited from the scheme.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-56) Parliament overwhelmingly voted in favour of a motion to censure Amin and investigate Obote's involvement. This led to raised tensions in the country.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

KY further demonstrated its ability to challenge Obote from within his party at the UPC Buganda conference, where the Attorney General, Godfrey Binaisa, was ousted by a faction believed to have the backing of KY, Ibingira and other anti-Obote elements in Buganda.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-kasozi-49):63 Obote's response was to arrest Ibingira and other ministers at a cabinet meeting and to assume special powers in February 1966. In March 1966, Obote also announced that the offices of President and vice-president would cease to exist – effectively dismissing the Kabaka.

Obote also gave Amin more power – giving him the Army Commander position over the previous holder, Opolot, who had relations to Buganda through marriage, possibly believing Opolot would be reluctant to take military action against the Kabaka if it came to that. Obote abolished the constitution and effectively suspended elections due in a few months. Obote went on television and radio to accuse the Kabaka of various offences including requesting foreign troops which appears to have been explored by the Kabaka following the rumours of Amin plotting a coup. Obote further dismantled the authority of the Kabaka by announcing among other measures:

*   The abolition of independent public service commissions for federal units. This removed the Kabaka's authority to appoint civil servants in Buganda.
*   The abolition of the Buganda High Court – removing any judicial authority the Kabaka had.
*   The bringing of Buganda financial management under further central control.
*   Abolition of lands for Buganda chiefs. Land is one of the key sources of Kabaka's power over his subjects.

This set the stage for a conflict between Buganda and the central government. Within Buganda's political institutions, rivalries driven by religion and personal ambition made the institutions ineffective and unable to respond to the central government moves. The Kabaka was often regarded as aloof and unresponsive to advice from the younger Buganda politicians who better understood the new post-Independence politics, unlike the traditionalists who were ambivalent to what was going on as long as their traditional benefits were maintained. The Kabaka favoured the neo-traditionalists.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-kasozi-49):64

In May 1966, the Kabaka asked for foreign help, and the Buganda parliament demanded that the Uganda government leave Buganda, including the capital, Kampala. In response Obote ordered Idi Amin to attack the Kabaka's palace. The battle for the Kabaka's palace was fierce – the Kabaka's guards putting up more resistance than had been expected. The British trained Captain – the Kabaka with about 120 armed men kept Idi Amin at bay for twelve hours.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-kasozi-49):85 It is estimated that up to 2,000 people died in the battle which ended when the army called in heavier guns and overran the palace. The anticipated countryside uprising in Buganda did not materialise and a few hours later a beaming Obote met the press to relish his victory. The Kabaka escaped over the palace walls and was transported into exile in London by supporters.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Before the coup (1966–1971)

In 1966, following a power struggle between the Obote-led government and King Muteesa, Obote suspended the constitution and removed the ceremonial president and vice-president. In 1967, a new constitution proclaimed Uganda a republic and abolished the traditional kingdoms. Obote was declared the president.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Background-27)

### Idi Amin's regime (1971–1979)

After a [military coup on 25 January 1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Ugandan_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1971 Ugandan coup d'état"), Obote was deposed from power and General [Idi Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idi_Amin "Idi Amin") seized control of the country. Amin ruled Uganda as dictator with the support of the military for the next eight years.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-loc-57) He carried out mass killings within the country to maintain his rule. An estimated 80,000–500,000 Ugandans died during his regime.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-58) Aside from his brutalities, he [forcibly removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_of_Asians_in_Uganda_in_1972 "Expulsion of Asians in Uganda in 1972") the entrepreneurial [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_people "Indian people") minority from Uganda.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-59)

In June 1976, Palestinian terrorists hijacked an [Air France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_France "Air France") flight and forced it to land at [Entebbe airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entebbe_International_Airport "Entebbe International Airport"). One hundred of the 250 passengers originally on board were held hostage until an [Israeli commando raid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Entebbe "Operation Entebbe") rescued them ten days later.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-60)

Amin's reign ended in 1979 during the [Uganda–Tanzania War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda%E2%80%93Tanzania_War "Uganda–Tanzania War"), in which Tanzanian forces aided by Ugandan exiles invaded the country.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-kasozi-49):125–127 Tanzanian president [Julius Nyerere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Nyerere "Julius Nyerere") supported the intervention with the hope of returning his ally, Obote, to power.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-61)

### 1979–present

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Second_Congo_War_Africa_map_en.svg/500px-Second_Congo_War_Africa_map_en.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Second_Congo_War_Africa_map_en.svg)

Belligerents of the Second Congo War. In 2005, the [International Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice "International Court of Justice") ruled against Uganda, in a case brought by the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), for illegal invasion of its territory, and violation of human rights.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-62)

In 1980, the [Ugandan Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugandan_Bush_War "Ugandan Bush War") broke out, leading to [Yoweri Museveni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoweri_Museveni "Yoweri Museveni") becoming president. His forces toppled the previous regime in January 1986.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-63)

From 1986, [political parties in Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_political_parties_in_Uganda "List of political parties in Uganda") were restricted in their activities, in a measure ostensibly designed to reduce sectarian violence. In the [non-party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-partisan_democracy "Non-partisan democracy") "Movement" system instituted by Museveni, political parties continued to exist, but they could operate only a headquarters office. They could not open branches, hold rallies, or field candidates directly, although electoral candidates could belong to political parties. In July 2005, a constitutional referendum cancelled this nineteen-year ban on multi-party politics.

In the mid-to-late 1990s, Museveni was lauded by Western countries as part of a new generation of African leaders.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-64) His presidency has been marred, however, by invading and occupying the Democratic Republic of the Congo during the [Second Congo War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Congo_War "Second Congo War"), resulting in an estimated 5.4 million deaths since 1998, and by participating in other conflicts in the [Great Lakes region of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_(Africa) "Great Lakes (Africa)"). He has struggled for years in the civil war against the Lord's Resistance Army, which has been guilty of numerous crimes against humanity, including [child slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_slavery "Child slavery"), the [Atiak massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atiak_massacre "Atiak massacre"), and other mass murders. Conflict in northern Uganda has killed thousands and displaced millions.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-65)

Parliament abolished presidential term limits in 2005, allegedly because Museveni used public funds to pay US$2,000 to each member of parliament who supported the measure.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-66) Presidential [elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Ugandan_general_election "2006 Ugandan general election") were held in February 2006. Museveni ran against several candidates, the most prominent of them being [Kizza Besigye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kizza_Besigye "Kizza Besigye").

On 20 February 2011, the Uganda Electoral Commission declared Museveni the winning candidate of the 2011 [elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Ugandan_general_election "2011 Ugandan general election") that were held on 18 February 2011. The opposition were not satisfied with the results, condemning them as full of sham and rigging. According to the official results, Museveni won with 68 per cent of the votes. This easily topped his nearest challenger, Besigye, who had been Museveni's physician and told reporters that he and his supporters "downrightly snub" the outcome as well as the unremitting rule of Museveni or any person he may appoint. Besigye added that the rigged elections would definitely lead to an illegitimate leadership and that it is up to Ugandans to critically analyse this. The European Union's Election Observation Mission reported on improvements and flaws of the Ugandan electoral process: "The electoral campaign and polling day were conducted in a peaceful manner. However, the electoral process was marred by avoidable administrative and logistical failures that led to an unacceptable number of Ugandan citizens being disfranchised."[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-67)

Since August 2012, hacktivist group [Anonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anonymous_(group) "Anonymous (group)") has threatened Ugandan officials and hacked official government websites over its anti-gay bills.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-68) Some international donors have threatened to cut financial aid to the country if anti-gay bills continue.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-69)

Indicators of a plan for succession by the president's son, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, have increased tensions.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-70)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-71)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Uganda_2012_Human_Rights_Report-72)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-73)

In [the 2021 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Ugandan_general_election "2021 Ugandan general election") Museveni won with 58% of the vote, while popstar-turned-politician [Bobi Wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobi_Wine "Bobi Wine") had 35%. The opposition challenged the result because of allegations of widespread fraud and irregularities.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-74)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-75) Another opposition candidate was 24-year-old John Katumba.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-76)

Museveni has ruled the country since 1986. He was last re-elected in the January 2026 presidential [elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Ugandan_general_election "2026 Ugandan general election").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-77)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-78)

## Geography

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Uganda%2C_2005.jpg/330px-Uganda%2C_2005.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uganda,_2005.jpg)

A topographic map of Uganda

Uganda is located in southeast Africa between 1º S and 4º N latitude, and between 30º E and 35º E longitude. Its geography is very diverse, consisting of volcanic hills, mountains, and lakes. The country sits at an average of 900 meters above sea level. Both the eastern and western borders of Uganda have mountains. The western [Ruwenzori mountain range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwenzori_Mountains "Rwenzori Mountains") contains [Mount Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Stanley "Mount Stanley"), the highest peak in both Uganda and the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), with an elevation of 5,109 metres (16,762 ft).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-79) The east on the border with Kenya has volcanic [Mount Elgon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Elgon "Mount Elgon") with its highest peak, Wagagai (4,321 metres (14,177 ft)), in Uganda.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-80)

### Lakes and rivers

Much of the south of the country is heavily influenced by one of the world's biggest lakes, Lake Victoria, which contains many islands. The most important cities are located in the south, near this lake, including the capital [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala")[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-81)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Amendment_2005-82) and the nearby city of [Entebbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entebbe "Entebbe").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-DataBasin-83)[Lake Kyoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Kyoga "Lake Kyoga") is in the centre of the country and is surrounded by extensive marshy areas.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-84)

Although landlocked, Uganda contains many large lakes. Besides Lakes Victoria and Kyoga, there are [Lake Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Albert_(Africa) "Lake Albert (Africa)"), [Lake Edward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Edward "Lake Edward"), and the smaller [Lake George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_George_(Uganda) "Lake George (Uganda)").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-DataBasin-83) It lies almost completely within the [Nile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile "Nile") basin. The Victoria Nile drains from Lake Victoria into Lake Kyoga and thence into Lake Albert on the Congolese border. It then runs northwards into [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan"). An area in eastern Uganda is drained by the [Suam River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkwel_River "Turkwel River"), part of the internal drainage basin of [Lake Turkana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Turkana "Lake Turkana"). The extreme north-eastern part of Uganda drains into the Lotikipi Basin, which is primarily in Kenya.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-DataBasin-83)

### Climate

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Koppen-Geiger_Map_UGA_present.svg/330px-Koppen-Geiger_Map_UGA_present.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Koppen-Geiger_Map_UGA_present.svg)

A map of Uganda's [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification") zones

Uganda has a warm [tropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_climate "Tropical climate") with temperatures falling in the 25 to 29°C (77.0 to 84.2°F) range on an average. The months from December to February are the hottest, but even during this season the evenings can be pleasant with temperatures in the 17 to 18°C (62.6 to 64.4°F) range.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-:0-85)

Most of Uganda receives an annual rainfall of 1,000 to 1,500 millimetres or 40 to 60 inches. The rainy seasons are March to May and September to November. During these months, heavy rains can make roads and terrains hard to traverse. January to February and June to August are dry.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-:0-85) In the north, there is one rainy season from March to November, and a dry season from December to February.
