### Biodiversity and conservation

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/033_Male_Ugandan_kob_trying_to_seduce_a_female_at_Queen_Elizabeth_National_Park_Photo_by_Giles_Laurent.jpg/250px-033_Male_Ugandan_kob_trying_to_seduce_a_female_at_Queen_Elizabeth_National_Park_Photo_by_Giles_Laurent.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:033_Male_Ugandan_kob_trying_to_seduce_a_female_at_Queen_Elizabeth_National_Park_Photo_by_Giles_Laurent.jpg)

A male kob trying to seduce a female at [Queen Elizabeth National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_National_Park "Queen Elizabeth National Park")

Uganda has [60 protected areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Protected_Areas_in_Uganda "List of Protected Areas in Uganda"), including ten national parks: [Bwindi Impenetrable National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bwindi_Impenetrable_National_Park "Bwindi Impenetrable National Park") and [Rwenzori Mountains National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwenzori_Mountains_National_Park "Rwenzori Mountains National Park") (both UNESCO [World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site")[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-92)), [Kibale National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kibale_National_Park "Kibale National Park"), [Kidepo Valley National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidepo_Valley_National_Park "Kidepo Valley National Park"), [Lake Mburo National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Mburo_National_Park "Lake Mburo National Park"), [Mgahinga Gorilla National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mgahinga_Gorilla_National_Park "Mgahinga Gorilla National Park"), [Mount Elgon National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Elgon_National_Park "Mount Elgon National Park"), [Murchison Falls National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murchison_Falls_National_Park "Murchison Falls National Park"), [Queen Elizabeth National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_National_Park "Queen Elizabeth National Park"), and [Semuliki National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semuliki_National_Park "Semuliki National Park").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-93)

Uganda is home to a vast number of species, including a population of [mountain gorillas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_gorillas "Mountain gorillas") in the Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, gorillas and [golden monkeys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_monkey "Golden monkey") in the Mgahinga Gorilla National Park, and [hippos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippo "Hippo") in the Murchison Falls National Park.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-94)[Jackfruit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackfruit "Jackfruit") can be found throughout Uganda.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-95) The country had a 2019 [Forest Landscape Integrity Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Landscape_Integrity_Index "Forest Landscape Integrity Index") mean score of 4.36/10, ranking it 128th globally out of 172 countries.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-FLII-Supplementary-96)

## Government and politics

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Yoweri_Museveni_2024.jpg/120px-Yoweri_Museveni_2024.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yoweri_Museveni_2024.jpg)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Alupo_Jessica_Rose_Epel.jpg/120px-Alupo_Jessica_Rose_Epel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alupo_Jessica_Rose_Epel.jpg)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Nabbanja_Robinah.jpg/250px-Nabbanja_Robinah.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nabbanja_Robinah.jpg)

The [president of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Uganda "President of Uganda") is both [head of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_state "Head of state") and [head of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_government "Head of government"). The president appoints a vice-president and a [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Uganda "Prime Minister of Uganda") to aid them in governing.

The [Parliament of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Uganda "Parliament of Uganda") has 557 members. These include [constituency representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_constituencies_in_Uganda "List of constituencies in Uganda"), district woman representatives and representatives of the Uganda People's Defense Forces. There are also 5 representatives of the youth, 5 representatives of workers, 5 representatives of persons with disabilities, and 18 [ex officio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex_officio_member "Ex officio member") members.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-97)

[Freedom of the press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Uganda#Freedom_of_the_press "Human rights in Uganda") has been continually infringed upon through the use of intimidation and the Public Order Management Act (2013).[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-98) Attacks on political freedom in the country, including the arrest and beating of opposition members of parliament, have led to international criticism, culminating in May 2005 in a decision by the British government to withhold part of its aid to the country. The arrest of the main opposition leader [Kizza Besigye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kizza_Besigye "Kizza Besigye") and the siege of the [High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_(Uganda)?action=edit&redlink=1 "High Court (Uganda) (page does not exist)") during a hearing of Besigye's case by heavily armed security forces – before the [February 2006 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Ugandan_general_election "2006 Ugandan general election") – led to condemnation.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-hrw1-99)

### Foreign relations

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/BushMuseveniEntebbe2003.jpg/250px-BushMuseveniEntebbe2003.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BushMuseveniEntebbe2003.jpg)

US President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") met with President Yoweri Museveni in Entebbe, Uganda, July 2003

Uganda is a member of the [East African Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Community "East African Community") (EAC), along with Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, and South Sudan. According to the East African Common Market Protocol of 2010, the free trade and free movement of people is guaranteed, including the right to reside in another member country for purposes of employment. This protocol has not been implemented because of work permit and other bureaucratic, legal, and financial obstacles. Uganda is a founding member of the [Intergovernmental Authority on Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergovernmental_Authority_on_Development "Intergovernmental Authority on Development") (IGAD), an eight-country bloc including governments from the [Horn of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horn_of_Africa "Horn of Africa"), [Nile Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile_Valley "Nile Valley"), and the [African Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Great_Lakes "African Great Lakes").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-100) Its headquarters are in Djibouti City. Uganda is also a member of the [Organization of Islamic Cooperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_of_Islamic_Cooperation "Organization of Islamic Cooperation").[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-oicmems-101)

In August 2025, Uganda made an agreement with the US to take in asylum seekers deported from the US.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-102) Migrants were to be of African origin and had to have no criminal record.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-ap-103) Critics including [Muwada Nkunyingi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muwada_Nkunyingi "Muwada Nkunyingi") have likened this arrangement to [human trafficking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_trafficking "Human trafficking").[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-ap-103)

### Military

The [Uganda People's Defence Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_People's_Defence_Force "Uganda People's Defence Force") serves as the military. The [number of military personnel in Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_number_of_military_and_paramilitary_personnel "List of countries by number of military and paramilitary personnel") is estimated at 45,000 soldiers on active duty. The Uganda army is involved in several peacekeeping and combat missions in the region, with commentators noting that only the [United States Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Armed_Forces "United States Armed Forces") is deployed in more countries. Uganda has soldiers deployed in the northern and eastern areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and in the [Central African Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_African_Republic "Central African Republic"), [Somalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia "Somalia"), and [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-104)

### Corruption

[Transparency International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_International "Transparency International") has rated Uganda's public sector as one of the most corrupt in the world. In 2016, Uganda ranked 151st best out of 176 and had a score of 25 on a scale from 0 (perceived as most corrupt) to 100 (perceived as clean).[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-CPI-105)

The [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank")'s 2015 Worldwide Governance Indicators ranked Uganda in the worst 12 percentile of all countries.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-106) In the [United States Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State")'s 2012 Human Rights Report on Uganda, "The World Bank's most recent Worldwide Governance Indicators reflected corruption was a severe problem" and that "the country annually loses 768.9 billion shillings ($286 million) to corruption."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Uganda_2012_Human_Rights_Report-72)

In 2014, Ugandan parliamentarians earned 60 times what was earned by most state employees, and they sought a major increase. This caused widespread criticism and protests, including the smuggling of two piglets into the parliament in June 2014 to highlight corruption amongst members of parliament. The protesters, who were arrested, used the word "MPigs" to highlight their grievance.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-UganadaMPs-107)

A specific scandal, which had significant international consequences and highlighted the presence of corruption in high-level government offices, was the embezzlement of $12.6 million of donor funds from the Office of the Prime Minister in 2012. These funds were "earmarked as crucial support for rebuilding northern Uganda, ravaged by a 20-year war, and Karamoja, Uganda's poorest region." This scandal prompted the EU, the United Kingdom, Germany, Denmark, Ireland, and Norway to suspend aid.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-108)

Widespread grand and petty corruption involving public officials and political patronage systems have also seriously affected the investment climate in Uganda. One of the high corruption risk areas is the public procurement in which non-transparent under-the-table cash payments are often demanded from procurement officers.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-109)

What may ultimately compound this problem is the availability of oil. The Petroleum Bill, passed by parliament in 2012 and touted by the NRM as bringing transparency to the oil sector, has failed to please domestic and international political commentators and economists. For instance, Angelo Izama, a Ugandan energy analyst at the US-based Open Society Foundation said the new law was tantamount to "handing over an ATM (cash) machine" to Museveni and his regime.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-110) According to Global Witness in 2012, a non-governmental organisation devoted to international law, Uganda now has "oil reserves that have the potential to double the government's revenue within six to ten years, worth an estimated US $2.4 billion per year."[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-111)

The Non-Governmental Organisations (Amendment) Act, passed in 2006, has stifled the productivity of NGOs through erecting barriers to entry, activity, funding and assembly within the sector. Burdensome and corrupt registration procedures (i.e. requiring recommendations from government officials; annual re-registration), unreasonable regulation of operations (i.e. requiring government notification prior to making contact with individuals in NGO's area of interest), and the precondition that all foreign funds be passed through the Bank of Uganda, among other things, are severely limiting the output of the NGO sector.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

A leaked confidential document exposes scandals in Uganda's Office of the Prime Minister, including distribution of rotten food, excessive spending, land grabbing allegations, and controversial handling of political matters. These revelations raise questions about the office's ethics and transparency and involves Charles Odongtho, the OPM's public relations expert.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-112)

### Human rights

There are many areas which continue to attract concern when it comes to human rights in Uganda.

Conflict in the northern parts of Uganda continues to generate reports of abuses by both the rebel [Lord's Resistance Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord's_Resistance_Army "Lord's Resistance Army") (LRA), led by [Joseph Kony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Kony "Joseph Kony"), and the [Ugandan Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_People's_Defence_Force "Uganda People's Defence Force"). A UN official accused the LRA in February 2009 of "appalling brutality" in the Democratic Republic of Congo.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-113)

The number of [internally displaced persons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internally_displaced_persons "Internally displaced persons") is estimated at 1.4 million. Torture continues to be a widespread practice amongst security organisations. [Child labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_labour "Child labour") is common in Uganda. Many child workers are active in agriculture.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-unhcr.org-114) Children who work on tobacco farms in Uganda are exposed to health hazards.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-unhcr.org-114) Child domestic servants in Uganda risk [sexual abuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_abuse "Sexual abuse").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-unhcr.org-114)[Trafficking of children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafficking_of_children "Trafficking of children") occurs.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-unhcr.org-114)[Slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery "Slavery") and [forced labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labour "Forced labour") are prohibited by the Ugandan constitution.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-unhcr.org-114)

In 2007, the US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants reported several violations of refugee rights, including forcible deportations by the Ugandan government and violence directed against refugees.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-World_Refugee_Survey_2008-115)

Torture and extrajudicial killings have been a pervasive problem in Uganda in recent years. For instance, in a 2012 US State Department report, "the African Center for Treatment and Rehabilitation for Torture Victims registered 170 allegations of torture against police, 214 against the UPDF, 1 against military police, 23 against the Special Investigations Unit, 361 against unspecified security personnel, and 24 against prison officials" between January and September 2012.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Uganda_2012_Human_Rights_Report-72)

Hillary Rodham Clinton with 2011 Human Rights Defender Award recipients

In September 2009, Museveni refused Kabaka Muwenda Mutebi, the Baganda king, permission to visit some areas of Buganda Kingdom, particularly the Kayunga district. Riots occurred and over 40 people were killed while others still remain imprisoned. 9 more people were killed during the April 2011 "Walk to Work" demonstrations. According to the Humans Rights Watch 2013 World Report on Uganda, the government has failed to investigate the killings associated with both of these events.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-116)

#### LGBT rights

![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Ambox_current_red_Asia_Australia.svg/60px-Ambox_current_red_Asia_Australia.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)This section needs to be **updated**. [![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Uganda_Anti-Homosexuality_Bill_protest.jpg/250px-Uganda_Anti-Homosexuality_Bill_protest.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uganda_Anti-Homosexuality_Bill_protest.jpg)

A 2009 protest in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") against Uganda's [first Anti-Homosexuality Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Homosexuality_Act,_2014 "Anti-Homosexuality Act, 2014")

In 2007, a newspaper, the _[Red Pepper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red\_Pepper\_(newspaper) "Red Pepper (newspaper)")_, published a list of allegedly gay men; as a result, many of the men listed suffered harassment.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-117)

On 9 October 2010, the Ugandan newspaper _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone\_(Uganda) "Rolling Stone (Uganda)")_ published a front-page article titled "100 Pictures of Uganda's Top Homos Leak" that listed the names, addresses, and photographs of 100 homosexuals alongside a yellow banner that read "Hang Them."[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Guardian-118) The paper also alleged [homosexual recruitment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexual_recruitment "Homosexual recruitment") of Ugandan children. The publication attracted international attention and criticism from human rights organisations, such as [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International"),[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-119)[No Peace Without Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Peace_Without_Justice "No Peace Without Justice")[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-120) and the [International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Lesbian,_Gay,_Bisexual,_Trans_and_Intersex_Association "International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association").[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-ILGA-121) According to [gay rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_rights "Gay rights") activists, many Ugandans have been attacked since the publication.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Independent-122) On 27 January 2011, gay rights activist [David Kato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Kato "David Kato") was murdered.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-BBC-123)

In 2009, the Ugandan parliament considered an [Anti-Homosexuality Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Anti-Homosexuality_Bill "Uganda Anti-Homosexuality Bill") which would have broadened the criminalisation of homosexuality by introducing the death penalty for people who have previous convictions, or are HIV-positive, and engage in same-sex sexual acts. The bill included provisions for Ugandans who engage in same-sex sexual relations outside of Uganda, asserting that they may be [extradited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extradition "Extradition") back to Uganda for punishment, and included penalties for individuals, companies, media organisations, or non-governmental organisations that support legal protection for homosexuality or sodomy. On 14 October 2009, MP [David Bahati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bahati "David Bahati") submitted the [private member's bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_member's_bill "Private member's bill") and was believed to have had widespread support in the Uganda parliament.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Harpers2010-124)

The hacktivist group [Anonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anonymous_(hacker_group) "Anonymous (hacker group)") hacked into Ugandan government websites in protest of the bill.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-125) In response to global condemnation the debate of the bill was delayed, but it was eventually passed on 20 December 2013 and President Museveni signed it on 24 February 2014. The death penalty was dropped in the final legislation. The law was widely condemned by the international community. Denmark, the Netherlands, and Sweden said they would withhold aid. On 28 February 2014, the [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank") said it would postpone a US$90 million loan, while the United States said it was reviewing ties with Uganda.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-WorldBankPostponesLOan-126)

On 1 August 2014, the [Constitutional Court of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Uganda "Constitutional Court of Uganda") ruled the bill invalid as it was not passed with the required [quorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quorum "Quorum").[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-127)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-128)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-129) A 13 August 2014 news report said that the Ugandan attorney general had dropped all plans to appeal, per a directive from President Museveni who was concerned about foreign reaction to the bill and who also said that any newly introduced bill should not criminalise same-sex relationships between consenting adults.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-130) As of 2019, adoption of LGBT rights on the African continent was slow but progressing with South Africa being the only country where same sex marriages are recognised.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-131)

##### Anti-Homosexuality Act, 2023

On 9 March 2023, [Asuman Basalirwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asuman_Basalirwa "Asuman Basalirwa") (a [member of parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Uganda "Parliament of Uganda") since 2018 from the opposition representing [Bugiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugiri "Bugiri") Municipality on Justice Forum party ticket) tabled a proposed law which sought to castigate gay sex and "the promotion or recognition of such relations" and he made remarks that, "In this country, or in this world, we talk about human rights. But it is also true that there are human wrongs. I want to submit that homosexuality is a human wrong that offends the laws of Uganda and threatens the sanctity of the family, the safety of our children and the continuation of humanity through reproduction."[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-132)

The speaker of parliament, [Annet Anita Among](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anita_Among "Anita Among"), referred the bill to a house committee for scrutiny, the first step in an accelerated process to pass the proposal into law. The parliament speaker had earlier noted that: "We want to appreciate our promoters of homosexuality for the social economic development they have brought to the country," in reference to western countries and donors. "But we do not appreciate the fact that they are killing morals. We do not need their money, we need our culture." - during a prayer service held in parliament and attended by several religious leaders.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-133) The Speaker vowed to pass the bill into law at whatever cost to shield Uganda's culture and its sovereignty.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-134)

On 21 March 2023, the Ugandan parliament approved a bill that would have made identifying as homosexual punishable by 20 year in prison and "aggravated homosexuality" by the death penalty.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-135)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-136)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-lancet-137) The bill was not approved by the President and, in the revised version which became law, identifying as homosexual was not a crime.

The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") strongly condemned the bill. During a [White House Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Press_Secretary "White House Press Secretary") briefing on 22 March 2023, [Karine Jean-Pierre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karine_Jean-Pierre "Karine Jean-Pierre") stated. "Human rights [are universal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_universalism "Moral universalism"). No one should be attacked, imprisoned, or killed simply because of who they are or whom they love."[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-138) Further criticism came from the United Kingdom,[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-139) Canada,[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-140) Germany,[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-141) and the European Union.

### Refugee policy

Uganda's approach to hosting refugees is among the most progressive globally.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-briefi-142) Despite limited international support, the country maintains an open door policy that is anchored in national law. Refugees have access to essential services, may apply for work permits and move freely within the country. They are allotted a plot of land and may live in settlements that are closely integrated with surrounding Ugandan communities. They are also allowed to form associations and civil society groups.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-onthef-143)[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-welhav-144) In this setting, many organisations created and run by refugees have developed, providing a range of support to their communities. These groups nonetheless face challenges such as scarce funding, barriers to registration and limited influence over decisions.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-onthef-143) The refugee policy does not provide a path to Ugandan citizenship.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-welhav-144)

Uganda has a long history of receiving [displaced people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_displacement "Forced displacement"). The country hosted refugees even before its independence in 1962, including groups fleeing [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and later people escaping violence in [Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda") and southern [Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan "Sudan"). Uganda also experienced periods when large numbers of its own citizens were displaced, particularly during the 1970s and 1980s and during the insurgency by the [Lord's Resistance Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord's_Resistance_Army "Lord's Resistance Army").[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-onthef-143) Regional conflicts throughout the 1990s and 2000s, including the [Rwandan genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_genocide "Rwandan genocide"), [Sudanese civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Second_Sudanese_Civil_War "The Second Sudanese Civil War") and the [Congolese wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congolese_Civil_War "Congolese Civil War"), continued to drive people into Uganda. By 2014, Uganda sheltered roughly 400,000 displaced people.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-onthef-143)

By October 2025, Uganda hosted roughly 1.95 million refugees,[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-ugasud-145) more than any other country in Africa.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-onthef-143) Most are rural groups mainly from [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan") and the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), as well as from [Somalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia "Somalia"), [Burundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burundi "Burundi"), and [Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda").[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-briefi-142)[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-onthef-143) From 2023, more than 90,000 refugees fleeing the [civil war in Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudanese_civil_war_(2023%E2%80%93present) "Sudanese civil war (2023–present)") have entered.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-ugasud-145)

### Administrative divisions

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Map_of_Ugandan_Kingdoms.png/250px-Map_of_Ugandan_Kingdoms.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_Ugandan_Kingdoms.png)

Map of the 17 officially recognised Kingdoms within Uganda. Areas without recognised Kingdoms in white

Uganda is divided into four [Regions of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_Uganda "Regions of Uganda") and [136 districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Districts_of_Uganda "Districts of Uganda").[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-district-146)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-factsheet-147) Rural areas of districts are subdivided [into sub-counties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-counties_of_Uganda "Sub-counties of Uganda"), parishes, and villages. Municipal and town councils are designated in urban areas of districts.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-148)

Political subdivisions in Uganda are officially served and united by the [Uganda Local Governments Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Local_Governments_Association "Uganda Local Governments Association") (ULGA), a voluntary and non-profit body which also serves as a forum for support and guidance for Ugandan sub-national governments.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-149)

Parallel with the state administration, [seventeen traditional kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_monarchies_in_Uganda "Traditional monarchies in Uganda") exist with official state recognition, enjoying some degrees of mainly cultural autonomy. The oldest and most prestigious of the kingdoms are [Buganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buganda "Buganda"), [Busoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Busoga "Busoga"), [Bunyoro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunyoro "Bunyoro"), [Tooro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toro_Kingdom "Toro Kingdom") and [Rwenzururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwenzururu "Rwenzururu"). Some groups attempt to restore [Ankole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankole "Ankole") as one of the officially recognised traditional kingdoms, to no avail yet.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-150) Several other kingdoms and chiefdoms are officially recognised by the government, including the [Alur Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alur_Kingdom "Alur Kingdom"), the [Iteso paramount chieftaincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teso_Kingdom "Teso Kingdom"), the [Lango monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lango_Kingdom "Lango Kingdom") and the [Padhola state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adhola_Kingdom "Adhola Kingdom").[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-151)

## Economy and infrastructure

The [Bank of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Uganda "Bank of Uganda") is the [central bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank") of Uganda and handles monetary policy along with the printing of the [Ugandan shilling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugandan_shilling "Ugandan shilling").[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-152)

In 2015, Uganda's economy generated export income from the following merchandise: coffee (US$402.63 million), oil re-exports (US$131.25 million), base metals and products (US$120.00 million), fish (US$117.56 million), maize (US$90.97 million), cement (US$80.13 million), tobacco (US$73.13 million), tea (US$69.94 million), sugar (US$66.43 million), hides and skins (US$62.71 million), cocoa beans (US$55.67 million), beans (US$53.88 million), [simsim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame "Sesame") (US$52.20 million), flowers (US$51.44 million), and other products (US$766.77 million).[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-153)

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/76/GDP_per_capita_development_of_Uganda.svg/250px-GDP_per_capita_development_of_Uganda.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GDP_per_capita_development_of_Uganda.svg)

Change in per capita GDP of Uganda, 1950–2018. Figures are inflation-adjusted to 2011 International dollars.

Uganda has been experiencing consistent economic growth. In fiscal year 2015–16, Uganda recorded gross domestic product growth of 4.6 per cent in real terms and 11.6 per cent in nominal terms. This compares to 5.0 per cent real growth in fiscal year 2014–15.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-154):vii

Uganda has largely untapped reserves of both [crude oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crude_oil "Crude oil") and natural gas.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-oilrush-155) While agriculture accounted for 56 per cent of the economy in 1986, with coffee as its main export, it has now been surpassed by the services sector, which accounted for 52 per cent of GDP in 2007.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-156) In the 1950s, the British colonial regime encouraged some 500,000 subsistence farmers to join co-operatives.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-157) Since 1986, the government, with the support of foreign countries and international agencies, has acted to rehabilitate an economy devastated during the regime of Idi Amin[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-158) and the subsequent civil war.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-cia-159)

In 2012, the World Bank listed Uganda on the [Heavily Indebted Poor Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavily_Indebted_Poor_Countries "Heavily Indebted Poor Countries") list.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-160)

Economic growth has not always led to [poverty reduction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_reduction "Poverty reduction"). Despite an average annual growth of 2.5 per cent between 2000 and 2003, poverty levels increased by 3.8 per cent during that time.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-ODI-161) This has highlighted the importance of avoiding [jobless growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jobless_growth "Jobless growth") and is part of the rising awareness in development circles of the need for [equitable growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Development_economics#equitable_growth "Development economics") not just in Uganda, but across the developing world.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-ODI-161)

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Uganda_GV5_lo_%284108162183%29.jpg/250px-Uganda_GV5_lo_%284108162183%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uganda_GV5_lo_(4108162183).jpg)

Coffee fields in southwestern Uganda

With the Uganda securities exchanges established in 1996, several equities have been listed. The government has used the stock market as an avenue for privatisation. All government treasury issues are listed on the securities exchange. The Capital Markets Authority has licensed 18 brokers, asset managers, and investment advisors including: African Alliance Investment Bank, Baroda Capital Markets Uganda Limited, Crane Financial Services Uganda Limited, Crested Stocks and Securities Limited, Dyer & Blair Investment Bank, Equity Stock Brokers Uganda Limited, Renaissance Capital Investment Bank and UAP Financial Services Limited.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-162) As one of the ways of increasing formal domestic savings, pension sector reform is the centre of attention (2007).[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-163)[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-164)

Uganda traditionally depends on Kenya for access to the Indian Ocean port of [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa"). Efforts have intensified to establish a second access route to the sea via the lakeside ports of [Bukasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukasa "Bukasa") in Uganda and [Musoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musoma "Musoma") in Tanzania, connected by railway to [Arusha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arusha "Arusha") in the Tanzanian interior and to the port of [Tanga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanga,_Tanzania "Tanga, Tanzania") on the Indian Ocean.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-165) Uganda is a member of the [East African Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Community "East African Community") and a potential member of the planned [East African Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Federation "East African Federation").

Uganda has a large diaspora, living mainly in the United States and the United Kingdom. This diaspora has contributed enormously to Uganda's economic growth through remittances and other investments, especially property. In 2016, Uganda received an estimated US$1.099 billion in remittances from abroad, second only to Kenya (US$1.574 billion) in the East African Community,[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-166) and seventh in Africa.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-167) Uganda also serves as an economic hub for a number of neighbouring countries like the Democratic Republic of the Congo,[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-168) South Sudan,[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-169) and Rwanda.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-170)

Inflation was 4.6 per cent in November 2016.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-171) In June 2018, inflation dropped to 3.4 per cent in the financial year ending 2017/18 compared to 5.7 per cent 2016/17.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-172)

In 2019, Uganda ranked as [number 102](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal) "List of countries by GDP (nominal)") among the countries of the world in nominal [Gross Domestic Product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_Domestic_Product "Gross Domestic Product") by the [International Monetary Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") with a [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP") of 26,349 (US$million).[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-GDP_by_IMF-173) In 2022, the [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank") ranked Uganda as number 99 in nominal GDP with a GDP of 25,891 (US$million).[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-GDP_by_World_Bank-174) In 2019, based on the GDP with [purchasing power parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity") the [IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMF "IMF") ranked Uganda as [number 86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP) "List of countries by GDP (PPP)") (91,212 million of current Int$). Since the 1990s, the economy in Uganda has grown. Real gross domestic product (GDP) grew at an average of 6.7% annually during the period 1990–2015. Real GDP per capita grew at 3.3% per annum during the same period.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-175)

### Poverty

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Kif20180421_114559.jpg/250px-Kif20180421_114559.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kif20180421_114559.jpg)

A school on the Nile River

Uganda is one of the poorest nations in the world. In 2012, 37.8 per cent of the population lived on less than $1.25 a day.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-176) Despite making enormous progress in reducing the countrywide poverty incidence from 56 per cent of the population in 1992 to 24.5 per cent in 2009, poverty remains deep-rooted in the country's rural areas, which are home to 84 per cent of Ugandans.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-177)

People in rural areas of Uganda depend on farming as the main source of income and 90 per cent of all rural women work in the agricultural sector.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-178) In addition to agricultural work, rural women are responsible for the caretaking of their families. The average Ugandan woman spends 9 hours a day on domestic tasks, such as preparing food and clothing, fetching water and firewood, and caring for the elderly, the sick as well as orphans.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-179)

Women on average work longer hours than men, between 12 and 18 hours per day, with a mean of 15 hours, as compared to men, who work between 8 and 10 hours a day, although urban men and women work very similar hours. In 2005, 26% of households were headed by women only (FHH), up from previous years as a result of death of men from AIDS. There were most FHHs in the top quintile, by income, (31%). Male only headed households in poverty were also increased to a similar level as FHH, though little research had been done.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-180)

To supplement their income, rural women may engage in small-scale entrepreneurial activities such as rearing and selling local breeds of animals. Nonetheless, because of their heavy workload, they have little time for these income-generating activities. The poor cannot support their children at school and in most cases, girls drop out of school to help out in domestic work or to get married. Other girls engage in sex work. As a result, young women tend to have older and more sexually experienced partners and this puts women at a disproportionate risk of getting affected by HIV, accounting for about 5.7 per cent of all adults living with HIV in Uganda.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-181)

Maternal health in rural Uganda lags behind national policy targets and the [Millennium Development Goals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennium_Development_Goals "Millennium Development Goals"), with geographical inaccessibility, lack of transport and financial burdens identified as key demand-side constraints to accessing maternal health services;[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-182) as such, interventions like intermediate transport mechanisms have been adopted as a means to improve women's access to maternal health care services in rural regions of the country.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-183)

Gender inequality is the main hindrance to reducing women's poverty. Women are subjected to an overall lower social status than men. Many women believe this reduces their power to act independently, participate in community life, become educated and escape reliance upon abusive men.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-184)

There are [36 airports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_airports_in_Uganda "List of airports in Uganda") in Uganda. Commercial airlines operate scheduled passenger services out of four airports. Uganda currently has one functioning international airport, [Entebbe International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entebbe_International_Airport "Entebbe International Airport"), which is located 25 miles (40 km) south-west of [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala"). In 2017, the airport traffic was 1.53 million passengers, 8% more than the previous year.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-185) A second international airport, [Hoima International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoima_International_Airport "Hoima International Airport"), is currently under construction.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-186) On 27 September 2026, Kabalega International Airport (also known as Hoima International Airport) received its first passenger aircraft, marking a significant milestone in the airport's operational history. The inaugural passenger arrivals occurred on Sunday, 27 September 2026, when aircraft carrying government officials and football teams landed at the airport. The event represented the airport's transition from construction and testing phases toward regular passenger operations and highlighted its growing role in supporting transportation and regional development in western Uganda.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-187)

### Road network

[![Image 37](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Wild_route.jpg/250px-Wild_route.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wild_route.jpg)

The road to Murchison

Roads are the main method of transportation in Uganda. 95% of freight and passenger traffic is handled by road traffic. The road network in Uganda is approximately 129,469 km (80,448 mi) long. About 4% of these roads are paved, which equates to only about 5,300 kilometres (3,300 mi) of paved road. The different types of roads are national roads (22,009 km (13,676 mi)—17%), district roads (33,661 km (20,916 mi)—26%), urban roads (9,062 km (5,631 mi)—7%), and community roads (64,734 km (40,224 mi)—50%).[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-188)

The national roads make up about 17% of the road network but carry over 80% of the total road traffic.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-189) In 2022, there were 83,000 private cars, which equates to 2.94 cars per 1,000 inhabitants.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-190)

### Railways

[![Image 38](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Uganda_railways_assessment_2010-2.jpg/250px-Uganda_railways_assessment_2010-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uganda_railways_assessment_2010-2.jpg)

Uganda Railway

The rail network in Uganda is approximately 1,260 kilometres (780 mi) long. The longest lines are the main line from [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala") to [Tororo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tororo "Tororo") (249 kilometres (155 mi)), the western line from Kampala to [Kasese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasese "Kasese") (333 kilometres (207 mi)), the northern line from Tororo to [Pakwach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakwach "Pakwach") (641 kilometres (398 mi)).[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-191)

### Communications

There are several systems of communication, including telephony, radio and television broadcasts, internet, mail, and newspapers. The use of phones and the internet has rapidly increased.

There are seven telecommunications companies. In 2018 there were over 24 million subscribers[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_][[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-3R-192)[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-:4-193) in a population of 48 million.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-:1-194) More than 95% of internet connections are made using mobile phones.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-195)

### Energy

[![Image 39](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Uganda_electricity_generation_by_source.png/250px-Uganda_electricity_generation_by_source.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uganda_electricity_generation_by_source.png)

Electricity generation in Uganda by source in terawatt-hours

Uganda has abundant energy resources, which are fairly distributed throughout the country. These include hydropower, biomass, solar, geothermal, peat and fossil fuels.

In the 1980s, the majority of energy in Uganda came from charcoal and wood. Oil was found in the [Lake Albert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Albert_(Africa) "Lake Albert (Africa)") area, totalling an estimated 95 million cubic metres (3.4×10 9 cu ft) of crude.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-oilrush-155)[Heritage Oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_Oil "Heritage Oil") discovered one of the largest crude oil finds in Uganda, and continues operations there.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-196)

Uganda and Tanzania signed a deal in September 2016 for the two countries build a 1,445 km, $3.5bn crude oil pipeline. The [Uganda–Tanzania Crude Oil Pipeline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Crude_Oil_Pipeline "East African Crude Oil Pipeline") (UTCOP), also known as the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), will be the first of its kind in East Africa, will connect Uganda's oil-rich Hoima region with the Indian Ocean through the Tanga port in Tanzania.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-197)[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-198)

Uganda's favourable enabling environment and broad presence of private sector investment presents a unique opportunity to deliver on [Power Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_Africa "Power Africa") goals.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-199) Uganda is one of the few sub-Saharan African countries to have liberalised and financially viable energy markets, with generation, transmission and supply segments unbundled since 2001.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-200) There is an independent [Electricity Regulatory Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity_Regulatory_Authority "Electricity Regulatory Authority") that undertakes sector regulation and oversight. The largest distribution company, [UMEME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umeme "Umeme") is privately owned and has a 20-year concession for distribution and retail. Uganda is divided into 13 rural service territories, and 6 of these are managed by small distribution companies. [Independent power producers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_power_producer "Independent power producer") (IPPs) currently account for nearly 60% of generation capacity. Issues with integrated planning and the financial ecosystem persist.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Water supply and sanitation

According to a 2006 report, the Ugandan water supply and sanitation sector had made substantial progress in urban areas since the mid-1990s, with substantial increases in coverage as well as in operational and commercial performance.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Mugisha-201):3–4 Sector reforms in the period 1998–2003 included the commercialisation and modernisation of the [National Water and Sewerage Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Water_and_Sewerage_Corporation "National Water and Sewerage Corporation") operating in cities and larger towns, and decentralisation and private sector participation in small towns.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-202):15

[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Rivers_and_lakes_of_Uganda.png/250px-Rivers_and_lakes_of_Uganda.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rivers_and_lakes_of_Uganda.png)

Main Rivers and Lakes of Uganda

Although these reforms have attracted significant international attention, 38 per cent of the population still had no access to an [improved water source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improved_water_source "Improved water source") in 2010. Concerning access to [improved sanitation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improved_sanitation "Improved sanitation"), figures have varied widely. According to government figures, it was 70 per cent in rural areas and 81 per cent in urban areas in 2011.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-SPR_2011-203) According to UN figures, it was only 34 per cent.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-JMP-204)

The water and sanitation sector was recognised as a key area under the 2004 Poverty Eradication Action Plan (PEAP), Uganda's main strategy paper to fight poverty.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-PEAP-205):182–188 In a 2006 report, a comprehensive expenditure framework had been introduced to co-ordinate financial support by external donors, the national government, and [nongovernmental organisations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NGO "NGO").[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-MWE_SWAP-206):5 The PEAP estimated that from 2001 to 2015, about US$1.4 billion, or US$92 million per year, was needed to increase water supply coverage up to 95 per cent, with rural areas needing US$956 million, urban areas and large towns needing US$281 million, and small towns needing US$136 million.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-PEAP-205):182–183

### Education

[![Image 41](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Makerere_University_Campus_Entrance_Road.JPG/250px-Makerere_University_Campus_Entrance_Road.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Makerere_University_Campus_Entrance_Road.JPG)

Makerere university Campus Entrance

Uganda's educational system, while lacking in many areas, has seen significant change since the late 1990s. Children spend seven years in primary school, six years in secondary school, and three to five years in post secondary school. In 1997, the government declared that primary school would be free for all children.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-207) This amendment has had huge benefits. In 1986, only two million children were attending primary school. By 1999, six million children were attending primary school, and this number has continued to climb.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 2007, following significant gains in access to primary education since 1997 when universal primary education (UPE) was introduced, Uganda became the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to introduce universal secondary education (USE).[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-208) This led to an increase in lower secondary enrolment of nearly 25% between 2007 and 2012.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/Uganda_students.jpg/250px-Uganda_students.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uganda_students.jpg)

Students in Uganda

At the 2002 census, Uganda had a [literacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy "Literacy") rate of 66.8 per cent, with 76.8 per cent male and 57.7 per cent female literacy.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-cia-159) Public spending on education was 5.2 per cent between 2002–2005 GDP.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-hdrstats.undp.org-209)

As of 2020, the [NCHE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_National_Council_for_Higher_Education "Uganda National Council for Higher Education") website listed 46 private accredited universities,[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-210) including [Makerere University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makerere_University "Makerere University"), [Mbarara University of science and technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mbarara_University "Mbarara University"), [Kyambogo University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyambogo_University "Kyambogo University"), [Gulu University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulu_University "Gulu University"), [Uganda Christian University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Christian_University "Uganda Christian University"), [Kampala international University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala_International_University "Kampala International University").

### Health

[![Image 43](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Aerial_view_of_old_Mulago_Hospital_in_Uganda.jpg/250px-Aerial_view_of_old_Mulago_Hospital_in_Uganda.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aerial_view_of_old_Mulago_Hospital_in_Uganda.jpg)

Mulago National Referral Hospital

There were eight physicians per 100,000 persons in the early 2000s.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-hdrstats.undp.org-209) Uganda's elimination of user fees at state health facilities in 2001 has resulted in an 80 per cent increase in visits, with over half of this increase coming from the poorest 20 per cent of the population.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-autogenerated1-211) This policy has been cited as a key factor in helping Uganda achieve its Millennium Development Goals and as an example of the importance of equity in achieving those goals.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-ODI-161) Despite this policy, many users are denied care if they do not provide their own medical equipment, as happened in the highly publicised case of Jennifer Anguko.[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-212) Poor communication within hospitals,[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-213) low satisfaction with health services[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-214) and distance to health service providers undermine the provision of quality health care to people living in Uganda, and particularly for those in poor and elderly-headed households.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-pariyo2009-215) The provision of subsidies for poor and rural populations, along with the extension of public private partnerships, have been identified as important provisions to enable vulnerable populations to access health services.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-pariyo2009-215)

The life expectancy of Uganda has increased from 39.3 in 1950 to 62.7 years in 2021.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Life_Expectancy-216) This is lower than the world average which is at 71.0 years.[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Life_Expectancy-216) The [fertility rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_fertility_rate "Total fertility rate") of Ugandan women slightly increased from an average of 6.89 babies per woman in the 1950s to about 7.12 in the 1970s before declining to an estimated 4.3 babies in 2019.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-217) This figure is higher than the world average of 2 and most world regions including [South East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia"), [Middle East and North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MENA "MENA"), [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") and [Central Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia "Central Asia") and [America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas "Americas").[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-218) The under-5-mortality-rate for Uganda has decreased from 191 deaths per 1000 [live births](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_birth_(human) "Live birth (human)") in 1970 to 41 deaths per 1000 live births in 2022.[](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/child-mortality?country)

[![Image 44](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Life_expectancy_chart_for_Uganda%2C_OWID.png/330px-Life_expectancy_chart_for_Uganda%2C_OWID.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Life_expectancy_chart_for_Uganda,_OWID.png)

Life expectancy of Uganda as per 2021

Uganda has been among the rare [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV "HIV") success stories.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-hdrstats.undp.org-209) Infection rates of 30 per cent of the population in the 1980s fell to 6.4 per cent by the end of 2008.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-219)[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-220) Meanwhile, the practice of abstinence was found to have decreased.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-221)

Less than half of all sexually active unmarried women use a modern contraceptive method, a fraction that has barely changed from 2000 to 2011. However, only ≈26% of married women used contraceptives in 2011. The use of contraceptives also differs substantially between poor (≈15%) and wealthy women (≈40%).[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-:2-222) As a result, Ugandan women have ≈6 children while they prefer to have around ≈4. According to the 2011 Uganda Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), more than 40% of births are unplanned. In 2010, the Ugandan Ministry of Health estimated that unsafe abortion accounted for 8% of the country's maternal deaths.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-:2-222) The 2006 Uganda Demographic Health Survey (UDHS) indicated that roughly 6,000 women die each year from pregnancy-related complications.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-223) Pilot studies in 2012 by Future Health Systems have shown that this rate could be significantly reduced by implementing a voucher scheme for health services and transport to clinics.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-224)[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-225)

The prevalence of [female genital mutilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Female_genital_mutilation "Female genital mutilation") (FGM) is low: according to a 2013 UNICEF report,[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-UNICEF2013p27-226) only 1 per cent of women in Uganda have undergone FGM, with the practice being illegal in the country.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-227)

Uganda's first confirmed [Ebola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebola "Ebola") outbreak occurred in 2000.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-228) Since then, Uganda has experienced several additional outbreaks, the [latest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Central_Africa_Ebola_epidemic "2026 Central Africa Ebola epidemic") in May 2026.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-229) Uganda's Ebola response has included isolation, contact tracing, infection control, public communication and, in some outbreaks, vaccine trials,[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-230) while outbreaks have also been associated with stigma against survivors and health workers.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-231)

The [Human Rights Measurement Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Measurement_Initiative "Human Rights Measurement Initiative") found that Uganda is fulfilling 80.0% of what it should be fulfilling for the right to health based on its level of income.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-232) Total health expenditure as a percentage of [gross domestic product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") (GDP) was 4.67% in 2021.[](https://apps.who.int/nha/database/country_profile/index/fr)

[Tourism in Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Uganda "Tourism in Uganda") is focused on Uganda's landscape and wildlife. It is a major driver of employment, investment and foreign exchange, contributing 4.9 trillion [Ugandan shillings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugandan_shilling "Ugandan shilling") (US$1.88 billion or €1.4 billion as of August 2013) to Uganda's [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") in the financial year 2012–13.[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Mutagamba-236) The Uganda Tourism Board is responsible for maintaining information pertaining to tourism in Uganda. The main attractions are photo safaris through the [National parks and game Reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_protected_areas_of_Uganda "List of protected areas of Uganda"). Other attractions include the Mountain Gorillas found in Bwindi Impenetrable National Park (BINP) and Mgahinga Gorilla National Park (MGNP), Uganda having some of the oldest cultural kingdom in Africa has many [Cultural sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Cultural_Sites_of_Uganda "National Cultural Sites of Uganda"). Uganda is a birding paradise boasting a massive bird list of more than 1073 recorded bird species ranking 4th in Africa's bird species and 16th internationally.[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-237) Uganda has landscapes ranging from white-capped [Rwenzori mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwenzori_Mountains "Rwenzori Mountains") to the [Great Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley "Great Rift Valley").

## Science and technology

The _National Science, Technology and Innovation Policy_ dates from 2009. Its overarching goal is to 'strengthen national capability to generate, transfer and apply scientific knowledge, skills and technologies that ensure sustainable utilisation of natural resources for the realisation of Uganda's development objectives.' The policy precedes Uganda Vision 2040, which was launched in April 2013 to transform 'Ugandan society from a peasant to a modern and prosperous country within 30 years,' in the words of the Cabinet. Uganda Vision 2040 vows to strengthen the private sector, improve education and training, modernise infrastructure and the underdeveloped services and agriculture sectors, foster industrialisation and promote good governance, among other goals. Potential areas for economic development include oil and gas, tourism, minerals and information and communication technologies (ICTs).[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-:12-238)

Uganda was ranked 124th in the [Global Innovation Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Innovation_Index "Global Innovation Index") in 2025,[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-239)[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-240) down from 102nd in 2019.[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-241) Research funding climbed between 2008 and 2010 from 0.33% to 0.48% of GDP. Over the same period, the number of researchers doubled (in head counts) from 1 387 to 2 823, according to the [UNESCO Institute for Statistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO_Institute_for_Statistics "UNESCO Institute for Statistics"). This represents a leap from 44 to 83 researchers per million inhabitants over the same period. One in four researchers is a woman.[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-:12-238)

## Demographics

[![Image 48](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Population_density_of_Uganda_districts.png/250px-Population_density_of_Uganda_districts.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Population_density_of_Uganda_districts.png)

The population density of Ugandan districts

Uganda's population grew from 9.5 million people in 1969 to 34.9 million in 2014. In 2024, the population was 45.9 million.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-census24-9) With respect to the census in 2002, the population increased by 21.7 million people in those 22 years.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-census24-9) Uganda's [median age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_age "Median age") of 15 years is the lowest in the world.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-cia-159) In 2014, Uganda had the fifth highest [total fertility rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_fertility_rate "Total fertility rate") in the world, at 5.97 children born per woman.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-cia-159)

Of Uganda's population, 23.6 million (51.4 per cent) were female and 22.3 million were male. In 2024, 49.5 per cent of Ugandans were under the age of 18, underscoring the country's very young age structure.[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-242)

There were about 80,000 [Indians in Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indians_in_Uganda "Indians in Uganda") before Idi Amin required the [expulsion of Ugandan-Asians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_of_Asians_from_Uganda "Expulsion of Asians from Uganda"), mostly of Indian origin, in 1972, which reduced the population to as low as 7,000. Many Indians returned to Uganda after Amin's ouster in 1979.[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-243) Around 90 per cent of Ugandan Indians reside in Kampala. There are a population of about 10,000 [white Africans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Africans "White Africans") and 3,000 Arabs in Uganda.[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-244)

In August 2021, Uganda hosted over 1.4 million refugees on its soil.[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-:3-245)[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-UNHCR_stats-246) Most come from neighbouring countries in the [African Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Great_Lakes "African Great Lakes") region, particularly [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan") (68.0 per cent) and [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "The Democratic Republic of the Congo") (24.6%).[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-UNHCR_stats-246) In August 2021, Uganda received some refugees from Afghanistan following the Taliban takeover.[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-:3-245)

### Languages

[![Image 49](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Languages_of_Uganda.png/330px-Languages_of_Uganda.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Languages_of_Uganda.png)

An ethnolinguistic map of Uganda

[Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_language "Swahili language"), a widely used language throughout the African Great Lakes region, was approved as the country's second official national language in 2005.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Amendment_2005-82)[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Kagonye_22_sw-247)[English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") was the only official language until the constitution was amended in 2005.[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-248)[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-cia-159)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Amendment_2005-82)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Republic-1)[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-249) Uganda has its own dialect of English, known as [Uglish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugandan_English "Ugandan English").[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-250)[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-251)

Swahili is not favoured by the Bantu-speaking populations of the south and south-west of Uganda, but is an important _[lingua franca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingua\_franca "Lingua franca")_ in the northern regions. Swahili is widely used in the police and military forces, which may be a historical result of the disproportionate recruitment of northerners into the security forces during the colonial period. The status of Swahili has thus alternated with the political group in power.[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-UCLA-252) For example, Idi Amin, who came from the north-west, declared Swahili to be the national language.[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-253)

### Religion

[![Image 50](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/Rubaga_Cthedral.jpg/250px-Rubaga_Cthedral.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rubaga_Cthedral.jpg)

[Saint Mary's Cathedral Rubaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubaga_Cathedral "Rubaga Cathedral") is the parent cathedral of the [Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Kampala "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Kampala").

The [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_Uganda "Catholic Church in Uganda") had the largest number of adherents (39.3 per cent, down from 41.6 in 2002), followed by the [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism "Anglicanism")[Church of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Uganda "Church of Uganda") (32 per cent, down from 35.9 per cent). The category of [Evangelical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical "Evangelical")/[Pentecostal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostal "Pentecostal")/[Born-Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born-Again "Born-Again") showed the most growth, rising from 4.7% in 2002 to 11.1% in 2018. [Adventist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventism "Adventism") and other [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism") churches claimed most of the remaining Christians, although there was also a small [Eastern Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church") community.[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Census_2014-254)[[252]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Census_2002-255)

The next most reported religion of Uganda was [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Uganda "Islam in Uganda"), with Muslims representing 14% per cent of the population, up from 12.1% in 2002.[[253]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-256)[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Census_2014-254)

The remainder of the population in the 2014 census followed traditional religions (0.1 per cent, down from 1% in 2002), other religions (1.4 per cent), or had no religious affiliation (0.2 per cent).[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda#cite_note-Census_2014-254)

### Media

Uganda has a number of media outlets that broadcast domestically and globally. They cover news, magazines, sports, business and entertainment.

Popular [Ugandan newspapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_newspapers_in_Uganda "List of newspapers in Uganda") include:

*   _[New Vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Vision\_(newspaper) "New Vision (newspaper)")_
*   _[Daily Monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Monitor "Daily Monitor")_
*   _[Bukedde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukedde "Bukedde")_
*   _[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Observer\_(Uganda) "The Observer (Uganda)")_
*   _[East African Business Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East\_African\_Business\_Week "East African Business Week")_
*   _[Red Pepper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red\_Pepper\_(newspaper) "Red Pepper (newspaper)")_

The most popular [television stations in Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_television_stations_in_Uganda "List of television stations in Uganda") include:

*   [Uganda Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_Broadcasting_Corporation "Uganda Broadcasting Corporation") (UBC)
*   [NTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NTV_Uganda "NTV Uganda")
*   [NBS Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBS_Television_(Uganda) "NBS Television (Uganda)")
