Since winning her first-ever marathon aged just 19 – Tegla Loroupe has broken world records and forged paths for women and people from African communities to follow in her footsteps. Now, she’s trailblazing a new kind of Olympic Team and fulfilling her childhood dream of being a peacemaker.
When Madina Biktagirova came in second place at the New York City marathon in 1994, she thought she’d won it. Little did she know that 2.5 minutes earlier, unknown Tegla Loroupe had already crossed the line, becoming the first black African woman ever to win a marathon on the world stage.
“I was just so excited that someone from such a small tribal community could run and defeat other women from across the world,” says Tegla, her trademark smile wide at the memory.
“I was always being dropped from the team,” she recalls, “they just didn’t believe that I would be someone to do good things. But winning the New York marathon opened doors not just for me but for other women.

## “I fought my way through not for myself, but for other women who couldn’t believe in themselves. For them to see that there was someone who has been there fighting for them, to make a difference.”
Tegla went on to become one of the most successful female athletes of the 90s and 2000s, winning many half- and full-marathon titles and setting world records for 25 km, 30 km and marathon distances.
“I think I found breaking records easier because I was always training with men, and I knew I could keep up with them,” she says.
Born in the West Pokot District of Kenya in 1973, Tegla was one of 24 siblings and had to fight to attend school, instead of following the usual path for women in her tribe – tending the animals, children and the land.
When she did start school, she walked or ran the 9 km journey every day, barefoot. Not until secondary school did she start to realize running was something that she was good at – easily winning races against the boys. But, even with this natural talent for running, her main childhood ambition was to be a peacemaker.
“I grew up in an area of conflict,” explains Tegla. “People would always be fighting over resources. Land, animals, water… And when men are fighting, it is the women who suffer… When I grew up, I wanted to find a way for people to listen to me – but for that to happen you need a title. At that time, I didn’t realize that sports could help me to be the way I am. Those two sides of myself came together, to help me work for peace.”
The path Tegla has taken gives her much-needed credibility within the local communities – to spread awareness about the importance of education, and sports.
When she first attended school, and later when she would travel for training, Tegla’s family were met with opposition from other members of their village, who didn’t understand why a girl should be allowed to abandon her duties to take care of her family and their animals.
“This was my true way,” she says. “It’s impossible to educate people about something you didn’t go through yourself. And now, when I talk about sports, people understand. They see that a girl from a tribe like theirs can bring wealth to a family through sports and education.”

## “I fought my way through not for myself, but for other women who couldn’t believe in themselves. For them to see that there was someone who has been there fighting for them, to make a difference.”
Competing in her first races at school, Tegla noticed the unique power of sports to bring people together. This was an opportunity for kids to be kids, to come together regardless of their tribes and cheer each other on.
“All through my training in Europe, I would be trying to find a way to bring this atmosphere home,” says Tegla. “I was always searching for what I could do to bring communities together to talk and appreciate each other.”
In 2003, Tegla began her Peace Foundation and launched the first Peace Race – a 10 km race in her home community of Pokot. Now held annually, it’s a day when tribes that would on any other day be at war, come together as comrades, and see each other as equals, not enemies. In just three years of races, two of Kenya’s most-wanted warriors had ceased fighting, and tribal deaths were almost down to zero.
The Peace Race continues to forge links between the tribes, reduce tension and encourage interaction across borders. Its success is improved by the miniature “Peace Ambassadors” – children from the Tegla Loroupe Peace Academy that opened in 2012, a school dedicated to education, sports and providing unity to the area.
Tegla continued to run and compete until she broke her last world record in 2006, and was also named a UN Ambassador of Sport in the same year. With fellow ambassador George Clooney, she traveled around the world speaking about the Darfur Crisis in China, Egypt and Turkey before visiting the refugees in Sudan.
“That’s when I realized that I could no longer focus 100% on sports,” says Tegla.
Refugees have always been close to Tegla’s heart. Many settled in her own community of West Pokot after fleeing the war in Sudan, and she went to school and trained with some of them.
“For me, I got to go to Europe and train but for them, they couldn’t go anywhere,” she says. “As an athlete, I always felt so bad that these kids are not criminals but they are stuck, so they are being wasted. I wished I had the power to get them out of the country, to pursue sports like me.”

## “I fought my way through not for myself, but for other women who couldn’t believe in themselves. For them to see that there was someone who has been there fighting for them, to make a difference.”
After training refugees herself; with the support of Thomas Bach, President of the International Olympic Committee, Tegla was able to create the Refugee Olympic Team in 2015. Now, together with the backing of the Kenyan government, Tegla is able to scout displaced athletes from UN refugee camps to train together – overcoming obstacles of sponsorship, prejudice and culture shock along the way.
“Refugees are very resilient people,” says Tegla. “They’ve been through hard lives, and they are still standing tall.”
Having just returned from national competition in Nairobi with their relay team, the 30-strong Athlete Refugee Team is now training with the Kenyans, and have the rescheduled 2020 games in their sights, with Tegla at the helm as Chef de Mission.
“It would be so encouraging for them,” she said. “To make it to the finals, representing the millions of refugees around the world.”
Along with her work with the Athlete Refugee Team, her Peace Foundation, the Peace Races, work with the Peace Academy and outreach work with the women of Kenya – how does this powerhouse of peace relax? Getting back to her roots. Staying with her family, her favorite moments are taking care of the animals, and collecting and cutting firewood with the local women.
She even tested out our new Cloudridge hiking boot on the tough Kenyan terrain. Her verdict? “You will not fall down, I am telling you!” It’s a comment that feels somehow poignant coming from a woman who has dedicated her life to helping others stand tall.
Learn more about [Tegla’s work with the Athlete Refugee Team, and find out how On is supporting the project](https://www.on.com/en-us/stories/run-the-athlete-refugee-team-story).

Tegla

Loroupe

Celebrated as a long distance athlete and advocate of peace and women’s rights, Tegla Loroupe is an icon of Kenya. She was the first African woman to win the New York Marathon.

*   Sport Athletics 
*   Country/Territory ![Image 21: Kenya](https://laureus-com-editor-images.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/layout/flags/kenya.svg) Kenya 
*   Born May 09, 1973 
*   Joined academy 2015 

*   [](https://twitter.com/LoroupeTegla?lang=en)
*   [](https://www.laureus.com/world-sports-academy/members/tegla-loroupe)

A member of the Pokot tribe, who live in northern Kenya, Tegla’s father had four wives and she grew up with 24 brothers and sisters. She spent her childhood working in the fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters. At the age of six, she started school, having to run 10km to and from class and becoming aware of her potential as an athlete. Initially a barefoot runner, she was 16 before she received her first pair of running shoes.

In 1994 and 1998, Tegla won the 10,000 metres at the Goodwill Games and bronze medals over the same distances at the World Athletics Championships in 1995 and 1999.

In 1994, she took part in and won her first major marathon in New York, becoming an icon for many young African women. She repeated the feat in 1995 and also won in Rotterdam three straight times from 1997 to 1999. She has also been a winner in Berlin, Boston, London and Rome.

She was favourite to win a gold medal in the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney in the the marathon, but she was ill the night before the race and could only finish 13th, still insisting on running barefoot.

In 2003, she created an annual series of peace marathons, sponsored by the Tegla Loroupe Foundation, involving warriors and nomadic groups in her native Kenya, Uganda and Sudan, in an effort to bring peace to an area plagued by raiding warriors from battling tribes. She has also established a school and orphanage for children from her own region of Kenya.

A highly committed woman, in 2006 she was named a United Nations sport ambassador and travelled with American actors George Clooney and Don Cheadle to Beijing, Cairo and New York on a diplomatic mission to bring an end to violence in Darfur. She is also an international ambassador for the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) and UNICEF.

Tegla has been an active Ambassador for the Laureus Sport for Good for many years. She was an enthusiastic supporter of International Inspiration in Tanzania, the official legacy programme of the London 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games, supported by Laureus, which reached out to 1.3 million young people by using physical education and sport to help develop leadership, education, work and life skills. She was elected a Laureus Academy Member in 2015.

Celebrated as a long distance athlete and advocate of peace and women’s rights, Tegla Loroupe is an icon of Kenya. She was the first African woman to win the New York Marathon.
*   Sport Athletics   
*   Country/Territory ![Image 21: Kenya](https://laureus-com-editor-images.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/layout/flags/kenya.svg) Kenya   
*   Born May 09, 1973   
*   Joined academy 2015 

*   [](https://twitter.com/LoroupeTegla?lang=en)

A member of the Pokot tribe, who live in northern Kenya, Tegla’s father had four wives and she grew up with 24 brothers and sisters. She spent her childhood working in the fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters. At the age of six, she started school, having to run 10km to and from class and becoming aware of her potential as an athlete. Initially a barefoot runner, she was 16 before she received her first pair of running shoes.
In 1994 and 1998, Tegla won the 10,000 metres at the Goodwill Games and bronze medals over the same distances at the World Athletics Championships in 1995 and 1999.

# Tegla Loroupe | Laureus
## 25 Years of Laureus
In 1994, she took part in and won her first major marathon in New York, becoming an icon for many young African women. She repeated the feat in 1995 and also won in Rotterdam three straight times from 1997 to 1999. She has also been a winner in Berlin, Boston, London and Rome.
She was favourite to win a gold medal in the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney in the the marathon, but she was ill the night before the race and could only finish 13th, still insisting on running barefoot.
In 2003, she created an annual series of peace marathons, sponsored by the Tegla Loroupe Foundation, involving warriors and nomadic groups in her native Kenya, Uganda and Sudan, in an effort to bring peace to an area plagued by raiding warriors from battling tribes. She has also established a school and orphanage for children from her own region of Kenya.
A highly committed woman, in 2006 she was named a United Nations sport ambassador and travelled with American actors George Clooney and Don Cheadle to Beijing, Cairo and New York on a diplomatic mission to bring an end to violence in Darfur. She is also an international ambassador for the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) and UNICEF.
Tegla has been an active Ambassador for the Laureus Sport for Good for many years. She was an enthusiastic supporter of International Inspiration in Tanzania, the official legacy programme of the London 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games, supported by Laureus, which reached out to 1.3 million young people by using physical education and sport to help develop leadership, education, work and life skills. She was elected a Laureus Academy Member in 2015.

state.next_chunk:
# No stopping Loroupe in her crusade for peace in sport
“I grew up in an area of conflict,” [she explained in a recent interview](https://www.on-running.com/en-us/articles/tegla-loroupe-creating-paths-of-peace). “People would always be fighting over resources: land, animals, water. When I grew up, I wanted to find a way for people to listen to me – but for that to happen you need a title. At that time, I didn’t realise that sports could help me to be the way I am. Those two sides of me came together, to help me work for peace.
“I always overcame obstacles because I stay focused on what I want and how to be better,” [she said](https://www.olympic.org/news/meet-the-extraordinary-women-hosting-olympian-and-paralympian-experiences). “I have proven to myself anything is possible if I put my mind to it. This is why I started the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation.”
Her foundation, which is supported by the **[Athletics for a Better World](https://www.worldathletics.org/athletics-better-world)** social responsibility programme, organises the annual ‘Loroupe Peace Race’. The event targets mainly the youth and aims to foster friendship networks among the warring communities on the Kenyan-Ugandan border.
The focal point of the event is the warriors’ 10km road race where rivalling factions put aside their differences and unite in the spirit of sport.
High-profile dignitaries from Uganda and Kenya have also supported and attended the race since the inaugural edition in 2003. The race has provided a much-needed platform to reflect and talk about peace and development, while some guests even ran alongside each other in the dignitaries’ 2km road race in a mark of improved diplomatic relations.
And while there’s work to be done, there is still palpable evidence of a soothing of relations since the foundation set up a series of Peace Races across Kenya.
One particular group of warriors from Kainuk in South Turkana district, who took part in the Moroto Peace Race, have remained staunch advocates of peace, helping to improve community relations between the Pokot and Turkana along Turkwel, Amolem and Kasei areas.

# No stopping Loroupe in her crusade for peace in sport
![Image 55](https://assets.aws.worldathletics.org/81d58842-a1e6-4f6f-ae54-1c89815e5768.png)
_Tegla Loroupe at the Loroupe Peace Race (© TLPF)_
In 2014 Loroupe took her peace-building efforts to refugee camps in Kenya where she discovered a great interest in athletics among refugee communities.
She then petitioned the International Olympic Committee to give refugees a chance to advance in their athletics careers by taking part in the Olympics. She established an athletics training camp for refugees in Ngong, in the outskirts of Nairobi, which is run by her foundation. Her hope was to help produce Olympic talent that would unite the people of countries that are at war.
Her vision was realised in 2016 when the first Refugee Olympic Team was constituted, comprising 10 refugees from Syria, Congo, Ethiopia and South Sudan, providing a symbol of hope to the more than 65 million people globally who are currently displaced by conflict. Five of the team members came from Kenya’s Kakuma refugee camp.
“My dream has been to help young people gain confidence and purpose through athletics,” said Loroupe. “I have learnt so much from my sport and I want to share this. When I was looking for financial support to start the training camps, World Athletics was generous and the Refugee Team that competed at the Rio 2016 Games owes its early steps to the funding and support from World Athletics.”
![Image 56](https://assets.aws.worldathletics.org/c9745253-8678-4ac9-ad87-83128ae2ca22.jpg)
_World Athletics President Sebastian Coe with Tegla Loroupe and athletes from the refugee camp in Ngong (© Getty Images)_
Just seven months after the Olympic Games, Loroupe, with the help of World Athletics, formed the Athlete Refugee Team. Ever since, the Athlete Refugee Team has been invited to compete at all World Athletics Series events.

# No stopping Loroupe in her crusade for peace in sport
### ![Image 57: Tegla Loroupe](https://assets.aws.worldathletics.org/606b51f3ab4ebc95ab1c679f.jpg)Why Loroupe will raise a white card on 6 April
Each year on 6 April, Peace and Sport encourages sportspeople around the world to mark the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by holding up a white card.
Holding up a white card, just like a referee, is an action that symbolises the positive power of sport. In contrast to a red card, which signifies the most serious offense in sport, the white card is a gesture of inclusion, equity and peace.
Loroupe is **[one of many top athletes to join in with the campaign](https://www.peace-sport.org/our-champions-of-peace/)**. Hicham El Guerrouj, Paula Radcliffe, Marie-Jose Perec, Wilson Kipketer, Mutaz Barshim, Habiba Ghribi have also voiced their support.
More information can be found at **[peace-sport.org](https://www.peace-sport.org/)** and **[april6.org](https://www.april6.org/)**.

# No stopping Loroupe in her crusade for peace in sport
### ![Image 57: Tegla Loroupe](https://assets.aws.worldathletics.org/606b51f3ab4ebc95ab1c679f.jpg)Why Loroupe will raise a white card on 6 April
Each year on 6 April, Peace and Sport encourages sportspeople around the world to mark the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by holding up a white card.
Holding up a white card, just like a referee, is an action that symbolises the positive power of sport. In contrast to a red card, which signifies the most serious offense in sport, the white card is a gesture of inclusion, equity and peace.
Loroupe is **[one of many top athletes to join in with the campaign](https://www.peace-sport.org/our-champions-of-peace/)**. Hicham El Guerrouj, Paula Radcliffe, Marie-Jose Perec, Wilson Kipketer, Mutaz Barshim, Habiba Ghribi have also voiced their support.
More information can be found at **[peace-sport.org](https://www.peace-sport.org/)** and **[april6.org](https://www.april6.org/)**.

Since winning her first-ever marathon aged just 19 – Tegla Loroupe has broken world records and forged paths for women and people from African communities to follow in her footsteps. Now, she’s trailblazing a new kind of Olympic Team and fulfilling her childhood dream of being a peacemaker.
When Madina Biktagirova came in second place at the New York City marathon in 1994, she thought she’d won it. Little did she know that 2.5 minutes earlier, unknown Tegla Loroupe had already crossed the line, becoming the first black African woman ever to win a marathon on the world stage.
“I was just so excited that someone from such a small tribal community could run and defeat other women from across the world,” says Tegla, her trademark smile wide at the memory.
“I was always being dropped from the team,” she recalls, “they just didn’t believe that I would be someone to do good things. But winning the New York marathon opened doors not just for me but for other women.
state.next_chunk:
## “I fought my way through not for myself, but for other women who couldn’t believe in themselves. For them to see that there was someone who has been there fighting for them, to make a difference.”
Tegla went on to become one of the most successful female athletes of the 90s and 2000s, winning many half- and full-marathon titles and setting world records for 25 km, 30 km and marathon distances.
“I think I found breaking records easier because I was always training with men, and I knew I could keep up with them,” she says.
Born in the West Pokot District of Kenya in 1973, Tegla was one of 24 siblings and had to fight to attend school, instead of following the usual path for women in her tribe – tending the animals, children and the land.
When she did start school, she walked or ran the 9 km journey every day, barefoot. Not until secondary school did she start to realize running was something that she was good at – easily winning races against the boys. But, even with this natural talent for running, her main childhood ambition was to be a peacemaker.
“I grew up in an area of conflict,” explains Tegla. “People would always be fighting over resources. Land, animals, water… And when men are fighting, it is the women who suffer… When I grew up, I wanted to find a way for people to listen to me – but for that to happen you need a title. At that time, I didn’t realize that sports could help me to be the way I am. Those two sides of myself came together, to help me work for peace.”
The path Tegla has taken gives her much-needed credibility within the local communities – to spread awareness about the importance of education, and sports.
When she first attended school, and later when she would travel for training, Tegla’s family were met with opposition from other members of their village, who didn’t understand why a girl should be allowed to abandon her duties to take care of her family and their animals.
“This was my true way,” she says. “It’s impossible to educate people about something you didn’t go through yourself. And now, when I talk about sports, people understand. They see that a girl from a tribe like theirs can bring wealth to a family through sports and education.”

## “I fought my way through not for myself, but for other women who couldn’t believe in themselves. For them to see that there was someone who has been there fighting for them, to make a difference.”
Competing in her first races at school, Tegla noticed the unique power of sports to bring people together. This was an opportunity for kids to be kids, to come together regardless of their tribes and cheer each other on.
“All through my training in Europe, I would be trying to find a way to bring this atmosphere home,” says Tegla. “I was always searching for what I could do to bring communities together to talk and appreciate each other.”
In 2003, Tegla began her Peace Foundation and launched the first Peace Race – a 10 km race in her home community of Pokot. Now held annually, it’s a day when tribes that would on any other day be at war, come together as comrades, and see each other as equals, not enemies. In just three years of races, two of Kenya’s most-wanted warriors had ceased fighting, and tribal deaths were almost down to zero.
The Peace Race continues to forge links between the tribes, reduce tension and encourage interaction across borders. Its success is improved by the miniature “Peace Ambassadors” – children from the Tegla Loroupe Peace Academy that opened in 2012, a school dedicated to education, sports and providing unity to the area.
Tegla continued to run and compete until she broke her last world record in 2006, and was also named a UN Ambassador of Sport in the same year. With fellow ambassador George Clooney, she traveled around the world speaking about the Darfur Crisis in China, Egypt and Turkey before visiting the refugees in Sudan.
“That’s when I realized that I could no longer focus 100% on sports,” says Tegla.
Refugees have always been close to Tegla’s heart. Many settled in her own community of West Pokot after fleeing the war in Sudan, and she went to school and trained with some of them.
“For me, I got to go to Europe and train but for them, they couldn’t go anywhere,” she says. “As an athlete, I always felt so bad that these kids are not criminals but they are stuck, so they are being wasted. I wished I had the power to get them out of the country, to pursue sports like me.”

A member of the Pokot tribe, who live in northern Kenya, Tegla’s father had four wives and she grew up with 24 brothers and sisters. She spent her childhood working in the fields, tending cattle and looking after younger brothers and sisters. At the age of six, she started school, having to run 10km to and from class and becoming aware of her potential as an athlete. Initially a barefoot runner, she was 16 before she received her first pair of running shoes.
In 1994 and 1998, Tegla won the 10,000 metres at the Goodwill Games and bronze medals over the same distances at the World Athletics Championships in 1995 and 1999.

MASCOT 

Riku One, is a Shiba Inu, one of Japan’s most iconic and loved dog breeds, this energetic charac -

ter embodies the true spirit of sport - courageous, determined, and always pushing to reach their 

goals. With a heart as warm as their fur, the mascot makes friends everywhere they go. Full of life, 

they generate energy through moving their body and burst into an adorable little dance when fully 

charged! A big fan of Tokyo’s festivals, this mascot is especially excited to have the World Athletics 

Championships return to their beloved home city after 34 years. The mascot’s name was decided

# 1

# WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS AT A GLANCE T O K Y O 2 0 2 5 ★ F U N F A C T S 2

The United States is comfortably the most successful 

nation at the World Championships , with 195 gold, 134 silver 

and 114 bronze medals up to 2023, for a total of 443. It seems 

certain that this country will win a 200th gold in Tokyo 2025. Six 

other countries have more than 100 medals, in order the 

Germanies, Kenya, Jamaica, Russia, Great Britain & NI and 

Ethiopia. Japan’s total is 35 (eight gold, nine silver and 18 

bronze). The country with the most medals but no golds yet are 

the 2023 hosts Hungary, with 15 medals in all, seven silvers and 

eight bronzes. 

The biggest World Athletics Championships in terms of ath -

letes is Budapest 2023 with 1994 participants from 194 coun -

tries plus the Athlete Refugee Team. The most teams with at 

least one starter, 206, appeared at the 2019 edition in Doha. 

That included 204 countries, plus Authorised Neutral Athletes 

from Russia and the Athlete Refugee Team, The championships 

with the most countries winning gold medals is Eugene 2022 

with 29. The record for the number of countries winning medals 

is 46, at Osaka 2007 and Budapest 2023. The 2023 edition also 

saw a record number of countries providing finalists, 82. 

The first full, autonomous World Championships in 

Athletics were staged in 1983 in Helsinki . Until then, World 

Athletics declared that the Olympic Games should serve as 

their World Championships. Therefore, two World Athletics 

Presidents were World Champions. Lord Burghley (David 

Cecil), president in 1946-1976, was the 1928 champion at 400m 

Hurdles. Sebastian Coe’s 1500m win at Moscow 1980 meant 

that the current World Athletics President was both Olympic 

Champion and (until 1983) World Champion at that event. 

The most championships contested is 13 by 50 kilometre 

walker Jesús Ángel García (ESP). The most by a woman is 11 

by another race walker, Susana Feitór (POR). 

The bib which has won most World Championship golds is 

number 510. First when triple jumper Philips Idowu (GBR) wore 

it in 2009, and then five more times by one athlete: Shelly-Ann 

Fraser-Pryce (JAM). She was issued with that number at 

Moscow 2013, where she won the sprint treble. Then, by 

chance, she got 510 again at Beijing 2015 where she won the 

100m and 4x100m. Five different athletes have won World titles 

(one each) with bib number 956. 

The four athletes with the most World Championship 

medals are Allyson Felix (USA), Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce (JAM), 

Merlene Ottey (JAM/SLO) and Usain Bolt (JAM). Felix has 20 

medals across the 200m, 400m and three types of relays. This 

includes one awarded after she ran the heats only of the 2022 

women’s 4x400m, her final race. Fraser-Pryce has a total of 16 

medal from the 100m, 200m and 4x100m. Both Ottey and Bolt 

collected 14 medals, also from sprints and relays. 

Considering individual titles only , Usain Bolt is top of the list 

with seven golds. Four at 200m and three at 100m. Bolt also 

holds the men’s record for the most races contested at the 

World Championships, 44 including relays. He won 33 of those. 

The overall record is 59 races by Merlene Ottey (JAM/SLO). 

Six individual World Championship golds and no defeats is 

a record Sergey Bubka (URS/UKR) and Michael Johnson (USA) 

both have. They only ever won gold medals and were never 

beaten in a final at the championships. Johnson won at 200m & 

400m. In Bubka’s case, it was in a single event (the Pole Vault) 

and included the era in 1983-1991 when the championships 

were only staged every four years. 

Considering races run over 200m and 400m, only three 

golds have ever been won from the innermost two lanes . Ed 

Moses (USA) won the 400m Hurdles in 1983 from lane 2, Olga 

Bryzgina (URS) won the women’s flat 400m in 1987 from lane 2 

and Cathy Freeman (AUS) won the same event from lane 1 in 

1997. Four golds have been won from the outermost lane: The 

1987 men’s 200m (Calvin Smith (USA), lane 8), the 1997 men’s 

4x100m (Canada, lane 8), the 2015 men’s 400m Hurdles (the 

late Nicholas Bett (KEN), lane 9) and the 2017 women’s 400m 

Hurdles (Kori Carter (USA), lane 9). 

The most popular family name for World Championship 

competitors is Williams, with 73 athletes having that name. 

Next is Smith (46), Li (45), Garcia (43) and Kim (39). World 

Champions with the name Williams include Bernard, Danielle, 

Diane, Jesse, Lauryn, Novlene and Tonique. 

The first World Champion at Helsinki 1983 was the legendary 

marathoner Grete Waitz (NOR), but there were three champions 

at earlier separate events arranged by World Athletics outside 

the Olympic Games. First a men’s 50 Kilometres Walk at Malmö 

in 1976. The International Olympic Committee had dropped the 

event from the programme of the Montreal Olympics, so it was 

agreed that Sweden would organise a separate world champi -

onship race after those 1976 Games. That is how Venyamin 

Soldatenko (URS) became the first-ever World Champion out -

side of cross country. Attempts by athletics to add a 3000m and 

400m Hurdles to the women’s schedule for the 1980 Games 

failed, so later that month, in Sittard, there were two world cham -

pionship events, both won by Germans. Birgit Friedmann (FRG) 

took the 3000m and Bärbel Broschat (GDR) the 400m Hurdles. 

The most world records at a World Championship is five at 

Stuttgart 1993. Colin Jackson at the 110m Hurdles (12.91), both 

men’s relays (USA 37.40 & 2:54.29), Sally Gunnell at 400m 

Hurdles (52.74), and Anna Biryukova (RUS) at Triple Jump 

(15.09). That men’s 4x400m time, which Michael Johnson 

anchored with a world best split of 42.94, remains the world 

record as we head into Tokyo 2025. 

The longest-standing championship records are both from 

Helsinki 1983 and both by the same athlete, Czechoslovakia’s 

Jarmila Kratochvílová . On August 9 she won the 800m in 

1:54.68 and then on the 10th the 400m in 47.99. That was the 

first world record to be set at the championships. 

The oldest World Champion is Ellina Zvereva (BLR), winner of 

the 2001 Discus Throw at 40 years 269 days. The oldest male 

champion is Yohann Diniz (FRA), winner of the 2017 50 kilome -

tres walk at 39 years 224 days. The youngest is Merlene Frazer 

(JAM) who at 17 years 248 days was part of the winning 

Jamaican 4x100m squad in 1991. The youngest individual cham -

pion is Tirunesh Dibaba (ETH), 5000m winner in 2003 at 17 years 

333 days. The youngest male champion is Ismael Kirui (KEN), 

5000m winner in 1993 at 18 years 177 days. 

The only case of a shared gold medal as been that of the 

2023 women’s Pole Vault, when Katie Moon (USA) and Nina 

Kennedy (AUS) agreed on that outcome rather than contesting 

a jump off. On two occasions at the World Championships there 

have been jump-offs, the 1997 women’s High Jump and 2015 

men’s High Jump. There have been numerous ties for second 

and third places in both track and field events at past World 

Championships. At Doha 2019, two events (the men’s 110m 

Hurdles and Hammer Throw) featured two bronze medallists as 

it was judged that those awarded extra medals had been disad -

vantaged during the course of the competition.

MASCOT 

Riku One, is a Shiba Inu, one of Japan’s most iconic and loved dog breeds, this energetic charac -

ter embodies the true spirit of sport - courageous, determined, and always pushing to reach their 

goals. With a heart as warm as their fur, the mascot makes friends everywhere they go. Full of life, 

they generate energy through moving their body and burst into an adorable little dance when fully 

charged! A big fan of Tokyo’s festivals, this mascot is especially excited to have the World Athletics 

Championships return to their beloved home city after 34 years. The mascot’s name was decided 

through a nationwide voting campaign. The losing names were Pochichi and Sorashiba. Year Title Edition Venue Dates

# WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS AT A GLANCE T O K Y O 2 0 2 5 ★ F U N F A C T S 2

The United States is comfortably the most successful 

nation at the World Championships , with 195 gold, 134 silver 

and 114 bronze medals up to 2023, for a total of 443. It seems 

certain that this country will win a 200th gold in Tokyo 2025. Six 

other countries have more than 100 medals, in order the 

Germanies, Kenya, Jamaica, Russia, Great Britain & NI and 

Ethiopia. Japan’s total is 35 (eight gold, nine silver and 18 

bronze). The country with the most medals but no golds yet are 

the 2023 hosts Hungary, with 15 medals in all, seven silvers and

But the defining feature of her life eventually became something much larger than running.

In the 1990s, Loroupe helped transform perceptions of African women in international road racing.

She won the New York City Marathon on her marathon debut.

Then she won it again.

She became a three-time consecutive world half marathon champion.

She won bronze medals over 10,000 metres at two World Athletics Championships.

And in 1998, she broke one of women’s marathon running’s longest-standing global marks.

A year later, she broke her own record.

World Athletics currently lists Loroupe’s marathon best at 2:20:43, recorded in Berlin on September 26, 1999. Her profile also includes a 30:32.03 personal best over 10,000 metres and identifies her as a three-time World Half Marathon champion and two-time World Championships bronze medallist.

Yet Loroupe’s greatest influence may ultimately come from what happened after her peak competitive years.

In 2003, she founded the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation.

The organisation began using athletics as a way to bring together pastoralist communities affected by conflict over cattle, pasture, water and other resources. It later expanded into education, women’s empowerment, livelihood programmes and refugee sport.

Then, in 2016, Loroupe stepped onto an entirely different Olympic stage.

She served as Chef de Mission of the first-ever Refugee Olympic Team at the Rio Games.

Ten displaced athletes entered the Olympics not under the flag of the countries they had fled, but as an international refugee team.

Loroupe helped lead them.

The United Nations later named her its 2016 Person of the Year in Kenya for using athletics in peacebuilding and helping make refugee participation in the Olympics possible.

Today, the Tegla Loroupe biography connects two careers that would each be remarkable on their own.

One is the story of a pioneering Kenyan runner who changed women’s distance running.

The other is the story of an athlete who turned sporting fame into a long-term platform for peace.

## Who Is Tegla Loroupe?

Tegla Loroupe is a Kenyan former elite long-distance runner and international peace advocate.

She is the founder and president of the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation, which works primarily through sport, education and community programmes in areas affected by violence and social conflict.

Loroupe belongs to an important generation of Kenyan distance runners who established the country as a global force in road racing.

But her significance is different from that of many champions.

She was not simply successful.

She was a pioneer.

When Loroupe won New York in 1994, World Athletics says she became the first African woman to win a major marathon.

That achievement came before Kenyan women had developed the extraordinary global dominance in marathon running seen in later decades.

## How Old Is Tegla Loroupe?

Loroupe was born on May 9, 1973.

World Athletics gives that date on her official athlete profile.

She therefore turned 53 in May 2026.

## Where Is Tegla Loroupe From?

Loroupe comes from Kenya’s West Pokot region.

The Foundation describes her origins more specifically around Kapsait in the former West Pokot District, while United Nations and UNHCR biographies identify her broadly with the Pokot region of north-western Kenya.

That geographical background later became fundamental to her peace work.

Loroupe grew up in an area where competition over livestock, pasture and water could result in conflict between neighbouring pastoralist communities.

Her Foundation eventually focused directly on those problems.

## Tegla Loroupe’s Childhood

World Athletics describes Loroupe as growing up in a very large family and later recalled that running provided an escape from some of the challenges of childhood.

UNHCR has similarly documented an upbringing involving household work, caring for younger children and travelling substantial distances to school.

Those experiences are important because Loroupe later linked her humanitarian work to what she witnessed growing up.

She has explained that she wanted communities experiencing conflict to have opportunities beyond violence and competition over scarce resources.

## Running to School

Stories about Loroupe running long distances barefoot to reach school have appeared repeatedly in profiles of her life.

UNHCR describes her beginning school at seven and running long distances to attend classes.

The broader fact is well documented.

Running existed in Loroupe’s life before it became competition.

What changed was discovering that the endurance developed through ordinary life could become an international sporting talent.

## When Did Tegla Loroupe Start Competitive Running?

World Athletics’ historical profile says Loroupe was selected to represent Kenya in the junior race at the 1989 World Cross Country Championships after gaining attention through barefoot racing.

Her early career focused heavily on cross-country and track.

She was not originally known primarily as a marathon runner.

That came later.

## From Track Running to the Marathon

Loroupe first developed internationally as a 5,000m and 10,000m athlete.

World Athletics notes that she competed in the 10,000 metres at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics before progressing into the top ranks of global track distance running.

At the 1993 World Championships in Stuttgart, she finished fourth in the 10,000 metres.

That placed her just outside the medals.

Her greatest international breakthrough came the following year.

And it happened on the roads.

## Tegla Loroupe’s New York Marathon Debut

Loroupe made her marathon debut at the 1994 New York City Marathon.

She won.

Her finishing time was 2:27:37.

World Athletics later described the victory as making Loroupe the first African woman to win a major marathon.

She was only 21.

The achievement changed her career completely.

## Why the 1994 New York Victory Mattered

African men were already enormously successful in long-distance running.

Women had not yet achieved the same visibility in the international marathon.

Loroupe’s victory challenged that imbalance.

Her win showed that an East African woman could travel to one of the world’s most famous marathons and defeat an elite international field.

It also created a platform for the generation of Kenyan women who followed.

## Loroupe Wins New York Again

Loroupe returned in 1995.

She won again.

World Athletics records her second victory at 2:28:06.

She became the first woman since Grete Waitz in the 1980s to win consecutive New York City Marathon titles.

The back-to-back victories transformed what might have been seen as one remarkable upset into evidence of sustained world-class ability.

## World Championships Bronze in 1995

Loroupe was also still an elite track runner.

At the 1995 World Athletics Championships in Gothenburg, she finished third in the women’s 10,000 metres.

Fernanda Ribeiro won.

Derartu Tulu finished second.

Loroupe took bronze in 31:17.66.

That medal demonstrated something unusual.

She was simultaneously one of the world’s leading marathon runners and competitive with the best 10,000-metre runners on the track.

## Atlanta 1996 Olympics

Loroupe reached the 10,000m final at the Atlanta Olympics in 1996.

She finished sixth in 31:23.22.

An Olympic medal would remain absent from her career despite her extraordinary success elsewhere.

That is an important distinction.

Loroupe was an Olympian and an elite Olympic finalist, but she was not an Olympic medallist.

## Was Tegla Loroupe a Boston Marathon Champion?

No.

This is one of the corrections needed in some modern biographies.

Loroupe ran brilliantly at the 1996 Boston Marathon but finished second.

She had built a substantial late-race lead before Germany’s Uta Pippig caught her and won.

Catherine Ndereba later became the first Kenyan woman to win Boston in 2000.

Therefore, Boston should not appear on Loroupe’s list of marathon victories.

## World Half Marathon Champion

Loroupe’s road-running dominance extended well beyond the full marathon.

She won three consecutive World Half Marathon Championships.

World Athletics describes her as the only athlete in that period to complete the three-title sequence and highlights the Palermo 1999 victory as her third in succession.

That achievement is one of the most important parts of her competitive record.

## Rotterdam 1998: A World Marathon Best

April 1998 became one of the defining moments of Loroupe’s career.

In Rotterdam, she ran 2:20:47.

The mark broke Ingrid Kristiansen’s long-standing 2:21:06 world best from 1985.

This is where the supplied profile needs a precise correction.

The 2:21:06 figure belonged to Kristiansen.

Loroupe’s new mark was 2:20:47.

## Why Loroupe’s Rotterdam Record Was Historic

Kristiansen’s mark had stood for almost 13 years.

World Athletics described it as the longest-standing marathon best among the men’s and women’s records at the time.

Loroupe reduced it by 19 seconds.

The performance established her not merely as a major-race champion but as the fastest female marathon runner in the world under the standards used at that time.

## One-Hour World Record

Loroupe’s record-breaking 1998 season did not stop with the marathon.

In August, she ran 18,340 metres in one hour in Borgholzhausen, Germany.

World Athletics reported it as a new women’s world record for the one-hour event.

The performance illustrated again how unusually broad her endurance range was.

## Rotterdam Champion Again

Loroupe returned to Rotterdam in 1999.

She won again, this time in 2:22:49.

The weather prevented another record attempt from succeeding.

But a few months later, she would return to world-record pace.

## Second World Championships Bronze

At the 1999 World Athletics Championships in Seville, Loroupe won another 10,000m bronze medal.

She ran 30:32.03, which World Athletics lists as her personal best.

Gete Wami won the race.

Paula Radcliffe took silver.

Loroupe finished third.

The medal came only a month before another historic marathon performance.

## Berlin 1999: Loroupe Breaks Her Own Record

On September 26, 1999, Loroupe won the Berlin Marathon in 2:20:43.

She had broken her own world marathon best by four seconds.

World Athletics noted that she became the first woman since Grete Waitz in 1980 to improve her own global marathon mark.

The 2:20:43 remains Loroupe’s career personal best.

## Was 2:20:43 a World Record?

At the time, international reporting often used the term “world best” for road marathon performances because of how road records were officially treated.

Modern World Athletics historical material routinely describes Loroupe as a former marathon world record-holder.

The important factual point is simpler:

2:20:43 was the fastest recognised women’s marathon performance in the world when she ran it.

## Three Consecutive Half Marathon World Titles

One week after her Berlin performance, Loroupe competed in Palermo.

She won the World Half Marathon Championship again.

It was her third consecutive title.

That sequence is remarkable because marathon record attempts normally require considerable recovery.

Loroupe’s racing frequency became one of the characteristics for which she was known.

## London Marathon Victory

Loroupe also won the London Marathon.

World Athletics’ career retrospective lists one London victory among her principal marathon honours.

By 2000, she had accumulated wins across several of Europe and America’s most important road races.

## Rome Marathon Victory

World Athletics records also describe Loroupe winning the Rome Marathon in 2000.

Her marathon résumé therefore reached well beyond New York and the record-setting courses in Rotterdam and Berlin.

## How Many Times Did Loroupe Win Rotterdam?

Three times.

World Athletics’ 2003 career summary lists three Rotterdam victories.

Rotterdam was particularly important because it was there that she first broke the global marathon best.

## Sydney 2000 Olympics

Loroupe attempted an unusually demanding programme at the Sydney Olympics.

She competed in both the marathon and 10,000 metres.

In the 10,000m final, she finished fifth in 30:37.26.

That was her strongest Olympic track finish.

## Why Loroupe Never Won an Olympic Medal

Major championships and city marathons demand different racing conditions.

Loroupe could dominate road events and set global marathon marks without automatically producing the same result in an Olympic championship race.

World Athletics nevertheless records her with two Olympic top-eight finishes.

Her lack of an Olympic medal does little to diminish her importance in distance-running history.

## Tegla Loroupe’s Major Marathon Victories

The best-supported core list includes:

New York City — 1994 and 1995.

Rotterdam — three victories.

Berlin — one victory.

London — one victory.

Rome — documented victory in 2000.

Boston should not be included as a victory.

## Tegla Loroupe’s Personal Bests

World Athletics currently lists:

10,000 metres — 30:32.03.

3,000 metres — 8:30.95.

Marathon — 2:20:43.

Indoor 5,000 metres — 14:51.69.

10km road — 31:02.

These figures underline how much more Loroupe was than a marathon specialist.

## The Transition From Athlete to Peace Advocate

Loroupe’s humanitarian work did not begin only after she stopped competing.

Her peace activities increasingly overlapped with the latter stages of her athletics career.

She had grown up around conflict between pastoralist communities.

Sport gave her something those communities often lacked:

an internationally recognised platform.

She eventually decided to use that visibility deliberately.

## Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation

Loroupe founded the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation in 2003.

The organisation says its mission centres on peacebuilding, livelihoods and resilience for people affected by conflict and violence.

The Foundation is particularly associated with pastoralist communities in Kenya and neighbouring parts of East Africa.

Its philosophy is based on the idea that sport can create neutral spaces where people who might otherwise meet as rivals can instead meet as competitors.

## What Does the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation Do?

The Foundation describes several areas of work.

Peace races.

Education.

Women’s and girls’ empowerment.

Sports training.

Livelihood programmes.

Refugee-athlete development.

Environmental and resilience projects.

The organisation’s current website lists a Nairobi office in Lavington and an Olympic Refugee Training Camp in Ngong.

## The Peace Races

Loroupe’s peace races became one of the Foundation’s signature programmes.

The Foundation says the events bring together pastoralist communities affected by cattle raiding and competition over natural resources.

Sport is used as the meeting point.

Traditional enemies can enter the same race.

Community leaders attend.

Women and girls participate.

And peace discussions accompany competition.

World Athletics has also documented the peace-race programme and its aim of building connections between communities along Kenya’s north-western border regions.

## The Warrior’s Training Center

The Foundation says its Warrior’s Training Center works with people who put down weapons and choose alternatives to cattle raiding.

Its stated programmes include athletics training, farming, ranching and other livelihoods.

These are the Foundation’s own programme descriptions.

A responsible biography should distinguish those descriptions from independent measurement of long-term outcomes.

## Education and Girls

Education became another major pillar of Loroupe’s peace work.

At a United Nations social-development session in 2025, Loroupe discussed the Foundation’s school for girls and said the programme had supported more than 7,000 children.

The figure comes from Loroupe’s organisation/public presentation rather than an independent audit.

But it demonstrates that education remains part of her active public work more than two decades after the Foundation was established.

## Refugee Athletes

Loroupe’s involvement with refugee sport developed into one of her most internationally visible projects.

UNHCR worked with the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation to identify and train displaced athletes based in Kenya.

Several eventually qualified for Olympic refugee teams.

The Ngong training centre became an important pathway connecting refugees in East Africa with elite competition.

## The First Refugee Olympic Team

The IOC created its first Refugee Olympic Team for Rio 2016.

Ten athletes competed.

Loroupe served as the team’s Chef de Mission.

It was a historic Olympic initiative.

The athletes entered the Games representing displaced people around the world rather than a single national Olympic committee.

## Loroupe’s Role at Rio 2016

Loroupe was not simply an honorary figure attached to the team.

UNHCR described her as its leader and documented her work helping prepare refugee athletes for the Games.

Several of the runners had trained through her Foundation.

For Loroupe, the project connected her athletics background directly with her peace and refugee advocacy.

## Was [Loroupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tegla_Loroupe)Chef de Mission at Paris 2024?

No.

This needs clarification in profiles that loosely associate Loroupe with every subsequent Refugee Olympic Team.

Masomah Ali Zada was appointed Chef de Mission for the Paris 2024 Refugee Olympic Team.

Loroupe’s defining Chef de Mission role was with the inaugural team at Rio 2016.

Her Foundation nevertheless remained connected with refugee athletes and training pathways after Rio.

## UN Person of the Year in Kenya

The United Nations in Kenya named Tegla Loroupe its Person of the Year for 2016.

The UN specifically cited her peacebuilding work and leadership in helping ensure refugees participated in the Olympics for the first time.

This is one of the strongest recognitions of the bridge between her athletics and humanitarian careers.

## IOC World Trophy

In June 2011, Loroupe received the International Olympic Committee’s World Trophy at the Women and Sport Awards.

World Athletics reported that the award recognised her work increasing opportunities and participation for women and girls through sport.

The IOC also highlighted her Foundation’s peace, education and women’s empowerment work.

## Abebe Bikila Award

Loroupe received the Abebe Bikila Award in 1999.

World Athletics reported that New York Road Runners honoured her for her contribution to long-distance running shortly after she had broken her own marathon world best in Berlin.

The award added to a remarkable year that also included World Championships bronze and a third consecutive World Half Marathon title.

## AIMS Athlete Recognition

Loroupe was also repeatedly recognised by the Association of International Marathons and Distance Races.

World Athletics’ historical award list records her as its female World Athlete of the Year in 1995, 1997, 1998 and 1999.

That sequence reflects just how dominant her road-racing reputation became during the second half of the 1990s.

## Environmental Work

Loroupe’s Foundation has expanded beyond its original peace-race model.

A 2025 Foundation project describes restoration and afforestation work in Kamatira Forest in West Pokot.

The initiative links environmental degradation, climate resilience and conflict-prone pastoralist communities.

That expansion makes sense within the Foundation’s wider mission.

Scarcity of water, pasture and other resources can contribute to conflict.

Environmental resilience therefore connects directly with peacebuilding.

## Is Tegla Loroupe Still Running the Foundation?

Yes.

The Foundation currently identifies Loroupe as its president and founder, while some pages also use the title chairman.

The United Nations also introduced her in 2025 as President and Founder of the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation.

Therefore, “Founder and President” is the strongest current short description.

## Is Tegla Loroupe Still Competing Professionally?

No.

Loroupe’s elite record-breaking years are behind her.

World Athletics’ profile shows her historic performances rather than current competitive seasons, and the Foundation now forms the centre of her public activity.

She is best described today as a former elite distance runner.

## Tegla Loroupe’s International Legacy

Loroupe’s international importance has three dimensions.

First, performance.

She broke the women’s marathon world best twice and won elite races across multiple continents.

Second, representation.

Her New York victory showed that African women could dominate the international marathon long before that became commonplace.

Third, public service.

She turned the status gained through running into an institution devoted to peace and refugees.

Few elite athletes have built such a clear bridge between competition and long-term humanitarian work.

## Did Tegla Loroupe Open the Door for Kenyan Women Marathoners?

No single athlete can claim sole responsibility for an entire national tradition.

But Loroupe was undoubtedly an important pioneer.

World Athletics explicitly describes her 1994 New York victory as the first major marathon win by an African woman.

Later Kenyan champions—including Catherine Ndereba and generations after her—would establish Kenya as one of the dominant countries in women’s road running.

Loroupe’s achievements came near the beginning of that transformation.

## Tegla Loroupe and Catherine Ndereba

Loroupe and Catherine Ndereba belong to overlapping generations of Kenyan distance-running history.

Loroupe became the first Kenyan and African woman to win major international marathons at the level she did.

Ndereba later became the first Kenyan woman to win Boston and went on to collect World Championship and Olympic medals.

Their achievements should not be merged.

Loroupe did not win Boston.

Ndereba did.

## Tegla Loroupe’s Family

Public sources describe Loroupe growing up in a very large family.

World Athletics says she was one of 24 siblings.

Beyond information Loroupe has chosen to make part of her public story, detailed private-family material is not necessary for understanding her career.

There is no need to speculate about her spouse, children or other private relationships where strong documentation is absent.

## Tegla Loroupe’s Education

Reliable public biographies focus primarily on Loroupe’s childhood schooling and athletics development.

I did not find sufficiently authoritative evidence establishing a conventional university degree that should be inserted into her biography as fact.

Some organisations use the honorific “Dr.” when referring to her, including her own Foundation.

Unless the awarding institution and honorary or earned status are independently documented, that should not be converted into a claim that she completed an academic doctorate.

## Does Tegla Loroupe Have a Doctorate?

Her Foundation styles her “Dr. Ambassador Tegla Loroupe.”

That does not, by itself, establish an earned PhD or academic doctorate.

A publication should identify the specific institution and whether the award is honorary before adding a doctorate to an education table.

Without that verification, it is safer to omit it.

## Tegla Loroupe’s Net Worth

There is no authoritative public record establishing Tegla Loroupe’s complete personal net worth.

Prize money earned during an elite athletics career is not equivalent to present personal wealth.

Likewise, Foundation budgets and charitable funds should never be treated as Loroupe’s private assets.

Precise celebrity net-worth estimates are therefore inappropriate unless supported by verified financial disclosure.

## Tegla Loroupe Career Timeline

Loroupe was born on May 9, 1973 in Kenya’s West Pokot region.

She emerged as a competitive runner in her youth and represented Kenya in international cross-country competition before becoming a major 10,000m athlete.

She competed at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics.

In 1993, she finished fourth in the World Championships 10,000 metres.

In 1994, she won the New York City Marathon on her debut, becoming the first African woman to win a major marathon.

She defended the New York title in 1995 and won 10,000m bronze at the World Championships that year.

She finished sixth in the 10,000m at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics.

Loroupe won three consecutive World Half Marathon titles from 1997 through 1999.

In 1998, she set a new marathon world best of 2:20:47 in Rotterdam.

Later that year, she set a world record in the one-hour race.

In 1999, Loroupe won another World Championships 10,000m bronze medal in a personal-best 30:32.03.

A month later, she improved her own marathon world best to 2:20:43 in Berlin.

She finished fifth in the Sydney Olympic 10,000m final in 2000.

In 2003, she established the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation.

In 2011, the IOC honoured her with its World Trophy at the Women and Sport Awards.

In 2016, she served as Chef de Mission of the first Refugee Olympic Team in Rio.

Later that year, the United Nations in Kenya named her Person of the Year.

Her Foundation continues working in peacebuilding, education, refugee sport and community resilience, while Loroupe remains its public leader.

## What Is Tegla Loroupe Doing Now?

As of August 2026, Tegla Loroupe is best described as a former elite Kenyan distance runner and active peace advocate.

She remains founder and president of the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation.

The organisation continues to maintain its Nairobi base and Ngong refugee-athlete training centre and has broadened its work into areas including environmental resilience and education.

Loroupe also continues appearing in international sport-for-development discussions.

The United Nations featured her in its 2025 Second World Summit for Social Development programming, where she discussed using sport to advance education and opportunity.

Tegla Loroupe’s athletics record would have been enough to establish a major legacy.

Two New York Marathon victories.

Three World Half Marathon championships.

Two global marathon bests.

Two World Championships bronze medals.

Multiple major-city marathon victories.

And three Olympic appearances.

But the second half of her public life altered how those achievements are understood.

Loroupe did not simply use sport to escape a difficult environment.

She eventually returned to the problems associated with that environment and attempted to use sport to address them.

The same running that once carried her onto podiums became a way to bring rival communities together.

The fame built through New York, Rotterdam and Berlin became a platform for refugee athletes.

And an elite career measured in minutes and seconds became a humanitarian career measured in institutions, programmes and people.

That combination is what makes Tegla Loroupe more than a former marathon record-holder.

She is one of the clearest Kenyan examples of an athlete turning sporting influence into long-term public service.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Tegla Loroupe

### Who is Tegla Loroupe?

Tegla Loroupe is a former Kenyan elite distance runner, former marathon world-best holder and founder and president of the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation.

### How old is Tegla Loroupe?

She was born on May 9, 1973, making her 53 years old as of August 2026.

### Where is Tegla Loroupe from?

She comes from West Pokot in north-western Kenya.

### What is Tegla Loroupe famous for?

She is famous both for her elite distance-running career and for her later peace and refugee advocacy. She broke the women’s marathon world best twice and founded the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation.

### What is Tegla Loroupe’s marathon personal best?

2:20:43, set in Berlin on September 26, 1999.

### What record did Tegla Loroupe break in Rotterdam?

In 1998, she ran 2:20:47, breaking Ingrid Kristiansen’s previous 2:21:06 world marathon best.

### Did Tegla Loroupe break her own marathon record?

Yes. She improved her 2:20:47 mark to 2:20:43 in Berlin in 1999.

### Did Tegla Loroupe win the New York City Marathon?

Yes. She won in 1994 and 1995.

### Why was her first New York win historic?

World Athletics says the 1994 victory made her the first African woman to win a major marathon.

### Did Tegla Loroupe win the Boston Marathon?

No. She finished second to Uta Pippig in 1996.

### Who was the first Kenyan woman to win Boston?

Catherine Ndereba, in 2000.

### How many World Half Marathon titles did Tegla Loroupe win?

Three, consecutively in 1997, 1998 and 1999.

### Did Tegla Loroupe win World Championship medals?

Yes. She won bronze in the 10,000 metres in 1995 and again in 1999.

### Did Tegla Loroupe win an Olympic medal?

No. World Athletics records two Olympic top-eight finishes, but no Olympic medal.

### What was her best Olympic finish?

She finished fifth in the 10,000 metres at Sydney 2000.

### Did Tegla Loroupe compete at the Sydney Olympics?

Yes. She was selected for both the marathon and 10,000 metres.

### How many times did Tegla Loroupe win Rotterdam?

World Athletics lists three Rotterdam Marathon victories.

### Did Tegla Loroupe win the Berlin Marathon?

Yes. Her 1999 Berlin victory produced her 2:20:43 world-best performance.

### Did Tegla Loroupe win the London Marathon?

Yes. World Athletics includes one London victory in its summary of her major marathon wins.

### What is the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation?

It is a charitable organisation established by Loroupe in 2003 that uses sport, education and livelihood programmes to support peace and resilience in conflict-affected communities.

### Is Tegla Loroupe still president of her Foundation?

Yes. The Foundation currently identifies her as president, while some of its pages also use chairman.

### Where is the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation based?

Its current website lists its main office in Lavington, Nairobi, and a refugee training camp in Ngong.

### What are Tegla Loroupe Peace Races?

They are races designed to bring together communities affected by conflict, particularly pastoralist groups dealing with cattle raiding and competition over resources.

### Did Tegla Loroupe lead the Refugee Olympic Team?

Yes. She was Chef de Mission of the first Refugee Olympic Team at Rio 2016.

### Was Tegla Loroupe Chef de Mission at Paris 2024?

No. Masomah Ali Zada was Chef de Mission for the Paris 2024 Refugee Olympic Team.

### Was Tegla Loroupe named UN Person of the Year?

Yes. The United Nations in Kenya named her its 2016 Person of the Year for peacebuilding and her leadership connected with the first Refugee Olympic Team.

### What IOC award did Tegla Loroupe receive?

She received the IOC World Trophy at the 2011 Women and Sport Awards.

### Did Tegla Loroupe win the Abebe Bikila Award?

Yes. She received the award in 1999 for her contribution to long-distance running.

### Does Tegla Loroupe have a university degree?

I found no sufficiently authoritative record establishing a conventional university qualification that should be presented as verified fact.

### Is Tegla Loroupe a doctor?

Her Foundation sometimes styles her “Dr. Ambassador Tegla Loroupe,” but the material reviewed does not establish an earned academic doctorate. A specific institution and award type should be verified before adding a doctorate to her education record.

### What is Tegla Loroupe’s net worth?

There is no authoritative public financial disclosure establishing her complete personal net worth. Exact figures published by celebrity websites should be treated as speculative.

### What is Tegla Loroupe doing now?

As of August 2026, Loroupe remains founder and president of the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation and continues public work involving peacebuilding, education, refugee sport and community resilience.

Then she won it again.

She became a three-time consecutive world half marathon champion.

She won bronze medals over 10,000 metres at two World Athletics Championships.

And in 1998, she broke one of women’s marathon running’s longest-standing global marks.

A year later, she broke her own record.

Riku One, is a Shiba Inu, one of Japan’s most iconic and loved dog breeds, this energetic charac -

> T O K Y O 2 0 2 5 ★W O R L D C H A M P I O N S H I P A T AG L A N C E

# 1

# WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS AT A GLANCE T O K Y O 2 0 2 5 ★ F U N F A C T S 2

The United States is comfortably the most successful 

nation at the World Championships , with 195 gold, 134 silver 

and 114 bronze medals up to 2023, for a total of 443. It seems 

certain that this country will win a 200th gold in Tokyo 2025. Six 

other countries have more than 100 medals, in order the 

Germanies, Kenya, Jamaica, Russia, Great Britain & NI and 

Ethiopia. Japan’s total is 35 (eight gold, nine silver and 18 

bronze). The country with the most medals but no golds yet are 

the 2023 hosts Hungary, with 15 medals in all, seven silvers and 

eight bronzes. 

The biggest World Athletics Championships in terms of ath -

letes is Budapest 2023 with 1994 participants from 194 coun -

tries plus the Athlete Refugee Team. The most teams with at 

least one starter, 206, appeared at the 2019 edition in Doha. 

That included 204 countries, plus Authorised Neutral Athletes 

from Russia and the Athlete Refugee Team, The championships 

with the most countries winning gold medals is Eugene 2022 

with 29. The record for the number of countries winning medals 

is 46, at Osaka 2007 and Budapest 2023. The 2023 edition also 

saw a record number of countries providing finalists, 82. 

The first full, autonomous World Championships in 

Athletics were staged in 1983 in Helsinki . Until then, World 

Athletics declared that the Olympic Games should serve as 

their World Championships. Therefore, two World Athletics 

Presidents were World Champions. Lord Burghley (David 

Cecil), president in 1946-1976, was the 1928 champion at 400m 

Hurdles. Sebastian Coe’s 1500m win at Moscow 1980 meant 

that the current World Athletics President was both Olympic 

Champion and (until 1983) World Champion at that event. 

The most championships contested is 13 by 50 kilometre 

walker Jesús Ángel García (ESP). The most by a woman is 11 

by another race walker, Susana Feitór (POR). 

The bib which has won most World Championship golds is 

number 510. First when triple jumper Philips Idowu (GBR) wore 

it in 2009, and then five more times by one athlete: Shelly-Ann 

Fraser-Pryce (JAM). She was issued with that number at 

Moscow 2013, where she won the sprint treble. Then, by 

chance, she got 510 again at Beijing 2015 where she won the 

100m and 4x100m. Five different athletes have won World titles 

(one each) with bib number 956. 

The four athletes with the most World Championship 

medals are Allyson Felix (USA), Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce (JAM), 

Merlene Ottey (JAM/SLO) and Usain Bolt (JAM). Felix has 20 

medals across the 200m, 400m and three types of relays. This 

includes one awarded after she ran the heats only of the 2022 

women’s 4x400m, her final race. Fraser-Pryce has a total of 16 

medal from the 100m, 200m and 4x100m. Both Ottey and Bolt 

collected 14 medals, also from sprints and relays. 

Considering individual titles only , Usain Bolt is top of the list 

with seven golds. Four at 200m and three at 100m. Bolt also 

holds the men’s record for the most races contested at the 

World Championships, 44 including relays. He won 33 of those. 

The overall record is 59 races by Merlene Ottey (JAM/SLO). 

Six individual World Championship golds and no defeats is 

a record Sergey Bubka (URS/UKR) and Michael Johnson (USA) 

both have. They only ever won gold medals and were never 

beaten in a final at the championships. Johnson won at 200m & 

400m. In Bubka’s case, it was in a single event (the Pole Vault) 

and included the era in 1983-1991 when the championships 

were only staged every four years. 

Considering races run over 200m and 400m, only three 

golds have ever been won from the innermost two lanes . Ed 

Moses (USA) won the 400m Hurdles in 1983 from lane 2, Olga 

Bryzgina (URS) won the women’s flat 400m in 1987 from lane 2 

and Cathy Freeman (AUS) won the same event from lane 1 in 

1997. Four golds have been won from the outermost lane: The 

1987 men’s 200m (Calvin Smith (USA), lane 8), the 1997 men’s 

4x100m (Canada, lane 8), the 2015 men’s 400m Hurdles (the 

late Nicholas Bett (KEN), lane 9) and the 2017 women’s 400m 

Hurdles (Kori Carter (USA), lane 9). 

The most popular family name for World Championship 

competitors is Williams, with 73 athletes having that name. 

Next is Smith (46), Li (45), Garcia (43) and Kim (39). World 

Champions with the name Williams include Bernard, Danielle, 

Diane, Jesse, Lauryn, Novlene and Tonique. 

The first World Champion at Helsinki 1983 was the legendary 

marathoner Grete Waitz (NOR), but there were three champions 

at earlier separate events arranged by World Athletics outside 

the Olympic Games. First a men’s 50 Kilometres Walk at Malmö 

in 1976. The International Olympic Committee had dropped the 

event from the programme of the Montreal Olympics, so it was 

agreed that Sweden would organise a separate world champi -

onship race after those 1976 Games. That is how Venyamin 

Soldatenko (URS) became the first-ever World Champion out -

side of cross country. Attempts by athletics to add a 3000m and 

400m Hurdles to the women’s schedule for the 1980 Games 

failed, so later that month, in Sittard, there were two world cham -

pionship events, both won by Germans. Birgit Friedmann (FRG) 

took the 3000m and Bärbel Broschat (GDR) the 400m Hurdles. 

The most world records at a World Championship is five at 

Stuttgart 1993. Colin Jackson at the 110m Hurdles (12.91), both 

men’s relays (USA 37.40 & 2:54.29), Sally Gunnell at 400m 

Hurdles (52.74), and Anna Biryukova (RUS) at Triple Jump 

(15.09). That men’s 4x400m time, which Michael Johnson 

anchored with a world best split of 42.94, remains the world 

record as we head into Tokyo 2025. 

The longest-standing championship records are both from 

Helsinki 1983 and both by the same athlete, Czechoslovakia’s 

Jarmila Kratochvílová . On August 9 she won the 800m in 

1:54.68 and then on the 10th the 400m in 47.99. That was the 

first world record to be set at the championships. 

The oldest World Champion is Ellina Zvereva (BLR), winner of 

the 2001 Discus Throw at 40 years 269 days. The oldest male 

champion is Yohann Diniz (FRA), winner of the 2017 50 kilome -

tres walk at 39 years 224 days. The youngest is Merlene Frazer 

(JAM) who at 17 years 248 days was part of the winning 

Jamaican 4x100m squad in 1991. The youngest individual cham -

pion is Tirunesh Dibaba (ETH), 5000m winner in 2003 at 17 years 

333 days. The youngest male champion is Ismael Kirui (KEN), 

5000m winner in 1993 at 18 years 177 days. 

The only case of a shared gold medal as been that of the 

2023 women’s Pole Vault, when Katie Moon (USA) and Nina 

Kennedy (AUS) agreed on that outcome rather than contesting 

a jump off. On two occasions at the World Championships there 

have been jump-offs, the 1997 women’s High Jump and 2015 

men’s High Jump. There have been numerous ties for second 

and third places in both track and field events at past World 

Championships. At Doha 2019, two events (the men’s 110m 

Hurdles and Hammer Throw) featured two bronze medallists as 

it was judged that those awarded extra medals had been disad -

vantaged during the course of the competition.

# WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS AT A GLANCE T O K Y O 2 0 2 5 ★ F U N F A C T S 2
The United States is comfortably the most successful
nation at the World Championships , with 195 gold, 134 silver
and 114 bronze medals up to 2023, for a total of 443. It seems
certain that this country will win a 200th gold in Tokyo 2025. Six
other countries have more than 100 medals, in order the
Germanies, Kenya, Jamaica, Russia, Great Britain & NI and
Ethiopia. Japan’s total is 35 (eight gold, nine silver and 18
bronze). The country with the most medals but no golds yet are
the 2023 hosts Hungary, with 15 medals in all, seven silvers and
eight bronzes.
The biggest World Athletics Championships in terms of ath -
letes is Budapest 2023 with 1994 participants from 194 coun -
tries plus the Athlete Refugee Team. The most teams with at
least one starter, 206, appeared at the 2019 edition in Doha.
That included 204 countries, plus Authorised Neutral Athletes
from Russia and the Athlete Refugee Team, The championships
with the most countries winning gold medals is Eugene 2022
with 29. The record for the number of countries winning medals
is 46, at Osaka 2007 and Budapest 2023. The 2023 edition also
saw a record number of countries providing finalists, 82.
The first full, autonomous World Championships in
Athletics were staged in 1983 in Helsinki . Until then, World
Athletics declared that the Olympic Games should serve as
their World Championships. Therefore, two World Athletics
Presidents were World Champions. Lord Burghley (David
Cecil), president in 1946-1976, was the 1928 champion at 400m
Hurdles. Sebastian Coe’s 1500m win at Moscow 1980 meant
that the current World Athletics President was both Olympic

The most championships contested is 13 by 50 kilometre

The bib which has won most World Championship golds is
number 510. First when triple jumper Philips Idowu (GBR) wore
it in 2009, and then five more times by one athlete: Shelly-Ann
Fraser-Pryce (JAM). She was issued with that number at
Moscow 2013, where she won the sprint treble. Then, by
chance, she got 510 again at Beijing 2015 where she won the
100m and 4x100m. Five different athletes have won World titles
(one each) with bib number 956.
The four athletes with the most World Championship
medals are Allyson Felix (USA), Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce (JAM),
Merlene Ottey (JAM/SLO) and Usain Bolt (JAM). Felix has 20
medals across the 200m, 400m and three types of relays. This
includes one awarded after she ran the heats only of the 2022
women’s 4x400m, her final race. Fraser-Pryce has a total of 16
medal from the 100m, 200m and 4x100m. Both Ottey and Bolt
collected 14 medals, also from sprints and relays.
Considering individual titles only , Usain Bolt is top of the list
with seven golds. Four at 200m and three at 100m. Bolt also
holds the men’s record for the most races contested at the
World Championships, 44 including relays. He won 33 of those.
The overall record is 59 races by Merlene Ottey (JAM/SLO).

Six individual World Championship golds and no defeats is
a record Sergey Bubka (URS/UKR) and Michael Johnson (USA)
both have. They only ever won gold medals and were never
beaten in a final at the championships. Johnson won at 200m &
400m. In Bubka’s case, it was in a single event (the Pole Vault)
and included the era in 1983-1991 when the championships
were only staged every four years.
Considering races run over 200m and 400m, only three
golds have ever been won from the innermost two lanes . Ed
Moses (USA) won the 400m Hurdles in 1983 from lane 2, Olga
Bryzgina (URS) won the women’s flat 400m in 1987 from lane 2
and Cathy Freeman (AUS) won the same event from lane 1 in
1997. Four golds have been won from the outermost lane: The
1987 men’s 200m (Calvin Smith (USA), lane 8), the 1997 men’s
4x100m (Canada, lane 8), the 2015 men’s 400m Hurdles (the
late Nicholas Bett (KEN), lane 9) and the 2017 women’s 400m
Hurdles (Kori Carter (USA), lane 9).
The most popular family name for World Championship
competitors is Williams, with 73 athletes having that name.
Next is Smith (46), Li (45), Garcia (43) and Kim (39). World
Champions with the name Williams include Bernard, Danielle,
Diane, Jesse, Lauryn, Novlene and Tonique.
The first World Champion at Helsinki 1983 was the legendary
marathoner Grete Waitz (NOR), but there were three champions
at earlier separate events arranged by World Athletics outside
the Olympic Games. First a men’s 50 Kilometres Walk at Malmö

The most world records at a World Championship is five at
Stuttgart 1993. Colin Jackson at the 110m Hurdles (12.91), both
men’s relays (USA 37.40 & 2:54.29), Sally Gunnell at 400m
Hurdles (52.74), and Anna Biryukova (RUS) at Triple Jump
(15.09). That men’s 4x400m time, which Michael Johnson
anchored with a world best split of 42.94, remains the world
record as we head into Tokyo 2025.
The longest-standing championship records are both from
Helsinki 1983 and both by the same athlete, Czechoslovakia’s
Jarmila Kratochvílová . On August 9 she won the 800m in
1:54.68 and then on the 10th the 400m in 47.99. That was the
first world record to be set at the championships.
